docs.title: The story in one minute
docs.text:
Java 8 gave us composable asynchrony (CompletableFuture, parallel streams, StampedLock, LongAdder), but every blocking call still tied up an expensive platform (OS) thread. So high-throughput services moved to reactive code, which scales but is hard to write, debug, and profile. Java 21 made virtual threads final: cheap, JVM-scheduled threads, so plain blocking code now scales like reactive code. Java 24 removed the biggest caveat: synchronized no longer pins a virtual thread to its carrier. Structured concurrency (preview) and scoped values (final in Java 25) finish the picture.

Java 5 · 2004java.util.concurrentExecutors, locks, atomics, the modern memory model (JSR-133) Java 7 · 2011Fork/JoinWork stealing, Phaser, TransferQueue Java 8 · 2014CompletableFutureParallel streams, StampedLock, LongAdder, ConcurrentHashMap rewrite Java 9 · 2017Flow API & VarHandleCompletableFuture timeouts, onSpinWait Java 21 LTS · 2023Virtual threads finalStructured concurrency and scoped values in preview Java 24 · 2025No pinning on synchronizedJEP 491: monitors owned by the virtual thread Java 25 LTS · 2025Scoped values finalStructured concurrency 5th preview, new Joiner API

docs.title: Common Bugs Gallery
docs.text:
L2 → L4

Each entry shows the bug, the symptom, and the fix.

docs.title: 1. Check-then-act on a concurrent map
docs.text:
if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, create());       // ❌ two creates
map.computeIfAbsent(k, key -> create());             // ✅

docs.title: 2. Non-volatile stop flag
docs.text: boolean running read in a loop → the loop never ends after the JIT hoists the read. ✅ Use volatile, or interruption.

docs.title: 3. SimpleDateFormat shared across threads
docs.text: Garbled dates and NumberFormatException. ✅ Use DateTimeFormatter.

docs.title: 4. HashMap modified by several threads
docs.text: Lost entries, and an infinite loop on Java ≤ 7 during resize. ✅ Use ConcurrentHashMap.

docs.title: 5. Swallowed InterruptedException
docs.text:
catch (InterruptedException e) { }                                // ❌ cancellation lost
catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; }  // ✅

docs.title: 6. Exceptions lost in submit()
docs.text: executor.submit(task) with a throwing task, and nobody calls get() → silent failure. ✅ Call get(), use execute() with an uncaught exception handler, or use structured scopes.

docs.title: 7. Periodic task dies silently
docs.text: scheduleAtFixedRate stops forever after one exception. ✅ Wrap the body in try/catch (Throwable).

docs.title: 8. Unbounded queue in newFixedThreadPool
docs.text: OOM under load. ✅ Use a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue + a rejection policy, or VTs + semaphores.

docs.title: 9. Nested submit().get() on the same pool
docs.text: Pool deadlock. ✅ Use separate pools, or VTs.

docs.title: 10. Blocking IO in parallelStream()
docs.text: Starves the common pool JVM-wide. ✅ Use a VT executor.

docs.title: 11. Blocking inside ConcurrentHashMap.compute
docs.text: Freezes other keys in the bin, and a recursive update throws IllegalStateException. ✅ Compute the value outside, then putIfAbsent.

docs.title: 12. this escaping the constructor
docs.text:
public Listener(EventBus bus) { bus.register(this); this.state = init(); } // ❌ events see null state
✅ Use a factory method that registers after construction.

docs.title: 13. Lock held across a network call
docs.text: Every thread blocks behind one slow call, and VTs get pinned on JDK 21–23. ✅ Narrow the critical section, and do IO outside it.

docs.title: 14. Pooling virtual threads / ThreadLocal caches on VTs
docs.text: See L7 pitfalls.

docs.title: 15. Missing timeouts with virtual threads
docs.text: A downstream hangs → hundreds of thousands of parked VTs, heap growth, then OOM. ✅ Put a timeout on every IO call, and deadlines on fan-out.

docs.title: 16. @Transactional + forking work to another thread
docs.text: The forked work runs outside the transaction (the connection is thread-bound). ✅ Fan out reads before the transaction, and write sequentially.

docs.title: 17. Double-checked locking without volatile
docs.text: Another thread can see a partially constructed object. ✅ Use volatile, the holder idiom, or StableValue.

docs.title: Reading a platform thread dump
docs.text:
"order-worker-3" #41 prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=1203.44ms elapsed=360.12s tid=0x... nid=0x2b03 waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at com.acme.Inventory.reserve(Inventory.java:58)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000071a2b3c40> (a com.acme.Inventory)
        at com.acme.OrderService.place(OrderService.java:31)

"order-worker-7" #45 ... runnable
        at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0(Native Method)
        ...
        at com.acme.Inventory.reserve(Inventory.java:61)
        - locked <0x000000071a2b3c40> (a com.acme.Inventory)      ← holding the lock during socket IO!

Diagnosis: a lock is held across a network call, and every other worker is BLOCKED. Fix: move the IO outside the critical section.

docs.text:
A single dump is a snapshot. Threads stuck in the same frame across all three are the real problem.

docs.title: Progress guarantees
docs.text: Guarantee Meaning Example Blocking A stalled thread can stop everyone synchronized, ReentrantLock Obstruction-free A thread running alone finishes Some STM designs Lock-free Some thread always makes progress CAS loops: ConcurrentLinkedQueue, AtomicLong.incrementAndGet Wait-free Every thread finishes in bounded steps AtomicLong.getAndAdd on x86 (LOCK XADD), LongAdder.increment mostly

docs.title: Treiber stack (lock-free)
docs.text:
public final class TreiberStack<E> {
    private record Node<E>(E item, Node<E> next) {}
    private final AtomicReference<Node<E>> top = new AtomicReference<>();

    public void push(E item) {
        Node<E> oldTop, newTop;
        do {
            oldTop = top.get();
            newTop = new Node<>(item, oldTop);
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(oldTop, newTop));   // retry if another thread won
    }

    public E pop() {
        Node<E> oldTop;
        do {
            oldTop = top.get();
            if (oldTop == null) return null;
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(oldTop, oldTop.next()));
        return oldTop.item();
    }
}

The garbage collector makes ABA harmless here: a node can't be reused while a thread still holds a reference to it. In C/C++ you'd need hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation.

docs.title: Michael–Scott queue
docs.text: ConcurrentLinkedQueue implements it: two CAS-updated pointers (head and tail), where a lagging tail is "helped" forward by other threads. Study the JDK source for a production-quality example, including the VarHandle relaxed reads.

docs.title: When not to go lock-free
docs.text:
• Multi-variable invariants: a lock is far simpler and usually fast enough.
  • Under heavy contention, CAS retry storms can be slower than a lock that parks waiters.
  • Readability and reviewability: few engineers can verify a lock-free algorithm. Prove it with jcstress.

docs.title: Single-writer principle
docs.text: The fastest concurrent code avoids contention entirely: one thread owns each piece of mutable state, and others communicate with it through queues. This is the core idea of LMAX Disruptor, actors, and Kafka partitions. With VTs, a "single writer per key" lane is cheap (see Case Studies).

docs.title: Balking example
docs.text:
private final AtomicBoolean refreshing = new AtomicBoolean();
public void refreshIfIdle() {
    if (!refreshing.compareAndSet(false, true)) return;     // someone else is refreshing: balk
    try { cache.reload(); } finally { refreshing.set(false); }
}

docs.title: Active object with a VT lane
docs.text:
final class AccountActor {
    private final BlockingQueue<Runnable> mailbox = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();
    private long balance;                                    // confined to the actor's VT, no locks
    AccountActor() {
        Thread.ofVirtual().name("account-actor").start(() -> {
            try { while (true) mailbox.take().run(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { /* stop */ }
        });
    }
    CompletableFuture<Long> deposit(long amt) {
        var cf = new CompletableFuture<Long>();
        mailbox.add(() -> cf.complete(balance += amt));
        return cf;
    }
}

docs.title: Choosing the primitive: the interviewer's hidden question
docs.text:
Most problems are really asking "do you know which coordination tool fits?"

flowchart TD Q{What must the threads coordinate?} Q -->|Take turns in a fixed order| T{How many threads?} T -->|2| SEM[Semaphore baton<br/>#1 odd/even] T -->|N, wake exactly one| COND[Lock + Condition per thread<br/>#2 round-robin] T -->|N, predicates overlap| MON[Monitor + notifyAll<br/>#3 FizzBuzz] Q -->|B waits until A happened once| LATCH[CountDownLatch / CompletableFuture<br/>#4 print in order] Q -->|Groups of exactly k| BAR[Semaphore slots + CyclicBarrier<br/>#5 H2O, #9 barrier] Q -->|Hand data from producers to consumers| BQ[BlockingQueue<br/>#6, #15] Q -->|Limit how many at once| SEMN[Semaphore N permits<br/>#13 barber, #19 crawler] Q -->|Several locks at once| ORD[Global lock order / tryLock<br/>#11, #12, #14] Q -->|Many readers, few writers| RW[Read-write lock<br/>#8] Q -->|Same expensive work requested concurrently| SF[putIfAbsent of a Future<br/>#18] Q -->|Wait until a time| TIME[Condition.awaitNanos / DelayQueue<br/>#10, #17]

docs.title: A five-step script for any concurrency coding question
docs.text:
1. Restate the invariant out loud: "at most 2 H per molecule", "total money is constant", "output is strictly ordered".
  2. Name the shared state and who guards it: write // guarded by lock next to every mutable field.
  3. Pick the primitive with the map above, and say why the alternatives are worse.
  4. Write the waiting loop correctly: while (!condition) await();, never if. Handle InterruptedException.
  5. Prove it: happens-before edges, no lost wake-ups, no deadlock (lock order), and how it shuts down. Then mention how you'd test it: hammer it with 1,000+ virtual threads and assert the invariant, as every solution here does.

docs.title: 1. Odd/Even Printer
docs.text: L1 ★☆☆ · wait/notifyAll · Semaphore

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Two threads print the numbers 1 to N. The odd thread prints only odd numbers and the even thread prints only even numbers. The output must be in order: 1 2 3 4 … N.

This is the "hello world" of thread coordination. The interviewer is checking three things: do you know that a thread has to wait for its turn (rather than busy-spin), that the turn must be handed over explicitly, and that both threads must terminate?

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
There is one piece of shared state, next, and it decides whose turn it is. A thread whose turn it isn't goes to sleep. After printing, a thread advances next and wakes the other thread.

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant O as odd thread participant M as monitor (next) participant E as even thread O->>M: lock, next=1 is odd → print 1, next=2, notifyAll E->>M: lock, next=2 is even → print 2, next=3, notifyAll O->>M: lock, next=3 → print 3, next=4, notifyAll E->>M: lock, next=3 is odd → not my turn → wait() (releases lock) Note over O,E: ...continues until next > N O->>M: next > N → notifyAll, return E->>M: woken, next > N → return

docs.title: Approach 1: monitor with wait/notifyAll
docs.text:
/** Approach 1: one monitor + wait/notifyAll. A shared counter decides whose turn it is. */
    static final class MonitorPrinter {
        private final int max;
        private int next = 1;                                   // guarded by "this"

        MonitorPrinter(int max) { this.max = max; }

        void print(boolean odd, List<String> out) throws InterruptedException {
            synchronized (this) {
                while (true) {
                    while (next <= max && isOdd(next) != odd) {
                        wait();                                 // not my turn: release monitor and sleep
                    }
                    if (next > max) {                           // finished: wake the other thread so it can exit too
                        notifyAll();
                        return;
                    }
                    out.add(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ":" + next);
                    next++;                                     // hand the turn over...
                    notifyAll();                                // ...and wake the other thread
                }
            }
        }

        private static boolean isOdd(int n) { return n % 2 == 1; }
    }

Line by line:

Code Why private int next = 1; // guarded by "this" The only shared mutable state. Every read and write happens inside synchronized (this), which gives both atomicity and visibility. synchronized (this) { while (true) { The thread holds the monitor for its whole life, except while it's inside wait(), which releases it. That's what lets the other thread in. while (next <= max && isOdd(next) != odd) wait(); The guarded wait. It's a while, not an if, because a thread can wake up spuriously, or wake because of a notifyAll meant for someone else. Re-check the condition every time. if (next > max) { notifyAll(); return; } Termination. Without the notifyAll here, the other thread could be left in wait() forever after the last number. out.add(...); next++; notifyAll(); Do the work, hand the turn over, and wake the waiter. notifyAll rather than notify: with two threads notify happens to work, but notifyAll is the safe default (see problem 3).

docs.title: Approach 2: two semaphores as a baton
docs.text:
/** Approach 2: two semaphores used as a baton. Exactly one of them has a permit at any time. */
    static final class SemaphorePrinter {
        private final Semaphore oddTurn = new Semaphore(1);    // odd goes first
        private final Semaphore evenTurn = new Semaphore(0);

        void odd(int max, List<String> out) throws InterruptedException {
            for (int i = 1; i <= max; i += 2) {
                oddTurn.acquire();                             // wait for the baton
                out.add("odd:" + i);
                evenTurn.release();                            // pass the baton
            }
        }

        void even(int max, List<String> out) throws InterruptedException {
            for (int i = 2; i <= max; i += 2) {
                evenTurn.acquire();
                out.add("even:" + i);
                oddTurn.release();
            }
        }
    }
stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> OddHasBaton: oddTurn=1, evenTurn=0 OddHasBaton --> EvenHasBaton: odd prints, evenTurn.release() EvenHasBaton --> OddHasBaton: even prints, oddTurn.release()
  • Invariant: the two semaphores together hold exactly one permit. Whoever can acquire it holds the baton.
  • There's no shared counter, because each thread knows its own numbers (i += 2).
  • Termination is automatic: each loop runs a fixed number of times.
  • Visibility: release() happens-before the matching acquire(), so the plain ArrayList writes are safely published from one thread to the other.

docs.title: The test harness
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int max = 10;

        List<String> out1 = new ArrayList<>();                 // only touched while holding the monitor
        var p = new MonitorPrinter(max);
        Thread odd = Thread.ofPlatform().name("odd").start(() -> run(() -> p.print(true, out1)));
        Thread even = Thread.ofPlatform().name("even").start(() -> run(() -> p.print(false, out1)));
        odd.join();
        even.join();                                           // join() = happens-before: safe to read out1
        System.out.println("monitor  : " + out1);
        check(out1, max);

        List<String> out2 = new ArrayList<>();                 // release()->acquire() gives happens-before
        var s = new SemaphorePrinter();
        Thread o = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> run(() -> s.odd(max, out2)));
        Thread e = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> run(() -> s.even(max, out2)));
        o.join();
        e.join();
        System.out.println("semaphore: " + out2);
        check(out2, max);
        System.out.println("PASS");
    }

The monitor version runs on platform threads and the semaphore version on virtual threads. Both work the same way. join() creates the happens-before edge that makes it safe for main to read the list afterwards.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake What goes wrong if (wrong turn) wait(); A spurious or misdirected wakeup prints out of turn Busy loop while (!myTurn) {} with a non-volatile flag 100% CPU, and the JIT may hoist the read, so the loop never ends volatile int next with no lock Visibility is fine, but check-then-increment still races Forgetting the final notifyAll The other thread hangs, and join() never returns Calling wait() without holding the monitor IllegalMonitorStateException

docs.title: Follow-up questions
2. Round-Robin with N Threads
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · ReentrantLock · one Condition per thread

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
N threads print the numbers 1 to M in strict rotation: T0 prints 1, T1 prints 2, …, T(N-1) prints N, then T0 prints N+1, and so on.

This is the generalization of problem 1. The interesting part is efficiency of wake-ups. With a single monitor and notifyAll, every print wakes all N threads, and N-1 of them immediately go back to sleep. That's a thundering herd. The better answer gives each thread its own wait-set and wakes exactly the next one.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
owner(number) = (number - 1) % N decides whose turn it is. Each thread waits on turn[id]. After printing, a thread signals turn[owner(next)], so only the next thread wakes up.

flowchart LR subgraph Lock["ReentrantLock (one lock, N wait-sets)"] C0[turn 0] C1[turn 1] C2[turn 2] C3[turn 3] end T0((T0)) -- prints 1, signal --> C1 T1((T1)) -- prints 2, signal --> C2 T2((T2)) -- prints 3, signal --> C3 T3((T3)) -- prints 4, signal --> C0 sequenceDiagram autonumber participant T0 participant T1 participant L as lock + next participant T2 T2->>L: lock, owner(1)=0 ≠ 2 → turn[2].await() T1->>L: lock, owner(1)=0 ≠ 1 → turn[1].await() T0->>L: lock, owner(1)=0 → print "T0:1", next=2 T0->>T1: turn[1].signal() (ONLY T1 wakes) T0->>L: owner(2)=1 ≠ 0 → turn[0].await() T1->>L: reacquire lock → print "T1:2", next=3, turn[2].signal()

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition[] turn;                  // one wait-set per thread: we wake exactly the next one
    private final int threads;
    private final int max;
    private int next = 1;                            // guarded by lock

    RoundRobinPrinter(int threads, int max) {
        this.threads = threads;
        this.max = max;
        this.turn = new Condition[threads];
        for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) turn[i] = lock.newCondition();
    }

    private int owner(int number) { return (number - 1) % threads; }

    void worker(int id, List<String> out) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (true) {
                while (next <= max && owner(next) != id) {
                    turn[id].await();                // releases the lock while waiting
                }
                if (next > max) {                    // done: wake everybody so they observe next > max and exit
                    for (Condition c : turn) c.signalAll();
                    return;
                }
                out.add("T" + id + ":" + next);
                next++;
                turn[owner(next)].signal();          // wake ONLY the thread whose turn it is now
            }
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
Code Why Condition[] turn created from one lock Conditions are wait-sets attached to a lock. One lock keeps next consistent, and N conditions give targeted wake-ups. owner(n) = (n - 1) % threads Maps number → thread id. next is the single source of truth. Threads don't keep their own counters. while (next <= max && owner(next) != id) turn[id].await(); Guarded wait. await() atomically releases the lock and parks. On wake-up it reacquires the lock before returning, then re-checks. if (next > max) { for (Condition c : turn) c.signalAll(); return; } Termination: whoever sees the end wakes everyone, so the sleepers re-check next > max and exit. Otherwise the remaining threads hang. turn[owner(next)].signal() The key optimization. Exactly one thread can make progress, so wake exactly that one. lock.lock(); try { … } finally { lock.unlock(); } Always unlock in finally. An exception must not leave the lock held forever.

docs.title: Why it's correct
docs.text:
• Mutual exclusion and visibility: every access to next and out happens while holding lock, and unlock→lock is a happens-before edge.
  • No lost wake-up: a thread checks its condition and calls await() while holding the lock. The signaller also holds the lock, so the signal can't slip in between "check" and "sleep".
  • Progress: exactly one thread is runnable at a time (the owner). After printing it signals the next owner, and that chain never breaks.
  • Termination: signalAll on every condition after the last number.

docs.text:
java RoundRobinPrinter.java

[T0:1, T1:2, T2:3, T3:4, T0:5, T1:6, T2:7, T3:8, T0:9, T1:10, T2:11, T3:12, T0:13, T1:14, T2:15, T3:16, T0:17, T1:18, T2:19, T3:20]
PASS

The threads are started in reverse order (T3 first) on purpose. The ordering comes only from the protocol, never from start order.

docs.title: notifyAll vs targeted signal: the cost
docs.text: Approach Wake-ups per printed number Context switches with N=100 Monitor + notifyAll N (all threads) ~100 per number Condition per thread + signal 1 ~1 per number

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• signal() on the same condition everyone waits on: it may wake a thread whose turn it isn't, and then the wake-up is lost.
  • Using if instead of while around await().
  • Forgetting the termination signalAll.
  • Calling await() without holding the lock → IllegalMonitorStateException.

3. Multithreaded FizzBuzz
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · generic turn-taking monitor · LeetCode 1195

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Four threads share one FizzBuzz object. Thread A calls fizz() (prints "Fizz" for numbers divisible by 3 but not 5), B calls buzz() (divisible by 5 but not 3), C calls fizzbuzz() (divisible by 15), and D calls number() (all others). Together they must print the normal FizzBuzz sequence for 1..n.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
This is the same pattern as odd/even, but with four predicates. Each number belongs to exactly one thread. Write the "wait for my turn → print → advance → wake others" loop once and pass in the predicate and the renderer.

flowchart LR I[current = i] --> P{which predicate<br/>matches i?} P -->|i%15==0| FB[fizzbuzz thread] P -->|i%3==0| F[fizz thread] P -->|i%5==0| B[buzz thread] P -->|otherwise| N[number thread] FB & F & B & N -->|print, current++, notifyAll| I sequenceDiagram participant N as number participant F as fizz participant B as buzz participant M as monitor(current) N->>M: 1 → "1", 2 → "2", current=3, notifyAll N->>M: 3 not mine → wait F->>M: 3 is mine → "Fizz", current=4, notifyAll B->>M: 4 not mine → wait N->>M: 4 → "4", current=5, notifyAll B->>M: 5 → "Buzz", current=6, notifyAll

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final int n;
    private int current = 1;                                  // guarded by this
    private final List<String> out;

    FizzBuzzMultithreaded(int n, List<String> out) { this.n = n; this.out = out; }

    /** Generic "my turn?" loop shared by all four threads. Only the predicate and the printer differ. */
    private synchronized void loop(IntPredicate mine, IntFunction<String> render) throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            while (current <= n && !mine.test(current)) wait();
            if (current > n) { notifyAll(); return; }
            out.add(render.apply(current));
            current++;
            notifyAll();                                      // 4 threads, 4 conditions: notify() could wake the wrong one
        }
    }

    void fizz()     throws InterruptedException { loop(i -> i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 != 0, i -> "Fizz"); }
    void buzz()     throws InterruptedException { loop(i -> i % 5 == 0 && i % 3 != 0, i -> "Buzz"); }
    void fizzbuzz() throws InterruptedException { loop(i -> i % 15 == 0,              i -> "FizzBuzz"); }
    void number()   throws InterruptedException { loop(i -> i % 3 != 0 && i % 5 != 0, Integer::toString); }
Code Why private synchronized void loop(IntPredicate mine, IntFunction<String> render) One method holds the entire protocol. synchronized on the method locks this, which is the same monitor that wait/notifyAll use. while (current <= n && !mine.test(current)) wait(); Each thread sleeps until the current number is its number, or until the sequence is finished. notifyAll() (not notify()) With four threads, notify() might wake e.g. buzz when the next number belongs to number. buzz sees it's not its turn and goes back to sleep, and nobody else was woken, so the program hangs. notifyAll wakes everyone, and exactly one proceeds. Four one-line public methods Each one is just a predicate plus a renderer. The predicates are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, which is what guarantees progress.

docs.title: Why notify() deadlocks here: a concrete trace
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     participant F as fizz (waiting)     participant B as buzz (waiting)     participant N as number     N->>N: prints 4, current=5     N->>F: notify() wakes fizz (arbitrary choice!)     F->>F: 5 is not mine → wait()     Note over B: buzz owns 5 but was never woken     Note over F,N: everyone is waiting → hang

PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Overlapping predicates (i % 3 == 0 for fizz and i % 15 == 0 for fizzbuzz): two threads both think it's their turn.
  • Loop condition while (current <= n) outside the synchronized block: you read current without the lock.
  • Using notify().

docs.title: Follow-up questions
4. Print in Order
docs.text: L1 ★☆☆ · CountDownLatch · CompletableFuture · LeetCode 1114

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The same Foo instance is passed to three threads. Thread A calls first(), B calls second(), and C calls third(). The threads may be scheduled in any order, but the output must always be first second third.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
This is a one-time dependency, not turn-taking: "second may run only after first has happened". A one-shot gate is exactly a CountDownLatch(1). Two gates give you a chain.

flowchart LR A[first] -->|countDown gate 1| G1{{gate 1}} G1 -->|await passes| B[second] B -->|countDown gate 2| G2{{gate 2}} G2 -->|await passes| C[third] sequenceDiagram participant C as thread C (third) participant B as thread B (second) participant A as thread A (first) C->>C: secondDone.await() → blocks B->>B: firstDone.await() → blocks A->>A: print "first" A->>B: firstDone.countDown() B->>B: print "second" B->>C: secondDone.countDown() C->>C: print "third"

docs.title: Code walkthrough: latches
docs.text:
static final class Foo {
        private final CountDownLatch firstDone = new CountDownLatch(1);
        private final CountDownLatch secondDone = new CountDownLatch(1);

        void first(Runnable printFirst) {
            printFirst.run();
            firstDone.countDown();                     // opens gate 1 (and publishes everything before it)
        }

        void second(Runnable printSecond) throws InterruptedException {
            firstDone.await();                         // blocks until gate 1 is open
            printSecond.run();
            secondDone.countDown();
        }

        void third(Runnable printThird) throws InterruptedException {
            secondDone.await();
            printThird.run();
        }
    }
Code Why new CountDownLatch(1) ×2 Each latch is a gate that opens once and stays open. A thread arriving after it opened passes straight through (no lost signal). printFirst.run(); firstDone.countDown(); The order matters: print then open the gate. countDown() happens-before a successful await() returns, so everything first did is visible to second. firstDone.await() Blocks (parks) until the count reaches zero. On a virtual thread, this unmounts and costs nothing.

docs.title: Code walkthrough: CompletableFuture
docs.text:
/** Same ordering expressed as a dependency chain of CompletableFutures. */
    static final class FooCf {
        private final CompletableFuture<Void> firstDone = new CompletableFuture<>();
        private final CompletableFuture<Void> secondDone = new CompletableFuture<>();

        void first(Runnable r)  { r.run(); firstDone.complete(null); }
        void second(Runnable r) { firstDone.join(); r.run(); secondDone.complete(null); }
        void third(Runnable r)  { secondDone.join(); r.run(); }
    }

A CompletableFuture<Void> is also a one-shot, publish-once gate: complete(null) opens it and join() waits on it. This version reads like a dependency graph, and it extends naturally to "third needs both first and second": CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join().

docs.title: Why not volatile boolean flags?
docs.text:
while (!firstDone) { }   // busy-wait: burns a CPU core, and with virtual threads it never yields the carrier

It's correct if the flag is volatile, but it wastes CPU. A latch parks the thread instead.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
5. Building H2O
docs.text: L2 ★★★ · Semaphore + CyclicBarrier · LeetCode 1117

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Hydrogen and oxygen threads arrive in random order. They must leave (call releaseHydrogen() / releaseOxygen()) in groups of three: exactly 2 H and 1 O. A group must finish leaving before atoms of the next group leave.

docs.title: Key idea: two separate concerns
docs.text:
1. Admission (who may join the current molecule): a Semaphore(2) for H and a Semaphore(1) for O. They act as "seats".
  2. Rendezvous (wait until the molecule is complete): a CyclicBarrier(3). All three seated atoms wait for each other, then leave together. The barrier resets itself for the next molecule.
flowchart LR subgraph Arrivals H1((H)) & H2((H)) & H3((H)) & O1((O)) & O2((O)) end H1 & H2 & H3 --> HS{{H seats: Semaphore 2}} O1 & O2 --> OS{{O seat: Semaphore 1}} HS -->|2 seated| B[[CyclicBarrier 3]] OS -->|1 seated| B B -->|trips| OUT[H H O leave, then release seats] H3 -. waits for a free seat .-> HS O2 -. waits for a free seat .-> OS sequenceDiagram autonumber participant H1 participant H2 participant H3 participant O1 participant Bar as barrier(3) H1->>Bar: seat 1/2 → await H2->>Bar: seat 2/2 → await H3->>H3: hydrogenSlots.acquire() blocks (no seat) O1->>Bar: seat 1/1 → await → barrier trips par molecule 1 leaves H1->>H1: releaseHydrogen, release seat H2->>H2: releaseHydrogen, release seat O1->>O1: releaseOxygen, release seat end H3->>Bar: gets a seat in molecule 2

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final Semaphore hydrogenSlots = new Semaphore(2);   // at most 2 H in the current molecule
    private final Semaphore oxygenSlots = new Semaphore(1);     // at most 1 O in the current molecule
    private final CyclicBarrier molecule = new CyclicBarrier(3); // the 3 atoms wait for each other

    void hydrogen(Runnable releaseHydrogen) throws Exception {
        hydrogenSlots.acquire();          // 1. claim a seat in the molecule being formed
        try {
            molecule.await();             // 2. wait until 2 H + 1 O are seated
            releaseHydrogen.run();        // 3. "bond" (print)
        } finally {
            hydrogenSlots.release();      // 4. free the seat for the NEXT molecule
        }
    }

    void oxygen(Runnable releaseOxygen) throws Exception {
        oxygenSlots.acquire();
        try {
            molecule.await();
            releaseOxygen.run();
        } finally {
            oxygenSlots.release();
        }
    }
Step Code Why 1 hydrogenSlots.acquire() A third H can't join the molecule being formed. It blocks until a seat is freed. 2 molecule.await() Waits until 3 atoms are seated. Because of the seat limits, those 3 are always 2 H + 1 O. 3 releaseHydrogen.run() "Bond": print after the barrier, so no atom of an incomplete molecule ever prints. 4 hydrogenSlots.release() in finally Free the seat after printing. That's what keeps molecule n+1 from printing before molecule n is done.

docs.title: Why groups can't interleave
docs.text:
The next molecule needs 2 free H seats and 1 free O seat, which are only released after their holders have printed. So molecule n+1's barrier can't trip until all three atoms of molecule n have printed. The test checks this over 500 shuffled molecules: every consecutive block of 3 outputs contains exactly 2 H.

500 molecules, every consecutive group of 3 is 2xH + 1xO, e.g. [H, O, H, H, H, O, H, H, O]
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Releasing the seat before printing: the next molecule can start printing in the middle of the current one.
  • Using only a barrier with no seats: three H atoms could trip the barrier together.
  • Counting atoms with int fields without a lock.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
6. Bounded Blocking Queue
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · ReentrantLock + two Conditions · circular buffer · LeetCode 1188

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Implement a thread-safe bounded queue: put(e) blocks while the queue is full, take() blocks while it's empty, and offer(e, timeout) gives up after the timeout. Don't use java.util.concurrent collections.

This is the most-asked "build it yourself" question, because the bounded queue is the backbone of producer/consumer systems, thread pools, and backpressure.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
• Storage: a fixed array used as a circular buffer (head, tail, count). Both operations are O(1) with no allocation.
  • Coordination: one lock, two wait-sets: producers wait on notFull, and consumers wait on notEmpty. A put wakes one consumer, and a take wakes one producer.
0· 1· 2Ahead → take() 3B 4C 5D 6E 7·tail ← put()

items[8] used as a ring · count = 5 · producers wait on notFull when count == 8 · consumers wait on notEmpty when count == 0

After put the tail moves to slot 0 (it wraps around: (7 + 1) % 8). After take the head moves to slot 3.

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant P as Producer participant Q as Queue (lock) participant C as Consumer C->>Q: take(): count==0 → notEmpty.await() P->>Q: put(x): enqueue, count=1 P->>C: notEmpty.signal() C->>Q: wakes, reacquires lock, re-checks count>0 → dequeue C->>P: notFull.signal()

docs.title: Fields and constructor
docs.text:
private final Object[] items;                 // circular buffer
    private int head;                             // next slot to take from
    private int tail;                             // next slot to put into
    private int count;                            // number of elements
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();   // producers wait here
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();  // consumers wait here

    public BoundedBlockingQueue(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        items = new Object[capacity];
    }
  • head, tail, and count are all guarded by lock. Write that comment in the interview. It shows you think about ownership.
  • Keeping count separately avoids the classic ambiguity of head == tail, which can mean either full or empty.

docs.title: put / take
docs.text:
public void put(E e) throws InterruptedException {
        if (e == null) throw new NullPointerException();
        lock.lockInterruptibly();                 // a blocked producer can still be cancelled
        try {
            while (count == items.length) {
                notFull.await();                  // queue full → wait for a consumer
            }
            enqueue(e);
            notEmpty.signal();                    // exactly one consumer can now make progress
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public E take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == 0) {
                notEmpty.await();                 // queue empty → wait for a producer
            }
            E e = dequeue();
            notFull.signal();                     // exactly one producer can now make progress
            return e;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
Code Why lock.lockInterruptibly() A producer blocked trying to get the lock can still be cancelled with interrupt(). Plain lock() would ignore it. while (count == items.length) notFull.await(); Guarded wait. await releases the lock, parks, and reacquires the lock before returning. Use while because of spurious wake-ups and because another producer may have filled the slot first. notEmpty.signal() after enqueue One new item means one consumer can progress, so use signal rather than signalAll (it's safe because all waiters on notEmpty wait for the same condition). finally { lock.unlock(); } Unlock on every path, including InterruptedException from await().

docs.title: Timed offer
docs.text:
/** Timed offer: gives up after the timeout. awaitNanos returns the time still left. */
    public boolean offer(E e, long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException {
        long nanos = unit.toNanos(timeout);
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) {
                if (nanos <= 0) return false;
                nanos = notFull.awaitNanos(nanos);
            }
            enqueue(e);
            notEmpty.signal();
            return true;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

awaitNanos(n) returns the remaining time. Looping with the returned value handles spurious wake-ups correctly without extending the total timeout. That detail separates good answers from great ones.

docs.title: Helpers
docs.text:
private void enqueue(E e) {                   // caller holds lock
        items[tail] = e;
        tail = (tail + 1) % items.length;
        count++;
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    private E dequeue() {                         // caller holds lock
        E e = (E) items[head];
        items[head] = null;                       // let GC reclaim it
        head = (head + 1) % items.length;
        count--;
        return e;
    }

    public int size() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return count; } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

items[head] = null prevents a memory leak: without it, the array keeps references to objects that were already taken.

docs.title: Why two Conditions beat wait/notifyAll
docs.text: With a single monitor, producers and consumers share one wait-set, so you must notifyAll. That wakes producers when only consumers can make progress. Two conditions let you signal exactly the right side. (This is how java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue is built.)

docs.text:
20 producers × 5,000 items flow through a capacity of 8 (heavy blocking), with 10 consumers, all on virtual threads:

20 producers x 5000 items through capacity 8: sum=250050000 (expected 250050000), timed offer on full queue=false
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• if instead of while around await().
  • signal() called before the state change, or outside the lock (IllegalMonitorStateException).
  • Unbounded ArrayList storage: that's not a bounded queue.
  • Using synchronized + wait() with thousands of virtual threads on JDK 21–23: Object.wait() pins carriers. Condition.await() doesn't.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
7. Build a Thread Pool
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · worker loop · FutureTask · shutdown race

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Implement a fixed-size thread pool with a bounded queue. submit(Callable) returns a Future. If the queue is full, reject. Support shutdown() (finish queued work), shutdownNow() (interrupt), and awaitTermination().

The interviewer wants to see that you understand what ThreadPoolExecutor does: worker lifecycle, result and exception propagation, rejection, and the subtle race between shutdown and submit.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: flowchart LR     C1[caller] -->|submit| S{shutdown?<br/>queue.offer ok?}     C2[caller] -->|submit| S     S -->|no / full| R[RejectedExecutionException]     S -->|yes| Q[(ArrayBlockingQueue)]     Q -->|poll 50ms| W1[worker-0]     Q -->|poll 50ms| W2[worker-1]     Q -->|poll 50ms| W3[worker-2]     W1 & W2 & W3 -->|run FutureTask| F[(Future result / exception)] stateDiagram-v2     [*] --> RUNNING     RUNNING --> SHUTDOWN: shutdown()  (reject new, drain queue)     RUNNING --> STOPPED: shutdownNow()  (drain to list, interrupt workers)     SHUTDOWN --> STOPPED: shutdownNow()     SHUTDOWN --> TERMINATED: queue empty, all workers exited     STOPPED --> TERMINATED: workers exited

docs.title: State and worker creation
docs.text:
private final BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue;
    private final List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Object stateLock = new Object();    // makes "check shutdown + enqueue" atomic
    private volatile boolean shutdown;

    public SimpleThreadPool(int threads, int queueCapacity) {
        queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(queueCapacity);
        for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) {
            workers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().name("pool-worker-", i).start(this::workerLoop));
        }
    }
  • Workers are platform threads named pool-worker-N. A pool exists to reuse expensive threads. (You never pool virtual threads.)
  • shutdown is volatile because workers read it without holding stateLock.

docs.title: The worker loop
docs.text:
private void workerLoop() {
        while (true) {
            Runnable task;
            try {
                task = queue.poll(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                return;                                // shutdownNow(): stop immediately
            }
            if (task == null) {
                if (shutdown && queue.isEmpty()) return;  // drained and no more submissions → exit
                continue;
            }
            try {
                task.run();                            // FutureTask captures exceptions into the Future
            } catch (Throwable t) {
                // a bare Runnable threw: keep the worker alive (a real pool would log this)
            }
        }
    }
Code Why queue.poll(50, ms) rather than take() A worker blocked in take() would never notice shutdown. Polling with a timeout lets it check the flag regularly. The alternative is to put one poison pill per worker on shutdown. catch (InterruptedException) → return shutdownNow() interrupts workers, and that's the signal to exit immediately. if (shutdown && queue.isEmpty()) return; Graceful exit: finish everything queued first. try { task.run(); } catch (Throwable t) A task exception must never kill the worker. (ThreadPoolExecutor replaces dead workers instead.) FutureTask already captures exceptions, so this guards only raw Runnables.

docs.title: submit, shutdown, termination
docs.text:
public <T> Future<T> submit(Callable<T> callable) {
        FutureTask<T> task = new FutureTask<>(callable);
        synchronized (stateLock) {                     // see "the shutdown race" in the docs
            if (shutdown) throw new RejectedExecutionException("pool is shut down");
            if (!queue.offer(task)) throw new RejectedExecutionException("queue full");  // AbortPolicy
        }
        return task;
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        synchronized (stateLock) { shutdown = true; }  // after this no task can be enqueued
    }

    public List<Runnable> shutdownNow() {
        shutdown();
        List<Runnable> pending = new ArrayList<>();
        queue.drainTo(pending);
        workers.forEach(Thread::interrupt);
        return pending;
    }

    public boolean awaitTermination(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException {
        long deadline = System.nanoTime() + unit.toNanos(timeout);
        for (Thread w : workers) {
            long left = deadline - System.nanoTime();
            if (left <= 0 || !w.join(java.time.Duration.ofNanos(left))) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    @Override
    public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        shutdown();
        if (!awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) shutdownNow();
    }
Code Why new FutureTask<>(callable) FutureTask is both a Runnable (for the worker) and a Future (for the caller). It stores the result or the exception, which get() rethrows as an ExecutionException. synchronized (stateLock) { check shutdown; offer } Makes "is it open? then enqueue" atomic with respect to shutdown(). See the race below. queue.offer(task) → false ⇒ reject The bounded queue gives backpressure. offer doesn't block, so holding stateLock while calling it is fine. shutdownNow(): drainTo + interrupt Returns the never-started tasks to the caller, like the JDK does. awaitTermination uses Thread.join(Duration) It shares one deadline across all workers (JDK 19+ join returns a boolean).

docs.title: The shutdown race (the question that separates seniors)
docs.text:
Without stateLock, this interleaving loses a task forever:

sequenceDiagram participant S as submit() participant P as shutdown() participant W as last worker S->>S: reads shutdown == false ✔ P->>P: shutdown = true W->>W: shutdown && queue.isEmpty() → exits S->>S: queue.offer(task) ✔ ← nobody will ever run it, so future.get() hangs

With stateLock, shutdown = true can't happen between the check and the offer. So either the task is enqueued before shutdown (and a worker will drain it, because workers only exit when the queue is empty), or the submit is rejected. ThreadPoolExecutor solves the same problem with a single atomic ctl word that packs the run state and worker count together.

docs.text:
failure captured in Future: java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom
500 tasks ok (sum of squares=41541750), queue-full rejection=true, post-shutdown rejection=true
PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Workers blocked in take() forever: the pool never shuts down.
  • Letting a task's exception propagate out of the worker loop: the pool silently shrinks.
  • An unbounded queue: OOM under load, and rejection never happens.
  • shutdown that isn't volatile or synchronized: workers may never see it.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
8. Read-Write Lock
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · monitor with writer preference

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a lock that allows many concurrent readers or one exclusive writer. Writers must not starve when readers keep arriving.

docs.title: Key idea: three counters, one invariant
docs.text:
Invariant: writerActive ⇒ activeReaders == 0, and at most one writer.

  • A reader may enter if no writer is active and no writer is waiting. The second condition is writer preference. Without it, a constant stream of readers starves writers forever.
  • A writer may enter if no writer is active and there are no active readers.
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Free Free --> Reading: lockRead (no writer active/waiting) Reading --> Reading: lockRead (more readers) Reading --> Draining: a writer arrives (waitingWriters++) Draining --> Draining: new readers BLOCKED (writer preference) Draining --> Writing: last reader leaves Free --> Writing: lockWrite Writing --> Free: unlockWrite (notifyAll) sequenceDiagram participant R1 as Reader 1 participant R2 as Reader 2 participant W as Writer participant R3 as Reader 3 R1->>R1: lockRead → readers=1 R2->>R2: lockRead → readers=2 W->>W: lockWrite → waitingWriters=1, wait (readers>0) R3->>R3: lockRead → waitingWriters>0 → wait (no starvation) R1->>R1: unlockRead → readers=1 R2->>R2: unlockRead → readers=0 → notifyAll W->>W: enters, writerActive=true W->>W: unlockWrite → notifyAll R3->>R3: enters

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private int activeReaders;          // readers currently holding the lock
    private int waitingWriters;         // writers queued: new readers must back off (writer preference)
    private boolean writerActive;       // a writer holds the lock

    public synchronized void lockRead() throws InterruptedException {
        while (writerActive || waitingWriters > 0) {
            wait();
        }
        activeReaders++;
    }

    public synchronized void unlockRead() {
        if (activeReaders <= 0) throw new IllegalMonitorStateException("no read lock held");
        activeReaders--;
        if (activeReaders == 0) notifyAll();          // last reader out lets a writer in
    }

    public synchronized void lockWrite() throws InterruptedException {
        waitingWriters++;
        try {
            while (writerActive || activeReaders > 0) {
                wait();
            }
        } finally {
            waitingWriters--;                          // also on interrupt, or readers would block forever
        }
        writerActive = true;
    }

    public synchronized void unlockWrite() {
        if (!writerActive) throw new IllegalMonitorStateException("no write lock held");
        writerActive = false;
        notifyAll();                                   // wake both readers and writers
    }
Code Why All four methods synchronized The counters are guarded by this. The lock is held only briefly inside these methods, not while the caller reads or writes the data. Reader waits while a writer is active or waiting Readers yield to writers that are queued, not only to the active one. That's writer preference. if (activeReaders == 0) notifyAll(); Only the last reader leaving can unblock a writer, so there's no need to notify earlier. waitingWriters-- in finally If a waiting writer is interrupted, it must still decrement. Otherwise readers would wait forever for a writer that no longer exists. IllegalMonitorStateException checks Unlocking a lock you don't hold is a programming error. Fail loudly.

docs.title: A real lesson: this code hangs with 2,000 virtual threads on JDK 21
docs.text:
The first version of the test used Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() with 2,000 tasks, and it hung. The reason:

flowchart LR VT1[VT in Object.wait] -->|pins| C1[carrier 1] VT2[VT in Object.wait] -->|pins| C2[carrier 2] VTn[... 256 VTs in wait] -->|pins| C256[carrier 256 = maxPoolSize] W[writer VT that would<br/>call notifyAll] -. no carrier left .-> X((stuck))

On JDK 21–23, Object.wait() pins the virtual thread to its carrier (the scheduler compensates by adding carriers, up to 256). With hundreds of readers parked in wait(), every carrier is pinned, and the thread that would call notifyAll() never gets to run. JEP 491 (JDK 24) fixes this. On JDK 21 the options are:

  • run monitor-based code on platform threads (what the test does now, with a pool of 64), or
  • build it with ReentrantLock + Condition, whose await() unmounts the virtual thread instead of pinning it.

The test asserts that no reader ever overlaps a writer, that writers are exclusive, and that readers really do run concurrently (max > 1).

docs.title: Follow-up questions
9. Implement a Cyclic Barrier
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · ReentrantLock + Condition · generation object

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement CyclicBarrier(parties, action). await() blocks until parties threads have called it, then runs action once and releases them all. The barrier must be reusable for the next round.

docs.title: Key idea: the generation
docs.text:
The naive version waits with while (waiting < parties) await();. That fails because the last thread resets waiting to 0 for the next round, so the woken threads see 0 < parties and go back to sleep forever.

The fix is to tag each round with a generation object. A waiter remembers its generation and waits until the generation changes. Fast threads that start the next round get a new generation, and they can't be confused with the old one.

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant A participant B participant C as C (last) participant G as barrier state A->>G: gen=g1, waiting=1 → await while gen==g1 B->>G: gen=g1, waiting=2 → await while gen==g1 C->>G: waiting=3 == parties → run action C->>G: waiting=0, gen=g2, signalAll A->>A: wakes: gen(g2) != g1 → return B->>B: wakes: gen(g2) != g1 → return Note over A,C: A can immediately call await() for round 2 (gen g2) stateDiagram-v2 direction LR g1: generation g1 (filling 0..parties-1) g2: generation g2 g1 --> g2: last arrival runs action, waiting=0, new Generation, signalAll g2 --> g3: next round...

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private static final class Generation {}           // identity object: one per "round"

    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition tripped = lock.newCondition();
    private final int parties;
    private final Runnable barrierAction;
    private int waiting;                               // guarded by lock
    private Generation generation = new Generation();  // guarded by lock

    public CustomCyclicBarrier(int parties, Runnable barrierAction) {
        if (parties <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        this.parties = parties;
        this.barrierAction = barrierAction;
    }

    /** @return arrival index: parties-1 for the first to arrive, 0 for the last (same as the JDK) */
    public int await() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Generation myGeneration = generation;
            int index = parties - 1 - waiting;
            waiting++;
            if (waiting == parties) {                  // last to arrive: trip the barrier
                if (barrierAction != null) barrierAction.run();   // runs before anyone is released
                waiting = 0;
                generation = new Generation();         // start the next round
                tripped.signalAll();
                return 0;
            }
            while (myGeneration == generation) {       // NOT "while waiting < parties": waiting was reset to 0!
                tripped.await();
            }
            return index;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
Code Why private static final class Generation {} An empty class whose identity is the round id. A counter (long round) works too. Generation myGeneration = generation; Captured under the lock when the thread arrives. int index = parties - 1 - waiting; Arrival index, matching the JDK's contract (the last arrival gets 0). It's handy for "elect one thread to do X". if (waiting == parties) { action; waiting = 0; generation = new Generation(); signalAll(); } The last thread trips the barrier. The action runs before anyone is released, so it sees the results of all parties (they all held the lock before it). while (myGeneration == generation) tripped.await(); The correct wait condition. It handles spurious wake-ups and is immune to the waiting reset.

docs.text:

8 parties x 1000 rounds: rounds completed=1000, ordering violations=0

docs.title: What the JDK version adds
docs.text:
• Broken barrier: if a waiter is interrupted or times out, the generation is marked broken, and all waiters get BrokenBarrierException. Otherwise the others would wait forever for a party that left.
  • Timed await(timeout).
  • reset(): break the current generation and start a new one.
Follow-up: add broken-barrier semantics.

Add boolean broken to Generation. In the catch (InterruptedException) around await, if the generation is unchanged, set broken = true, signalAll(), and rethrow. After waking, if myGeneration.broken, throw BrokenBarrierException.

CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Phaser?

A latch is one-shot, and waiters wait for events. A barrier is reusable, and parties wait for each other. A Phaser is a reusable barrier with dynamic registration and phase numbers (used in problem 19).

Full source: CustomCyclicBarrier.java 
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

/**
 * Implement a reusable CyclicBarrier (with a barrier action) from scratch. The key insight: a GENERATION object,
 * so threads from the next round can't be confused with threads still leaving the current round.
 * Run: java CustomCyclicBarrier.java
 */
public class CustomCyclicBarrier {

    private static final class Generation {}           // identity object: one per "round"

    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition tripped = lock.newCondition();
    private final int parties;
    private final Runnable barrierAction;
    private int waiting;                               // guarded by lock
    private Generation generation = new Generation();  // guarded by lock

    public CustomCyclicBarrier(int parties, Runnable barrierAction) {
        if (parties <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        this.parties = parties;
        this.barrierAction = barrierAction;
    }

    /** @return arrival index: parties-1 for the first to arrive, 0 for the last (same as the JDK) */
    public int await() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Generation myGeneration = generation;
            int index = parties - 1 - waiting;
            waiting++;
            if (waiting == parties) {                  // last to arrive: trip the barrier
                if (barrierAction != null) barrierAction.run();   // runs before anyone is released
                waiting = 0;
                generation = new Generation();         // start the next round
                tripped.signalAll();
                return 0;
            }
            while (myGeneration == generation) {       // NOT "while waiting < parties": waiting was reset to 0!
                tripped.await();
            }
            return index;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int parties = 8, rounds = 1_000;
        AtomicInteger roundsCompleted = new AtomicInteger();
        int[] perRound = new int[rounds];                           // each worker increments its round's slot
        AtomicInteger violations = new AtomicInteger();
        var barrier = new CustomCyclicBarrier(parties, () -> {
            int r = roundsCompleted.get();
            if (perRound[r] != parties) violations.incrementAndGet();   // all parties finished round r?
            roundsCompleted.incrementAndGet();
        });
        Object lock = new Object();
        List<Thread> ts = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int p = 0; p < parties; p++) {
            ts.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
                try {
                    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++) {
                        synchronized (lock) { perRound[r]++; }
                        barrier.await();                            // nobody starts round r+1 before all finish r
                    }
                } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            }));
        }
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
        System.out.printf("%d parties x %d rounds: rounds completed=%d, ordering violations=%d%n",
                parties, rounds, roundsCompleted.get(), violations.get());
        if (roundsCompleted.get() != rounds || violations.get() != 0) throw new AssertionError();
        System.out.println("PASS");
    }
}

docs.title: 10. Delayed Task Scheduler
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · PriorityQueue · Condition.awaitNanos

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement schedule(task, delay). Tasks must run as close as possible to their due time, in due-time order. A task scheduled later with a shorter delay must still run first. Don't use ScheduledExecutorService or DelayQueue.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
• A min-heap (PriorityQueue) ordered by due time gives the next task in O(1), and insertion costs O(log n).
  • One dispatcher thread sleeps exactly until the head is due, using awaitNanos(head.due - now).
  • When schedule() inserts a task that becomes the new head, it signals the dispatcher so it can recompute a shorter sleep. This is the important part.
  • Due tasks run on virtual threads, so a slow task never delays the next one.
sequenceDiagram autonumber participant M as main participant S as schedule() participant D as dispatcher participant VT as task VT M->>S: C @300ms, A @100ms, E @500ms S->>D: A is the new head → signal D->>D: awaitNanos(100ms) M->>S: (t=50) B @150ms Note over S: B (150) is not earlier than A (100) → no signal needed D->>D: t=100 → poll A D->>VT: start A D->>D: head = B → awaitNanos(50ms) D->>VT: t=150 start B, then C, D, E... flowchart TD L[dispatcher loop: lock] --> S{shutdown?} S -->|yes| X[exit] S -->|no| E{queue empty?} E -->|yes| W1[changed.await()] W1 --> S E -->|no| D{head due?} D -->|no| W2["changed.awaitNanos(head.due - now)"] W2 --> S D -->|yes| P[poll head, unlock] P --> R[start on virtual thread] R --> L

docs.title: Data structures
docs.text:
private record Job(long dueNanos, long seq, Runnable task) implements Comparable<Job> {
        public int compareTo(Job o) {
            int c = Long.compare(dueNanos, o.dueNanos);
            return c != 0 ? c : Long.compare(seq, o.seq);      // FIFO for equal due times
        }
    }

    private final PriorityQueue<Job> queue = new PriorityQueue<>();   // min-heap by due time, guarded by lock
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition changed = lock.newCondition();           // "new head or shutdown"
    private final AtomicLong seq = new AtomicLong();
    private final Thread dispatcher;
    private boolean shutdown;                                        // guarded by lock

    public DelayedTaskScheduler() {
        dispatcher = Thread.ofPlatform().name("scheduler-dispatcher").daemon(true).start(this::dispatchLoop);
    }
  • Job is a record with compareTo by dueNanos, then by a sequence number, so tasks with equal due times run FIFO (a PriorityQueue isn't stable by itself).
  • System.nanoTime(), not currentTimeMillis(): it's monotonic and unaffected by wall-clock adjustments.

docs.title: schedule()
docs.text:
public void schedule(Runnable task, long delay, TimeUnit unit) {
        Job job = new Job(System.nanoTime() + unit.toNanos(delay), seq.getAndIncrement(), task);
        lock.lock();
        try {
            if (shutdown) throw new IllegalStateException("scheduler is shut down");
            queue.add(job);
            if (queue.peek() == job) changed.signal();   // new earliest job → dispatcher must re-compute its sleep
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

if (queue.peek() == job) changed.signal(); means we only wake the dispatcher if the new job is now the earliest. Otherwise the dispatcher's current sleep is already correct.

docs.title: The dispatcher
docs.text:
private void dispatchLoop() {
        while (true) {
            Job due;
            lock.lock();
            try {
                while (true) {
                    if (shutdown) return;
                    Job head = queue.peek();
                    if (head == null) {
                        changed.await();                              // nothing scheduled: sleep until schedule()
                        continue;
                    }
                    long wait = head.dueNanos() - System.nanoTime();
                    if (wait <= 0) {
                        due = queue.poll();                           // it's time
                        break;
                    }
                    changed.awaitNanos(wait);                         // sleep until due, or until a new head arrives
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                return;
            } finally {
                lock.unlock();
            }
            Thread.ofVirtual().start(due.task());                     // never run user code on the dispatcher
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        lock.lock();
        try { shutdown = true; changed.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
Code Why changed.await() when empty No busy waiting. It sleeps until something is scheduled. changed.awaitNanos(wait) Sleeps until the head is due, or until signalled about a new head, or spuriously. In every case, loop and recompute. due = queue.poll(); break; then unlock Take the job out under the lock, but run it outside the lock. Thread.ofVirtual().start(due.task()) User code never runs on the dispatcher: a slow or failing task can't delay the others.

docs.text:

PASS

B was scheduled 50 ms after A, C, and E, yet it ran in the correct place.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
11. Deadlock: Create, Detect, Fix
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · ThreadMXBean · lock ordering · tryLock

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Write a program that always deadlocks. 2. Detect the deadlock programmatically. 3. Fix it in two different ways.

Interviewers ask "write a deadlock" to see whether you can make it deterministic rather than "usually happens". Then they move on to the Coffman conditions and the fixes.

docs.title: The four Coffman conditions
docs.text:
A deadlock needs all four. Break any one of them and the deadlock is impossible.

Condition Meaning Broken by Mutual exclusion Locks are exclusive Lock-free/immutable data Hold and wait Holding A while waiting for B tryLock + release + retry (fix 2) No preemption Locks can't be taken away Timeouts / interruptible locks Circular wait A→B and B→A Global lock ordering (fix 1)

docs.title: 1. Creating a guaranteed deadlock
docs.text:
static void createDeadlock(Object a, Object b) {
        CountDownLatch bothHoldFirstLock = new CountDownLatch(2);   // guarantees the bad interleaving
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("worker-A").daemon(true).start(() -> {
            synchronized (a) {
                bothHoldFirstLock.countDown();
                await(bothHoldFirstLock);
                synchronized (b) { System.out.println("never printed"); }
            }
        });
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("worker-B").daemon(true).start(() -> {
            synchronized (b) {                                      // opposite order → cycle
                bothHoldFirstLock.countDown();
                await(bothHoldFirstLock);
                synchronized (a) { System.out.println("never printed"); }
            }
        });
    }
sequenceDiagram participant A as worker-A participant LA as lock a participant LB as lock b participant B as worker-B A->>LA: synchronized(a) ✔ B->>LB: synchronized(b) ✔ A->>A: latch.countDown, await B->>B: latch.countDown, await → both hold their first lock A--xLB: synchronized(b) → BLOCKED (held by B) B--xLA: synchronized(a) → BLOCKED (held by A) Note over A,B: circular wait → stuck forever

The CountDownLatch(2) is the trick that makes it deterministic: neither thread tries its second lock until both hold their first one. Without it, one thread might grab both locks before the other starts, and the deadlock wouldn't happen. The threads are daemon so the demo JVM can still exit.

docs.title: 2. Detecting it
docs.text:
static long[] detect() throws InterruptedException {
        ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
        for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) {                              // poll up to ~5 s
            long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads();                // monitors AND j.u.c locks
            if (ids != null) {
                for (ThreadInfo info : mx.getThreadInfo(ids, true, true)) {
                    System.out.printf("  DEADLOCK: %s is waiting for %s held by %s%n",
                            info.getThreadName(), info.getLockName(), info.getLockOwnerName());
                }
                return ids;
            }
            Thread.sleep(100);
        }
        return null;
    }
  • ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() finds cycles across both synchronized monitors and java.util.concurrent locks (findMonitorDeadlockedThreads covers monitors only).
  • ThreadInfo tells you who waits for which lock and who owns it. That's the same information jstack prints as "Found one Java-level deadlock".
  • In production you'd run this in a health check or a scheduled task and alert. The JVM can't resolve a deadlock; you restart the process.
  • It only sees platform threads. For virtual threads, use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json.

Real output:

1) creating a deadlock...
  DEADLOCK: worker-B is waiting for java.lang.Object@1e683a3e held by worker-A

docs.title: 3a. Fix: global lock ordering (breaks circular wait)
docs.text:
/** Fix 1: every thread acquires locks in the same global order (here: by id). No cycle is possible. */
    record Resource(int id, ReentrantLock lock) {}

    static void withBoth(Resource x, Resource y, Runnable action) {
        Resource first = x.id() < y.id() ? x : y;
        Resource second = first == x ? y : x;
        first.lock().lock();
        try {
            second.lock().lock();
            try { action.run(); } finally { second.lock().unlock(); }
        } finally {
            first.lock().unlock();
        }
    }
flowchart LR subgraph Before A1[T1: a then b] --> X((cycle)) B1[T2: b then a] --> X end subgraph After["After: always lower id first"] A2[T1: r1 then r2] --> OK((no cycle)) B2["T2: asked for (r2, r1) → takes r1 then r2"] --> OK end

If every thread acquires locks in the same total order, a cycle in the wait-for graph is impossible. Use a stable, unique key for the order (here an id). System.identityHashCode works but can collide, so a tie-breaker lock is then needed.

docs.title: 3b. Fix: tryLock with timeout and back-off (breaks hold-and-wait)
docs.text:
/** Fix 2: never wait for the second lock while holding the first: tryLock with timeout, back off, retry. */
    static boolean withBothTryLock(ReentrantLock x, ReentrantLock y, Runnable action) throws InterruptedException {
        long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(5);
        while (System.nanoTime() < deadline) {
            if (x.tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                try {
                    if (y.tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                        try { action.run(); return true; } finally { y.unlock(); }
                    }
                } finally {
                    x.unlock();                                     // release what we hold → breaks hold-and-wait
                }
            }
            Thread.sleep(java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 5)); // random backoff vs livelock
        }
        return false;
    }
Code Why x.tryLock(10, ms) Don't wait forever for the first lock. y.tryLock(10, ms) fails → finally x.unlock() Release what you hold if you can't get everything. That breaks hold-and-wait. Random sleep(1..5ms) back-off Without randomness, two threads can retry in lockstep forever. That's a livelock. Overall deadline Gives up eventually and reports failure instead of spinning.

docs.text:
2) lock ordering: 2 threads x 100k opposite-order acquisitions
  completed, counter=200000
3) tryLock + backoff: 2 threads x 10k opposite-order acquisitions
  completed, counter=20000

docs.title: Follow-up questions
12. Dining Philosophers
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · resource ordering · waiter semaphore · LeetCode 1226

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair. To eat, a philosopher needs both adjacent forks. Design a protocol with no deadlock (everyone stuck) and no starvation (someone never eats).

docs.title: Why the naive solution deadlocks
docs.text:
"Pick up the left fork, then the right fork." If all five pick up their left fork at the same moment, each waits for a right fork held by a neighbour, and the wait-for graph is a cycle.

flowchart LR P0((P0)) -- holds --> F0[fork 0] P0 -. wants .-> F1[fork 1] P1((P1)) -- holds --> F1 P1 -. wants .-> F2[fork 2] P2((P2)) -- holds --> F2 P2 -. wants .-> F3[fork 3] P3((P3)) -- holds --> F3 P3 -. wants .-> F4[fork 4] P4((P4)) -- holds --> F4 P4 -. wants .-> F0

docs.title: Solution 1: resource ordering
docs.text:
/** Solution 1: resource ordering. Everyone picks up the LOWER-numbered fork first, so no wait-for cycle exists. */
    static final class OrderedTable {
        private final ReentrantLock[] forks;

        OrderedTable(int n) {
            forks = new ReentrantLock[n];
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock(true);   // fair → no starvation
        }

        void dine(int philosopher, Runnable eat) {
            int left = philosopher;
            int right = (philosopher + 1) % forks.length;
            ReentrantLock first = forks[Math.min(left, right)];
            ReentrantLock second = forks[Math.max(left, right)];
            first.lock();
            try {
                second.lock();
                try { eat.run(); } finally { second.unlock(); }
            } finally {
                first.unlock();
            }
        }
    }

Everyone picks up the lower-numbered fork first. Philosophers 0–3 behave as before (left then right), but philosopher 4's neighbours are forks 4 and 0, so they pick up fork 0 first. That single asymmetry breaks the cycle:

flowchart LR P3((P3)) -->|1st| F3[fork 3] P3 -->|2nd| F4[fork 4] P4((P4)) -->|1st| F0[fork 0] P4 -->|2nd| F4 P0((P0)) -->|1st| F0 P0 -->|2nd| F1[fork 1]

P4 and P0 now compete for fork 0 first. Whoever loses holds nothing, so fork 4 stays free for P3. There's no cycle, so there's no deadlock. new ReentrantLock(true) (fair) hands each fork out FIFO, which prevents starvation.

docs.title: Solution 2: the waiter (limit the diners)
docs.text:
/** Solution 2: a "waiter" admits at most N-1 philosophers to the table, so at least one can always get both forks. */
    static final class WaiterTable {
        private final ReentrantLock[] forks;
        private final Semaphore seats;

        WaiterTable(int n) {
            forks = new ReentrantLock[n];
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock();
            seats = new Semaphore(n - 1, true);
        }

        void dine(int philosopher, Runnable eat) throws InterruptedException {
            seats.acquire();
            try {
                ReentrantLock left = forks[philosopher], right = forks[(philosopher + 1) % forks.length];
                left.lock();                      // naive left-then-right is now safe
                try {
                    right.lock();
                    try { eat.run(); } finally { right.unlock(); }
                } finally { left.unlock(); }
            } finally {
                seats.release();
            }
        }
    }

A Semaphore(N-1) lets at most four philosophers try to eat at once. By the pigeonhole principle, four philosophers holding five forks means at least one of them has both forks, so the system always makes progress. Inside, the naive left-then-right order is now safe.

sequenceDiagram participant W as waiter Semaphore(4) participant P0 participant P4 P0->>W: acquire (1/4) Note over W: P1, P2, P3 also seated (4/4) P4->>W: acquire → blocks (table full) Note over P0: at least one seated philosopher<br/>can always get both forks P0->>W: release after eating P4->>W: acquire succeeds
