13. Sleeping Barber
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · signalling semaphores · Dijkstra 1965

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A barbershop has one barber, one barber chair, and N waiting chairs. If there are no customers, the barber sleeps. An arriving customer wakes the barber, or sits in a free waiting chair, or leaves if all chairs are taken. Avoid races where the barber sleeps while a customer waits, or two customers sit in the same chair.

docs.title: Key idea: two "doorbells" and one counter
docs.text:
Shared item Type Role waiting int guarded by seatsLock How many waiting chairs are taken: decides "sit or leave" customersReady Semaphore(0) Customer → barber: "someone is waiting" (the barber sleeps on it) barberReady Semaphore(0) Barber → customer: "next please"

Semaphores count signals, so a release() that happens before the matching acquire() isn't lost. That's exactly the race that broke early solutions built on wait/notify.

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Customer participant L as seatsLock / waiting participant CR as customersReady participant BR as barberReady participant B as Barber B->>CR: acquire() → sleeps (no customers) C->>L: lock: waiting < chairs → waiting++ , unlock C->>CR: release() (doorbell) CR-->>B: wakes B->>L: lock: waiting-- , unlock B->>BR: release() ("next please") C->>BR: acquire() → called in B->>B: cut hair (outside any lock) flowchart TD A[customer arrives] --> L{lock: waiting == chairs?} L -->|yes| X[unlock, leave: turnedAway++] L -->|no| S[waiting++, unlock] S --> R[customersReady.release] R --> W[barberReady.acquire] W --> H[haircut: served++]

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final int chairs;
    private int waiting;                                       // guarded by seatsLock
    private final ReentrantLock seatsLock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Semaphore customersReady = new Semaphore(0); // counts waiting customers; barber sleeps on it
    private final Semaphore barberReady = new Semaphore(0);    // barber signals "next please"
    final AtomicInteger served = new AtomicInteger();
    final AtomicInteger turnedAway = new AtomicInteger();

    SleepingBarber(int chairs) { this.chairs = chairs; }

    void barber() {
        try {
            while (true) {
                customersReady.acquire();                      // sleep until a customer sits down
                seatsLock.lock();
                try {
                    waiting--;                                 // take one customer from the waiting room
                } finally {
                    seatsLock.unlock();
                }
                barberReady.release();                         // invite that customer into the chair
                Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(2));            // cut hair (outside the lock!)
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();                // shop closes
        }
    }

    void customer() throws InterruptedException {
        seatsLock.lock();
        try {
            if (waiting == chairs) {                           // no free chair → leave
                turnedAway.incrementAndGet();
                return;
            }
            waiting++;                                         // sit down in the waiting room
        } finally {
            seatsLock.unlock();
        }
        customersReady.release();                              // wake the barber if he's asleep
        barberReady.acquire();                                 // wait to be called
        served.incrementAndGet();                              // getting a haircut
    }
Code Why Customer: check-and-increment waiting under seatsLock "Is a chair free? Take it" must be atomic, or two customers take the last chair. Customer: customersReady.release() after unlocking Signals don't need the lock. Releasing outside it keeps the critical section tiny. Barber: customersReady.acquire() This is the barber's "sleep". The permit count equals the number of waiting customers, so no wake-up is lost. Barber: waiting-- then barberReady.release() Frees a waiting chair and calls exactly one customer in. Thread.sleep(2ms) outside the lock The haircut (the work) never holds a lock, so new customers can still check the chairs meanwhile. Barber exits on InterruptedException That's how the shop closes: the main thread interrupts the barber after all customers are done.

The invariant served + turnedAway == customers holds, so nobody is lost or double-counted.

Multiple barbers?

Start K barber threads with the same code. The semaphores already handle many-to-many. Each barberReady.release() admits one customer.

Where does this pattern appear in real systems?

In a bounded worker pool with a bounded queue and rejection: chairs = queue capacity, barber = worker, leaving = RejectedExecutionException. It's problem 7 in disguise.

Full source: SleepingBarber.java 
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

/**
 * Sleeping barber (Dijkstra): one barber, N waiting chairs. If no chair is free the customer leaves.
 * If nobody is waiting the barber sleeps. Classic semaphore signalling problem.
 * Run: java SleepingBarber.java
 */
public class SleepingBarber {

    private final int chairs;
    private int waiting;                                       // guarded by seatsLock
    private final ReentrantLock seatsLock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Semaphore customersReady = new Semaphore(0); // counts waiting customers; barber sleeps on it
    private final Semaphore barberReady = new Semaphore(0);    // barber signals "next please"
    final AtomicInteger served = new AtomicInteger();
    final AtomicInteger turnedAway = new AtomicInteger();

    SleepingBarber(int chairs) { this.chairs = chairs; }

    void barber() {
        try {
            while (true) {
                customersReady.acquire();                      // sleep until a customer sits down
                seatsLock.lock();
                try {
                    waiting--;                                 // take one customer from the waiting room
                } finally {
                    seatsLock.unlock();
                }
                barberReady.release();                         // invite that customer into the chair
                Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(2));            // cut hair (outside the lock!)
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();                // shop closes
        }
    }

    void customer() throws InterruptedException {
        seatsLock.lock();
        try {
            if (waiting == chairs) {                           // no free chair → leave
                turnedAway.incrementAndGet();
                return;
            }
            waiting++;                                         // sit down in the waiting room
        } finally {
            seatsLock.unlock();
        }
        customersReady.release();                              // wake the barber if he's asleep
        barberReady.acquire();                                 // wait to be called
        served.incrementAndGet();                              // getting a haircut
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var shop = new SleepingBarber(5);
        Thread barber = Thread.ofVirtual().name("barber").start(shop::barber);
        List<Thread> customers = new ArrayList<>();
        int total = 300;
        for (int i = 0; i < total; i++) {
            customers.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
                try { shop.customer(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            }));
            Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, 4)));   // random arrivals
        }
        for (Thread c : customers) c.join();
        barber.interrupt();
        barber.join();
        System.out.printf("customers=%d served=%d turnedAway=%d%n", total, shop.served.get(), shop.turnedAway.get());
        if (shop.served.get() + shop.turnedAway.get() != total || shop.served.get() == 0) throw new AssertionError();
        System.out.println("PASS");
    }
}

docs.title: 14. Bank Transfer
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · ordered locking · consistent snapshot

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement transfer(from, to, amount) for a bank with many accounts and thousands of concurrent transfers. Requirements: no lost updates, no negative balances, no deadlock, and the total money in the bank never changes, even when you audit it while transfers are running.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
• A lock per account gives fine-grained concurrency (transfers between unrelated accounts run in parallel).
  • A transfer needs two locks, so a deadlock is possible (A→B concurrently with B→A). Lock in id order.
  • "Check balance, then debit" is a check-then-act, so it's safe only while both locks are held.
  • The audit locks all accounts in the same id order to get a consistent snapshot.
sequenceDiagram participant T1 as transfer(A→B) participant LA as lock A (id 1) participant LB as lock B (id 2) participant T2 as transfer(B→A) T1->>LA: lock (lower id first) T2--xLA: lock A first too → waits T1->>LB: lock T1->>T1: check & move money T1->>LB: unlock T1->>LA: unlock T2->>LA: acquires A, then B → proceeds

docs.title: Account
docs.text:
static final class Account {
        private final long id;
        private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
        private long balanceMinor;                       // guarded by lock

        Account(long id, long openingMinor) { this.id = id; this.balanceMinor = openingMinor; }

        long balance() {
            lock.lock();
            try { return balanceMinor; } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        }
    }

The balance is a long in minor units (paise or cents). Never use double for money: 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text:
static final AtomicLong rejected = new AtomicLong();

    /** @return true if moved, false if insufficient funds */
    static boolean transfer(Account from, Account to, long amountMinor) {
        if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        if (from == to) return true;                     // same lock twice would be fine (reentrant) but pointless

        Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to;     // global lock order by id → no deadlock cycle
        Account second = first == from ? to : from;

        first.lock.lock();
        try {
            second.lock.lock();
            try {
                if (from.balanceMinor < amountMinor) {   // check-then-act is SAFE: both locks are held
                    rejected.incrementAndGet();
                    return false;
                }
                from.balanceMinor -= amountMinor;
                to.balanceMinor += amountMinor;
                return true;
            } finally {
                second.lock.unlock();
            }
        } finally {
            first.lock.unlock();
        }
    }
Code Why amountMinor <= 0 check Validate input before taking any lock. if (from == to) return true; Avoids locking the same account twice. It would work (the lock is reentrant), but it's pointless. first = from.id < to.id ? from : to Global lock ordering, which removes the circular wait. Ids are unique and stable, unlike identityHashCode. Balance check inside both locks No other thread can change either balance between the check and the update. Nested try/finally Each lock is released even if the inner code throws, in reverse acquisition order.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
/** Consistent snapshot of the total: lock ALL accounts in id order, then sum. */
    static long auditTotal(Account[] accounts) {
        for (Account a : accounts) a.lock.lock();        // accounts[] is sorted by id
        try {
            long total = 0;
            for (Account a : accounts) total += a.balanceMinor;
            return total;
        } finally {
            for (int i = accounts.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) accounts[i].lock.unlock();
        }
    }

Summing balances without locks can read A before a transfer and B after it, which double-counts the money in flight. Locking every account (in id order, so it can't deadlock with transfers) gives a moment where no transfer is half-done.

flowchart LR subgraph Unlocked sum a1[read A = 100] --> t[transfer A→B 50 happens] --> b1[read B = 150] --> s1[total off by +50] end subgraph Locked audit a2[lock A..Z in id order] --> s2[sum] --> u[unlock] --> ok[exact total] end

15. Producer-Consumer Pipeline with Poison Pills
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · BlockingQueue · poison pills · sealed types · virtual threads

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build a three-stage pipeline: a reader emits lines, N parser threads convert each line to a number, and an aggregator sums them. Stages must run concurrently, memory must stay bounded, and the pipeline must shut down cleanly when the input ends.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
• Bounded queues between the stages. A full queue blocks the upstream put, which is backpressure with no extra code.
  • Poison pills for shutdown: a special message that means "no more data". With N consumers you need N pills, one per consumer, because each consumer stops after swallowing one.
  • Fan-in from N parsers to one aggregator: only the last parser to finish sends the aggregator's pill.
flowchart LR R[reader<br/>1 VT] -->|put Line ... then N × POISON| Q1[(lines<br/>cap 100)] Q1 --> P1[parser 1] Q1 --> P2[parser 2] Q1 --> P8[parser 8] P1 & P2 & P8 -->|put Long| Q2[(numbers<br/>cap 100)] P8 -. last parser to finish sends END .-> Q2 Q2 --> A[aggregator<br/>1 VT] sequenceDiagram participant R as reader participant Q1 as lines participant P as parser k participant Q2 as numbers participant A as aggregator R->>Q1: Line("1") ... Line("100000") R->>Q1: POISON × 8 P->>Q1: take → Line → parse P->>Q2: put(n) P->>Q1: take → POISON → stop, finishedParsers.incrementAndGet() Note over P: the 8th parser to finish puts END P->>Q2: put(END) A->>Q2: take ... until END → total

docs.title: Message types
docs.text:
sealed interface Msg permits Line, Poison {}
    record Line(String text) implements Msg {}
    record Poison() implements Msg {}                       // "no more data" marker
    static final Poison POISON = new Poison();

A sealed interface makes "data or poison" explicit and type-safe. Java 21 record patterns then deconstruct it: if (m instanceof Line(String text)). Compare that with the Java 8 habit of using a magic "EOF" string, which could appear in real data.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
static long run(List<String> input, int parsers) throws Exception {
        BlockingQueue<Msg> lines = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);     // stage 1 → 2 (bounded = backpressure)
        BlockingQueue<Long> numbers = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);  // stage 2 → 3
        final long END = Long.MIN_VALUE;                               // poison for stage 3
        AtomicLong total = new AtomicLong();

        try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            // Stage 1: single producer
            ex.submit(() -> {
                for (String s : input) lines.put(new Line(s));
                for (int i = 0; i < parsers; i++) lines.put(POISON);   // ONE pill per consumer
                return null;
            });

            // Stage 2: N parallel parsers
            AtomicInteger finishedParsers = new AtomicInteger();
            for (int p = 0; p < parsers; p++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    while (true) {
                        Msg m = lines.take();
                        if (m instanceof Poison) break;                 // swallow my pill and stop
                        if (m instanceof Line(String text)) numbers.put(Long.parseLong(text.trim()));
                    }
                    if (finishedParsers.incrementAndGet() == parsers) {    // exactly ONE parser sees this
                        numbers.put(END);                                   // last parser out poisons stage 3
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }

            // Stage 3: single aggregator
            ex.submit(() -> {
                long sum = 0;
                for (long n; (n = numbers.take()) != END; ) sum += n;
                total.set(sum);
                return null;
            });
        }                                                              // close() waits for all stages
        return total.get();
    }
Code Why new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100) Bounded queues cap memory at roughly 200 in-flight items, whatever the input size. for (i < parsers) lines.put(POISON) One pill per consumer. A single pill would stop only one parser, and the others would block in take() forever. if (m instanceof Poison) break; The consumer swallows its own pill and doesn't pass it on. (The alternative design re-queues one shared pill.) if (finishedParsers.incrementAndGet() == parsers) numbers.put(END) Fan-in termination: the aggregator must stop only after every parser has flushed its numbers. incrementAndGet is atomic and returns each value 1..N exactly once, so exactly one parser sees N. (Incrementing, then reading a LongAdder.sum() separately, could let two parsers both see N.) try (var ex = newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) 10 stage threads, all virtual. Blocking put/take just parks them. close() waits for every stage. total as an AtomicLong Written by the aggregator thread, read by the caller after close() (which also gives happens-before).

PASS

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One poison pill for N consumers: N-1 consumers hang.
  • Unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue() without a capacity: a fast reader fills the heap.
  • Sending the aggregator's END from every parser: the aggregator stops early and loses numbers still in flight.
  • Swallowing InterruptedException in a consumer loop: the pipeline can't be cancelled.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
16. Thread-safe LRU Cache
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · LinkedHashMap access order · ReentrantLock

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a cache with a fixed capacity that evicts the least-recently used entry when full. It must be safe under concurrent get/put, and should offer getOrLoad(key, loader) where a slow loader doesn't block other keys.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
• LinkedHashMap(…, accessOrder = true) keeps entries in access order: every get moves the entry to the tail. Overriding removeEldestEntry evicts the head (the LRU entry) on insertion. That gives O(1) for everything.
  • LinkedHashMap isn't thread-safe, and get() mutates it (it reorders the list). So reads need the lock too, and a ReadWriteLock would be wrong here.
  • In getOrLoad, load outside the lock, then re-check before inserting.
flowchart LR subgraph "access-ordered list (head = LRU)" direction LR K2[2] --> K3[3] --> K1[1] end G["get(1)"] -.moves 1 to tail.-> K1 P["put(4) → size 4 > 3"] -.evicts head.-> K2 sequenceDiagram participant T1 as thread 1 participant C as cache (lock) participant DB as loader (slow) participant T2 as thread 2 T1->>C: get(k) → miss (lock held briefly) T1->>DB: load(k) — NO lock held T2->>C: get(other) → served immediately DB-->>T1: value T1->>C: lock, re-check k (another thread may have loaded it), put, unlock

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final int capacity;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final LinkedHashMap<K, V> map;              // guarded by lock

    public ConcurrentLruCache(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        // accessOrder=true: every get() moves the entry to the tail → head is the least-recently used
        this.map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
            @Override
            protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
                return size() > ConcurrentLruCache.this.capacity;   // evict after insertion overflows
            }
        };
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        lock.lock();                                    // even get() needs the lock: it MUTATES the access order
        try { return map.get(key); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public void put(K key, V value) {
        lock.lock();
        try { map.put(key, value); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    /** Load outside the lock so a slow loader never blocks other keys. Two threads may load the same key. */
    public V getOrLoad(K key, Function<K, V> loader) {
        V v = get(key);
        if (v != null) return v;
        V loaded = loader.apply(key);                   // potentially slow IO, no lock held
        lock.lock();
        try {
            V raced = map.get(key);                     // someone else loaded meanwhile? keep theirs
            if (raced != null) return raced;
            map.put(key, loaded);
            return loaded;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public int size() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return map.size(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
Code Why new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) The third argument true = access order (the default is insertion order). removeEldestEntry → size() > capacity Called by put after inserting. Returning true evicts the eldest (head = LRU) entry. get() takes the lock Because it writes (it reorders the linked list). Two unsynchronized gets could corrupt the list pointers. getOrLoad: get, then loader.apply with no lock A 200 ms DB load must not freeze every other key. Holding the lock during IO is the classic mistake (and it pins virtual threads on JDK 21–23 if the lock is synchronized). Re-check raced before put Another thread may have loaded the same key meanwhile, so keep the first value for consistency. Two loads of the same key can still happen. Problem 18 shows how to make that exactly once.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
sequential LRU semantics ok: 2 evicted, 1 kept
50,000 concurrent getOrLoad calls: size=100 (never above capacity 100)
PASS

docs.title: Scaling beyond one lock
docs.text:
One lock serializes every operation. Options, roughly in the order you'd mention them in an interview:

Approach Idea Striping N independent LRU segments chosen by hash(key) % N. This gives an approximate global LRU Read buffers (Caffeine) Record accesses in lock-free ring buffers and replay them under the lock in batches, so reads almost never contend Sampled eviction (Redis) No list at all: sample a few keys and evict the oldest ConcurrentHashMap + clock/second-chance Approximate LRU with a reference bit per entry

In production, use Caffeine: W-TinyLFU gets a better hit rate than LRU, and it has async loading and stampede protection.

Why not Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap(...))?

Single operations would be safe, but compound ones (getOrLoad's check-then-put) wouldn't be, and iteration still needs manual locking.

How would you add TTL expiry?

Store (value, expiresAt). On get, treat expired entries as a miss and remove them. Optionally run a background sweeper on a scheduler.

Full source: ConcurrentLruCache.java 
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * Thread-safe LRU cache with a fixed capacity.
 * Run: java ConcurrentLruCache.java
 */
public class ConcurrentLruCache<K, V> {

    private final int capacity;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final LinkedHashMap<K, V> map;              // guarded by lock

    public ConcurrentLruCache(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        // accessOrder=true: every get() moves the entry to the tail → head is the least-recently used
        this.map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
            @Override
            protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
                return size() > ConcurrentLruCache.this.capacity;   // evict after insertion overflows
            }
        };
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        lock.lock();                                    // even get() needs the lock: it MUTATES the access order
        try { return map.get(key); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public void put(K key, V value) {
        lock.lock();
        try { map.put(key, value); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    /** Load outside the lock so a slow loader never blocks other keys. Two threads may load the same key. */
    public V getOrLoad(K key, Function<K, V> loader) {
        V v = get(key);
        if (v != null) return v;
        V loaded = loader.apply(key);                   // potentially slow IO, no lock held
        lock.lock();
        try {
            V raced = map.get(key);                     // someone else loaded meanwhile? keep theirs
            if (raced != null) return raced;
            map.put(key, loaded);
            return loaded;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public int size() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return map.size(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var lru = new ConcurrentLruCache<Integer, String>(3);
        lru.put(1, "a"); lru.put(2, "b"); lru.put(3, "c");
        lru.get(1);                                     // 1 becomes most recently used
        lru.put(4, "d");                                // evicts 2 (the LRU), not 1
        if (lru.get(2) != null || !"a".equals(lru.get(1)) || lru.size() != 3) throw new AssertionError("LRU order");
        System.out.println("sequential LRU semantics ok: 2 evicted, 1 kept");

        var cache = new ConcurrentLruCache<Integer, Integer>(100);
        try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int t = 0; t < 50_000; t++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    int k = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(500);
                    Integer v = cache.getOrLoad(k, key -> key * 2);
                    if (v != k * 2) throw new AssertionError("wrong value");
                });
            }
        }
        System.out.println("50,000 concurrent getOrLoad calls: size=" + cache.size() + " (never above capacity 100)");
        if (cache.size() != 100) throw new AssertionError();
        System.out.println("PASS");
    }
}

docs.title: 17. Token Bucket Rate Limiter
docs.text: L3 ★★☆ · lazy refill · sleep outside the lock

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a rate limiter that allows on average R requests per second with bursts of up to B. Provide a non-blocking tryAcquire() (for an API that returns 429) and a blocking acquire() (for a client that must pace itself).

docs.title: Key idea: the token bucket
docs.text:
The bucket holds at most B tokens and gains R tokens per second. Each request takes one token, and an empty bucket means wait or reject. Instead of a background thread adding tokens, compute them lazily from the elapsed time on every call:

tokens = min(B, tokens + (now - lastRefill) × R)
flowchart LR T[time passes] -->|+R tokens/s, capped at B| BK[(bucket<br/>0..B tokens)] REQ[request] --> D{tokens ≥ 1?} BK --> D D -->|yes| OK[take 1 token → allowed] D -->|no, tryAcquire| NO[reject → 429] D -->|no, acquire| W[sleep until 1 token exists → retry] xychart-beta title "Tokens over time: burst 10, 100/s, greedy clients" x-axis "ms" [0, 1, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50] y-axis "tokens" 0 --> 10 line [10, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]

The bucket starts full, so the first 10 requests pass instantly (the burst). After that, the rate settles at one token every 10 ms.

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerNano;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private double tokens;                            // guarded by lock
    private long lastRefillNanos;                     // guarded by lock

    public TokenBucketRateLimiter(long capacity, long tokensPerSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerNano = tokensPerSecond / 1_000_000_000.0;
        this.tokens = capacity;                       // start full → allows an initial burst
        this.lastRefillNanos = System.nanoTime();
    }

    /** Lazy refill: no background thread; tokens are computed from elapsed time on each call. */
    private void refill(long now) {
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastRefillNanos) * refillPerNano);
        lastRefillNanos = now;
    }

    public boolean tryAcquire() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            refill(System.nanoTime());
            if (tokens >= 1) {
                tokens -= 1;
                return true;
            }
            return false;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public void acquire() throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            long waitNanos;
            lock.lock();
            try {
                refill(System.nanoTime());
                if (tokens >= 1) {
                    tokens -= 1;
                    return;
                }
                waitNanos = (long) Math.ceil((1 - tokens) / refillPerNano);   // time until 1 token exists
            } finally {
                lock.unlock();
            }
            Thread.sleep(Duration.ofNanos(waitNanos));   // sleep OUTSIDE the lock; cheap on a virtual thread
        }
    }
Code Why double tokens Fractional tokens accumulate between calls (for example, 0.3 tokens after 3 ms at 100/s). refill(now) under the lock Read-modify-write of tokens and lastRefillNanos must be atomic. System.nanoTime() Monotonic. currentTimeMillis() can jump backwards (NTP), which would mint or burn tokens. tryAcquire() never waits For server-side admission control: reject immediately with 429 + Retry-After. acquire(): compute waitNanos, unlock, then sleep Sleeping while holding the lock would block every other caller, including tryAcquire. After waking, loop: another thread may have taken the token. Thread.sleep(Duration) Cheap on a virtual thread. 10,000 clients pacing themselves cost almost nothing.

docs.text:
tryAcquire: 50 greedy clients for 500 ms -> allowed 59 (expected ~60)
acquire: 101 permits at 200/s took 533 ms (expected ~500)
PASS

Expected values: 10 (burst) + 0.5 s × 100/s = 60. For the blocking test, 1 initial token plus 100 more at 200/s ≈ 500 ms.

docs.title: Algorithm comparison (the follow-up you'll get)
18. Single-Flight Cache (Request Coalescing)
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent · CompletableFuture

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A popular product's cache entry expires, and 1,000 requests arrive at the same moment. Without care, all 1,000 hit the database (a cache stampede or thundering herd). Make sure the expensive load runs once per key, and every concurrent caller gets that same result. Failures must not be cached.

docs.title: Key idea: cache the future, not the value
docs.text:
Put a CompletableFuture<V> into the map before loading. putIfAbsent is atomic, so exactly one thread wins and loads. Everyone else finds the winner's future and waits on it.

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant W as Thread 1 (winner) participant M as ConcurrentHashMap participant L1 as Thread 2..1000 participant DB as Loader (200 ms) W->>M: putIfAbsent(k, future₁) → null (I won) L1->>M: putIfAbsent(k, futureₙ) → future₁ (lost) L1->>L1: future₁.get() → parks W->>DB: load(k) (no map lock held) DB-->>W: value W->>W: future₁.complete(value) W-->>L1: all 999 waiters wake with the same value flowchart TD G["get(key)"] --> P{"putIfAbsent(key, myFuture)"} P -->|returned existing| WAIT["existing.get() — wait for winner"] P -->|null: I'm the winner| LOAD[loader.apply(key)] LOAD -->|ok| C[myFuture.complete(v)] LOAD -->|throws| F["map.remove(key, myFuture)<br/>myFuture.completeExceptionally(e)"]

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Function<K, V> loader;

    public SingleFlightCache(Function<K, V> loader) { this.loader = loader; }

    public V get(K key) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        CompletableFuture<V> mine = new CompletableFuture<>();
        CompletableFuture<V> existing = cache.putIfAbsent(key, mine);   // atomic: exactly one thread wins
        if (existing != null) {
            return existing.get();                                       // losers wait for the winner's result
        }
        try {                                                            // winner loads OUTSIDE any map lock
            V value = loader.apply(key);
            mine.complete(value);
            return value;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            cache.remove(key, mine);                                     // don't cache failures: allow a retry
            mine.completeExceptionally(e);                               // ...but fail everyone currently waiting
            throw e;
        }
    }
Code Why new CompletableFuture<>() before loading A placeholder that other threads can wait on immediately. cache.putIfAbsent(key, mine) Atomic claim. Exactly one thread gets null back. Losers: existing.get() They park (cheaply, on virtual threads) until the winner completes the future. complete happens-before get returns. Winner loads outside any lock Unlike computeIfAbsent(key, k -> load(k)), which runs the loader while holding the map's bin lock. That blocks unrelated keys in the same bin, and a recursive load throws IllegalStateException. On failure: cache.remove(key, mine) Don't cache the failure, so the next caller can retry. The 2-arg remove only removes our future, never a newer one. mine.completeExceptionally(e) Callers already waiting must not hang: they get the same exception.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
1,000 concurrent gets on 3 keys: loader calls=3, correct=1000, took 220 ms (one 200 ms load per key, in parallel)
failed load not cached: retry succeeded
PASS

Without coalescing, that would be 1,000 database calls instead of 3.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• computeIfAbsent(key, k -> slowLoad(k)) on a ConcurrentHashMap: the slow IO runs inside the bin lock.
  • Caching exceptional futures forever: one DB hiccup poisons the key permanently.
  • Map<K,V> plus synchronized on the whole load: correct, but it serializes all keys.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
19. Concurrent Web Crawler
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · virtual threads · Phaser · Semaphore · concurrent set · LeetCode 1242

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given a start URL and a fetch(url) → links function (slow, blocking), crawl every page on the same host. Fetch concurrently, never fetch a page twice, limit the total number of in-flight requests (and the number per host), and return when the crawl is complete.

The hard parts are knowing when you're done (new work is discovered while you run) and doing dedup atomically.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: flowchart LR     S[start URL] --> SUB{visited.add&#40;url&#41;?}     SUB -->|false: already seen| DROP[skip]     SUB -->|true| REG[phaser.register&#40;&#41;]     REG --> VT[new virtual thread]     VT --> G{{global Semaphore 64}}     G --> H{{per-host Semaphore}}     H --> F[fetch&#40;url&#41; — blocking IO]     F --> LINKS[for each same-host link → submit]     LINKS --> SUB     F --> DONE[phaser.arriveAndDeregister&#40;&#41;] sequenceDiagram     participant C as caller (party 1)     participant P as Phaser     participant V1 as VT page 0     participant V2 as VT page 7     C->>P: new Phaser(1)     C->>P: register (page 0) → parties=2     C->>P: arriveAndAwaitAdvance() … waits     V1->>P: register (page 7) → parties=3     V1->>P: arriveAndDeregister (page 0 done) → parties=2     V2->>P: arriveAndDeregister (page 7 done) → parties=1     P-->>C: all parties arrived → advance → crawl complete

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
private final Fetcher fetcher;
    private final Set<String> visited = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();      // atomic "claim this URL"
    private final Semaphore globalInFlight;                                 // protects us and the network
    private final Map<String, Semaphore> perHost = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final int perHostLimit;
    private final AtomicInteger peakInFlight = new AtomicInteger();
    private final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger();

    ConcurrentWebCrawler(Fetcher fetcher, int maxInFlight, int perHostLimit) {
        this.fetcher = fetcher;
        this.globalInFlight = new Semaphore(maxInFlight);
        this.perHostLimit = perHostLimit;
    }

    Set<String> crawl(String startUrl) {
        Phaser pending = new Phaser(1);                    // party #1 = the caller
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            submit(startUrl, ex, pending);
            pending.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();               // returns when every registered page has arrived
        }
        return visited;
    }

    private void submit(String url, ExecutorService ex, Phaser pending) {
        if (!visited.add(url)) return;                     // someone else already claimed it
        pending.register();                                // one more page in flight (BEFORE submitting!)
        ex.submit(() -> {
            try {
                for (String link : fetch(url)) {
                    if (host(link).equals(host(url))) submit(link, ex, pending);   // stay on the start host
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            } finally {
                pending.arriveAndDeregister();             // this page is done
            }
        });
    }

    private List<String> fetch(String url) throws InterruptedException {
        Semaphore host = perHost.computeIfAbsent(host(url), h -> new Semaphore(perHostLimit));
        globalInFlight.acquire();
        try {
            host.acquire();
            try {
                peakInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max);
                return fetcher.links(url);                 // blocking IO: the virtual thread parks
            } finally {
                inFlight.decrementAndGet();
                host.release();
            }
        } finally {
            globalInFlight.release();
        }
    }

    static String host(String url) { return url.split("/")[2]; }
Code Why ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() + visited.add(url) add returns true for exactly one thread, so it's an atomic claim. "contains then add" would be a race that fetches pages twice. new Phaser(1) Party #1 is the caller. Each in-flight page is one more party. pending.register() before ex.submit(...) Crucial ordering. If the task were submitted first, it could finish and deregister before being registered, and the phase could advance early, so you'd return with work still running. arriveAndDeregister() in finally Every page arrives exactly once, even when fetch throws. Without the finally, a failure would hang the crawl. arriveAndAwaitAdvance() by the caller Returns when all registered parties have arrived: the dynamic version of CountDownLatch, which doesn't need to know the count up front. Global then per-host Semaphore The global limit protects us (sockets, memory). The per-host limit is politeness toward each site. Release in reverse order in finally. One virtual thread per page Fetching is blocking IO, so a VT parks for free. 2,000 pages means 2,000 cheap threads, with the concurrency limited by the semaphore.

Phaser limit

A Phaser supports up to 65,535 registered parties at once. For bigger crawls use a tiered phaser tree, or an AtomicInteger in-flight counter + CountDownLatch(1) released when the counter reaches zero.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
crawled 1952 pages in 361 ms (sequential would be ~19520 ms), peak in-flight=64 (limit 64)
PASS

The test computes the expected reachable set with a plain sequential DFS and checks that the crawler found exactly that set, without exceeding the in-flight limit.

docs.title: Java 8 version: what was harder
docs.text:
• A fixed ThreadPoolExecutor(64) had to be both the concurrency limit and the thread budget.
  • Completion detection needed an AtomicInteger pending + CountDownLatch, or a CompletableFuture graph.
  • Blocking fetches inside a 64-thread pool limited throughput to 64 / latency. That's the same here, but here the semaphore can be raised to 1,000 without 1,000 OS threads.
How would you add a depth limit or URL priority?

Carry depth with each URL and skip when it's above the limit. For priority, put URLs into a PriorityBlockingQueue frontier consumed by N worker VTs instead of spawning a VT per URL.

Distributed crawl?

Partition URLs by host hash across workers (which keeps politeness local), keep a shared seen-set (a Bloom filter + store), and use a durable frontier (Kafka or a DB) with checkpointing.

Full source: ConcurrentWebCrawler.java 
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Phaser;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

/**
 * LeetCode 1242 (web crawler multithreaded), production-flavoured: one virtual thread per page, a global limit on
 * in-flight fetches, a per-host politeness limit, a concurrent visited set, and a Phaser to know when we're done.
 * The "internet" is a simulated link graph where each fetch sleeps 5-15 ms.
 * Run: java ConcurrentWebCrawler.java
 */
public class ConcurrentWebCrawler {

    interface Fetcher { List<String> links(String url) throws InterruptedException; }

    private final Fetcher fetcher;
    private final Set<String> visited = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();      // atomic "claim this URL"
    private final Semaphore globalInFlight;                                 // protects us and the network
    private final Map<String, Semaphore> perHost = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final int perHostLimit;
    private final AtomicInteger peakInFlight = new AtomicInteger();
    private final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger();

    ConcurrentWebCrawler(Fetcher fetcher, int maxInFlight, int perHostLimit) {
        this.fetcher = fetcher;
        this.globalInFlight = new Semaphore(maxInFlight);
        this.perHostLimit = perHostLimit;
    }

    Set<String> crawl(String startUrl) {
        Phaser pending = new Phaser(1);                    // party #1 = the caller
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            submit(startUrl, ex, pending);
            pending.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();               // returns when every registered page has arrived
        }
        return visited;
    }

    private void submit(String url, ExecutorService ex, Phaser pending) {
        if (!visited.add(url)) return;                     // someone else already claimed it
        pending.register();                                // one more page in flight (BEFORE submitting!)
        ex.submit(() -> {
            try {
                for (String link : fetch(url)) {
                    if (host(link).equals(host(url))) submit(link, ex, pending);   // stay on the start host
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            } finally {
                pending.arriveAndDeregister();             // this page is done
            }
        });
    }

    private List<String> fetch(String url) throws InterruptedException {
        Semaphore host = perHost.computeIfAbsent(host(url), h -> new Semaphore(perHostLimit));
        globalInFlight.acquire();
        try {
            host.acquire();
            try {
                peakInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max);
                return fetcher.links(url);                 // blocking IO: the virtual thread parks
            } finally {
                inFlight.decrementAndGet();
                host.release();
            }
        } finally {
            globalInFlight.release();
        }
    }

    static String host(String url) { return url.split("/")[2]; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int pages = 2_000;
        Random rnd = new Random(42);
        Map<String, List<String>> graph = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < pages; i++) {
            List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) out.add("http://shop.test/p/" + rnd.nextInt(pages));
            out.add("http://other.test/p/" + i);           // off-host links must be ignored
            graph.put("http://shop.test/p/" + i, out);
        }
        Fetcher fetcher = url -> {
            Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(5 + Math.floorMod(url.hashCode(), 11)));   // 5-15 ms of "network"
            return graph.getOrDefault(url, List.of());
        };

        // expected = everything reachable from page 0 (plain BFS)
        Set<String> expected = new HashSet<>();
        var stack = new ArrayList<String>(List.of("http://shop.test/p/0"));
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            String u = stack.removeLast();
            if (!expected.add(u)) continue;
            for (String l : graph.getOrDefault(u, List.of())) if (host(l).equals("shop.test")) stack.add(l);
        }

        var crawler = new ConcurrentWebCrawler(fetcher, 64, 64);
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        Set<String> found = crawler.crawl("http://shop.test/p/0");
        long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
        System.out.printf("crawled %d pages in %d ms (sequential would be ~%d ms), peak in-flight=%d (limit 64)%n",
                found.size(), ms, found.size() * 10, crawler.peakInFlight.get());
        if (!found.equals(expected) || crawler.peakInFlight.get() > 64) throw new AssertionError();
        System.out.println("PASS");
    }
}

docs.title: 20. Parallel Merge Sort (Fork/Join)
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · RecursiveAction · work stealing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Sort a large int[] using all CPU cores. Explain how the work is split and how threads balance the load.

This is the canonical CPU-bound problem, the opposite of the IO-bound problems where virtual threads shine. The right tool is the Fork/Join framework (platform threads ≈ cores, work stealing).

docs.title: Key idea: divide and conquer
docs.text: flowchart TD     A["sort [0, 20M)"] --> B["sort [0, 10M)"]     A --> C["sort [10M, 20M)"]     B --> D["[0, 5M)"] & E["[5M, 10M)"]     C --> F["[10M, 15M)"] & G["[15M, 20M)"]     D & E --> M1((merge))     F & G --> M2((merge))     M1 & M2 --> M3((merge))     D -.->|... until ≤ 8192 elements| LEAF[Arrays.sort leaf]

docs.title: Work stealing
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph W1[worker 1 deque] direction LR a1[task L-L] --- a2[task L-R] --- a3[task R] end subgraph W2[worker 2 — idle] direction LR b0[empty] end W1 -- "owner pops newest (LIFO)" --> a1 W2 -- "thief steals oldest = biggest (FIFO)" --> a3

Each worker pushes subtasks onto its own deque and works on the newest one (cache-friendly). Idle workers steal the oldest task from another worker, which is the biggest chunk, so a single steal hands over a lot of work.

docs.title: Code walkthrough
docs.text:
static final class SortTask extends RecursiveAction {
        private static final int SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD = 8_192;    // below this, forking costs more than it saves
        private final int[] a;
        private final int[] tmp;                                  // shared scratch buffer, disjoint ranges per task
        private final int lo, hi;                                 // sorts a[lo, hi)

        SortTask(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {
            this.a = a; this.tmp = tmp; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi;
        }

        @Override
        protected void compute() {
            if (hi - lo <= SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD) {
                Arrays.sort(a, lo, hi);                           // leaf: sequential sort
                return;
            }
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;                            // >>> avoids int overflow for huge arrays
            invokeAll(new SortTask(a, tmp, lo, mid),              // fork left, run right, join both
                      new SortTask(a, tmp, mid, hi));
            merge(mid);                                           // both halves are sorted now
        }

        private void merge(int mid) {
            System.arraycopy(a, lo, tmp, lo, hi - lo);
            int i = lo, j = mid, k = lo;
            while (i < mid && j < hi) a[k++] = tmp[i] <= tmp[j] ? tmp[i++] : tmp[j++];   // <= keeps it stable
            while (i < mid) a[k++] = tmp[i++];
            while (j < hi) a[k++] = tmp[j++];
        }
    }

    static void parallelSort(int[] a) {
        ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SortTask(a, new int[a.length], 0, a.length));
    }
Code Why extends RecursiveAction A Fork/Join task with no result (it sorts in place). Use RecursiveTask<T> for a result, such as a sum. SEQUENTIAL_THRESHOLD = 8_192 Below this size, task overhead beats the parallel gain. The value is tuned empirically; 1k–10k elements is typical. int[] tmp shared One scratch buffer allocated once. Tasks touch disjoint ranges, so there's no data race and no locking. (lo + hi) >>> 1 Unsigned shift avoids overflow when lo + hi > Integer.MAX_VALUE. That's a famous bug in Arrays.binarySearch, fixed in 2006. invokeAll(left, right) Forks one half and computes the other in the current thread, then joins both. Better than left.fork(); right.fork(); join both, which wastes the current thread. merge(mid) after invokeAll join gives happens-before: both halves' writes are visible here. tmp[i] <= tmp[j] <= keeps equal elements in their original order, so the sort is stable.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
20M ints on 4 cores: sequential merge sort 3149 ms, fork/join 1332 ms (2.4x)
PASS

The speed-up is less than the 4× core count because the final merges are sequential (Amdahl's law), memory bandwidth is limited, and there's JIT warm-up. In real code, Arrays.parallelSort(a) does all of this for you.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
21. Best-Price Fan-out with a Deadline
docs.text: L3 ★★☆ · CompletableFuture (Java 8) vs virtual threads + invokeAll (Java 21)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Ask N vendors for a price in parallel. Return the cheapest quote that arrives within 300 ms. Ignore vendors that fail or are too slow. The total response time must be about 300 ms, regardless of how slow the slowest vendor is.

This is the most "real" interview question here: it's every price comparison, search aggregator, and BFF.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     autonumber     participant API as caller     participant A as fresh-mart (80 ms, ₹52)     participant B as green-grocer (120 ms, ₹47)     participant C as cheap-but-slow (2000 ms, ₹39)     participant D as broken (30 ms, fails)     participant E as daily-needs (60 ms, ₹49)     par fan-out at t=0       API->>A: quote       API->>B: quote       API->>C: quote       API->>D: quote       API->>E: quote     end     D--xAPI: t=30 exception → ignore     E-->>API: t=60 ₹49     A-->>API: t=80 ₹52     B-->>API: t=120 ₹47     Note over API,C: t=300 deadline → C cancelled     API->>API: min(₹49, ₹52, ₹47) = green-grocer ₹47

docs.title: Java 8: CompletableFuture
docs.text:
static Optional<Quote> bestJava8(List<Vendor> vendors, Duration deadline, ExecutorService pool) {
        List<CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>>> futures = vendors.stream()
                .map(v -> CompletableFuture
                        .supplyAsync(() -> {
                            try { return Optional.of(v.quote()); }
                            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return Optional.<Quote>empty(); }
                        }, pool)
                        .completeOnTimeout(Optional.empty(), deadline.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // too slow
                        .exceptionally(ex -> Optional.empty()))                                         // failed
                .toList();
        return CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new))
                .thenApply(ignored -> futures.stream()
                        .map(CompletableFuture::join)                 // all done: join() won't block
                        .flatMap(Optional::stream)
                        .min(Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceMinor)))
                .join();
        // Note: completeOnTimeout does NOT stop the slow vendor call; its pool thread stays busy.
    }
Code Why supplyAsync(..., pool) Always pass your own executor. The default common pool is meant for CPU work, and blocking calls starve it. Wrap the result in Optional Turns "no quote" into a value, so failures and timeouts become Optional.empty() instead of exceptions. .completeOnTimeout(Optional.empty(), 300ms) Java 9+. After 300 ms the future completes with empty. But the vendor call keeps running and keeps a pool thread busy. .exceptionally(ex -> Optional.empty()) A failed vendor doesn't fail the whole result. allOf(...).thenApply(... join ...) allOf returns CompletableFuture<Void>, so you collect the results yourself. join() can't block there because everything is already complete.

docs.title: Java 21: virtual threads + invokeAll
docs.text:
static Optional<Quote> bestJava21(List<Vendor> vendors, Duration deadline) throws InterruptedException {
        try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Callable<Quote>> calls = vendors.stream().<Callable<Quote>>map(v -> v::quote).toList();
            List<Future<Quote>> results = ex.invokeAll(calls, deadline.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            // invokeAll returns when all finished OR the deadline passed; unfinished ones are CANCELLED (interrupted)
            return results.stream()
                    .filter(f -> f.state() == Future.State.SUCCESS)   // skip FAILED and CANCELLED
                    .map(Future::resultNow)
                    .min(Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceMinor));
        }
    }
Code Why newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() One cheap thread per vendor call. Plain blocking code, no callbacks. invokeAll(calls, 300, ms) Returns when all tasks finish or the deadline passes. Unfinished tasks are cancelled (interrupted), so the slow vendor's thread actually stops. f.state() == SUCCESS Future.State (Java 19+) cleanly separates SUCCESS / FAILED / CANCELLED. resultNow() Java 19+: get the result of a completed future without checked exceptions. try-with-resources close() guarantees no vendor call outlives the method.

docs.title: Side by side
