docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Java 8 : Quote[vendor=green-grocer, priceMinor=4700] in 312 ms
Java 21: Quote[vendor=green-grocer, priceMinor=4700] in 303 ms
PASS

The cheapest vendor (₹39) missed the deadline, and the ₹10 one failed. Both versions correctly pick ₹47 in about 300 ms.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
Foundations
docs.text:
L1 L2

Everything else in this playbook, including virtual threads, builds on these six ideas:

  1. Thread: an independent path of execution that shares heap memory with other threads.
  2. Race condition: the result depends on how threads interleave.
  3. Visibility: one thread's writes are not automatically seen by another thread (JMM).
  4. Atomicity: a compound action (check-then-act, read-modify-write) must look indivisible.
  5. Ordering: compilers and CPUs reorder instructions unless a happens-before edge forbids it.
  6. Liveness: correct code can still get stuck (deadlock), spin uselessly (livelock), or never run (starvation).
flowchart LR subgraph Problems R[Race condition] --- V[Visibility] V --- O[Reordering] O --- L[Liveness] end subgraph Tools S[synchronized] --- VO[volatile] VO --- LK[Locks] LK --- AT[Atomics / VarHandle] AT --- IM[Immutability] IM --- CF[Confinement] end R -->|fixed by| S & LK & AT V -->|fixed by| VO & S & AT O -->|fixed by| VO & S L -->|avoided by| LK & CF

docs.title: Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
docs.text:
A single CPU instruction (LOCK CMPXCHG on x86, LDXR/STXR or CAS on ARM) that does this atomically: "if memory == expected, set it to newValue and report success". It is the basis of every lock-free algorithm.

AtomicLong seq = new AtomicLong();
long next = seq.incrementAndGet();                       // CAS loop inside
seq.updateAndGet(v -> Math.max(v, observed));            // functional update (Java 8)
seq.accumulateAndGet(5, Long::sum);

docs.title: The atomic family
docs.text: Class Use AtomicInteger/Long/Boolean Single counters and flags AtomicReference<V> Swap immutable snapshots (copy-on-write state) AtomicStampedReference Solves the ABA problem with a version stamp AtomicIntegerArray / AtomicLongArray Per-slot atomics AtomicXxxFieldUpdater CAS on a volatile field without allocating a wrapper per object (memory-efficient) LongAdder / LongAccumulator (8) High-contention counters: per-cell striping, then sum()

docs.title: AtomicLong vs LongAdder
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph AtomicLong T1a[T1] --> C[(single cell)] T2a[T2] --> C T3a[T3] --> C end subgraph LongAdder T1b[T1] --> c1[(cell 1)] T2b[T2] --> c2[(cell 2)] T3b[T3] --> c3[(cell 3)] c1 & c2 & c3 --> S[sum] end
  • AtomicLong: exact value on every read. CAS failures spike under contention.
  • LongAdder: writes scale with core count. sum() is not an atomic snapshot. Use it for metrics, not for IDs.

docs.title: Immutable snapshot pattern with AtomicReference
docs.text:
record RoutingTable(Map<String, URI> routes) {}

private final AtomicReference<RoutingTable> table =
        new AtomicReference<>(new RoutingTable(Map.of()));

void addRoute(String key, URI uri) {
    table.updateAndGet(old -> {
        var copy = new HashMap<>(old.routes());
        copy.put(key, uri);
        return new RoutingTable(Map.copyOf(copy));
    });
}
URI lookup(String key) { return table.get().routes().get(key); }   // lock-free reads

updateAndGet may call your function more than once

Keep the function pure. Don't log, send emails, or call IO inside it.

docs.title: VarHandle (Java 9+): the supported Unsafe
docs.text:
class Node {
    volatile Node next;
    private static final VarHandle NEXT;
    static {
        try {
            NEXT = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Node.class, "next", Node.class);
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); }
    }
    boolean casNext(Node expect, Node update) { return NEXT.compareAndSet(this, expect, update); }
    void lazySetNext(Node n) { NEXT.setRelease(this, n); }     // release store (cheaper than volatile)
}

Access modes: get/set (plain), getOpaque/setOpaque, getAcquire/setRelease, getVolatile/setVolatile, compareAndSet, compareAndExchange, weakCompareAndSet* (may fail spuriously, which makes it cheaper in loops), getAndAdd, getAndBitwiseOr, and so on. Fences: VarHandle.acquireFence(), releaseFence(), fullFence().

docs.title: ABA problem
docs.text: Thread 1 reads A. Thread 2 changes A→B→A. Thread 1's CAS(A→C) succeeds even though the state changed underneath it. This matters for pointer-based lock-free stacks that reuse nodes. Fixes: AtomicStampedReference, or never reuse nodes (the GC makes this mostly safe in Java).

docs.title: Java Memory Model (JMM)
docs.text:
L2 L3

The JMM (JSR-133, Java 5; JLS §17) defines which values a read may observe. Without it, the compiler (JIT), the CPU (store buffers, out-of-order execution), and caches are all free to reorder or delay writes.

docs.title: The visibility bug everyone hits once
docs.text:
class Worker {
    private boolean running = true;           // BUG: not volatile
    void stop() { running = false; }
    void loop() { while (running) { /* busy */ } } // JIT may hoist the read → infinite loop
}

Fix: private volatile boolean running = true;. Alternatively, use an AtomicBoolean or check Thread.interrupted().

docs.title: Happens-before rules (memorize these)
docs.text:
If action A happens-before B, then A's effects are visible to B and A is ordered before B.

Rule Edge Program order Each action in a thread → every later action in that thread Monitor lock unlock(m) → every subsequent lock(m) Volatile Write to v → every subsequent read of v Thread start t.start() → every action in t Thread join Every action in t → return from t.join() Interrupt t.interrupt() → t detects the interrupt Finalizer Constructor end → finalize() start final fields Constructor end (with no this escape) → any thread that sees the reference sees initialized finals j.u.c. Put into BlockingQueue → take; submit → task runs; task completes → Future.get returns; countDown → await returns Transitivity A → B and B → C ⇒ A → C sequenceDiagram participant T1 as Thread 1 participant M as Main memory participant T2 as Thread 2 T1->>T1: data = 42 (plain write) T1->>M: ready = true (volatile write — release) Note over T1,M: All writes before the volatile write<br/>are published with it T2->>M: read ready (volatile read — acquire) M-->>T2: true T2->>T2: read data → guaranteed 42

This is called safe publication through a volatile flag. It is the same mechanism ConcurrentHashMap.put/get, BlockingQueue, and CompletableFuture.complete/join give you for free.

docs.title: Safe publication idioms
docs.text:
1. Initialize from a static initializer (static final Foo FOO = new Foo();).
  2. Store the reference in a volatile field or an AtomicReference.
  3. Store it in a final field of a properly constructed object.
  4. Store it in a field guarded by a lock.
  5. Put it into a thread-safe collection.

docs.title: Double-checked locking: then and now
volatile is NOT atomicity
docs.text: volatile int x; x++; is still a read-modify-write race. volatile gives visibility and ordering, never mutual exclusion. Use AtomicInteger or a lock instead.

docs.title: Memory ordering modes (VarHandle, Java 9+)
docs.text: Mode Guarantees Use Plain None across threads Thread-confined data Opaque Coherence per variable, no reordering with itself Progress flags, statistics Acquire/Release One-way ordering fences Producer/consumer handoff (cheaper than volatile on ARM) Volatile Sequential consistency Default when in doubt

docs.title: Word tearing and long/double
docs.text: Non-volatile long and double writes may be split into two 32-bit writes on some JVMs (JLS §17.7). Declare them volatile or use atomics when sharing them. In practice 64-bit HotSpot doesn't tear, but the spec allows it.

docs.title: Liveness Hazards
docs.text:
L2 L3

Hazard Symptom Classic cause Fix Deadlock Threads stuck forever, CPU ~0% Lock-ordering cycle Global lock order, tryLock with timeout, single lock Livelock CPU high, no progress Threads politely back off in lockstep Randomized backoff Starvation Some threads never run Unfair locks, priority, greedy readers Fair locks, bounded queues Thread-pool deadlock Pool full of tasks waiting on tasks queued behind them Nested submit().get() on the same bounded pool Separate pools, or virtual threads Carrier starvation (VT) VTs runnable but not running Pinned VTs (JDK 21–23) or CPU-bound VTs that never yield JEP 491 (JDK 24), move CPU work to a platform pool Lost wakeup Waiter sleeps forever notify before wait, or if instead of while Condition loop, BlockingQueue

docs.title: Deadlock: anatomy
Thread-pool-induced deadlock (very common in Java 8 code)
docs.text:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
Future<String> outer = pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<String> inner = pool.submit(() -> "inner");  // queued behind the outer tasks
    return inner.get();                                 // all 2 threads wait here → deadlock
});

This kind of deadlock happens with CompletableFuture.join() on the common pool and with parallel streams calling blocking code. Virtual threads remove this class of bug, because there is no fixed thread count to exhaust.

docs.title: Livelock example and fix
docs.text:
// Two threads each try to acquire both locks, release on failure, and retry immediately → may loop forever
while (true) {
    if (a.tryLock()) {
        try {
            if (b.tryLock()) { try { work(); return; } finally { b.unlock(); } }
        } finally { a.unlock(); }
    }
    Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 10)); // randomized backoff breaks the symmetry
}

docs.title: ReentrantLock vs synchronized
Condition: separate wait sets
docs.text:
public class BoundedQueue<T> {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
    private final ArrayDeque<T> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int cap;

    public BoundedQueue(int cap) { this.cap = cap; }

    public void put(T t) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (q.size() == cap) notFull.await();
            q.addLast(t);
            notEmpty.signal();               // wake ONE consumer, not every thread
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (q.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await();
            T t = q.removeFirst();
            notFull.signal();
            return t;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

docs.title: ReentrantReadWriteLock
docs.text: Many readers or one writer. Good when reads are long and frequent and writes are rare. Watch for writer starvation in non-fair mode. A thread can downgrade a write lock to a read lock, but it can't upgrade a read lock to a write lock. Upgrading deadlocks.

docs.title: StampedLock (Java 8): optimistic reads
docs.text:
public class Point {
    private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
    private double x, y;

    public void move(double dx, double dy) {
        long stamp = sl.writeLock();
        try { x += dx; y += dy; } finally { sl.unlockWrite(stamp); }
    }

    public double distanceFromOrigin() {
        long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();       // no lock taken, just a version stamp
        double cx = x, cy = y;
        if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {                 // a writer intervened: fall back to a real read lock
            stamp = sl.readLock();
            try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
        }
        return Math.hypot(cx, cy);
    }
}

StampedLock is NOT reentrant and has no Conditions

Re-acquiring it from the same thread deadlocks. Use it for small, leaf-level, read-mostly state.

docs.title: Which lock? (decision table)
docs.text: Situation Choose Simple critical section, JDK 24+ synchronized Simple critical section with blocking IO inside, JDK 21–23 on VTs ReentrantLock Need timeout, tryLock, or interruptible acquire ReentrantLock Multiple wait conditions ReentrantLock + Condition Read-heavy, tiny critical section StampedLock (optimistic) Read-heavy map ConcurrentHashMap (no lock at all) Limit N concurrent holders Semaphore Cross-JVM exclusion DB row lock, Redis/ZooKeeper lease (Distributed concurrency)

docs.title: Intrinsic locks (monitors)
docs.text:
Every object has a monitor. synchronized gives you:

  • Mutual exclusion: only one thread at a time is inside the block for a given monitor.
  • Visibility: releasing the monitor happens-before the next acquisition.
  • Reentrancy: the owning thread can re-enter the block.
public class BankAccount {
    private long balancePaise;                     // guarded by this

    public synchronized void deposit(long paise) { balancePaise += paise; }

    public void transfer(BankAccount to, long paise) {
        // lock ordering prevents deadlock: always lock the lower id first
        BankAccount first  = System.identityHashCode(this) < System.identityHashCode(to) ? this : to;
        BankAccount second = first == this ? to : this;
        synchronized (first) {
            synchronized (second) {
                if (balancePaise < paise) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
                balancePaise -= paise;
                to.balancePaise += paise;
            }
        }
    }
}

Lock on a private final object

synchronized(this) and synchronized methods expose your lock to any caller. In libraries, use private final Object lock = new Object();. Never lock on String literals, boxed Integers, or value-based classes. They are shared or interned, so unrelated code can end up holding your lock.

docs.title: How HotSpot implements it (L3)
docs.text:
State When Cost ~~Biased~~ Removed in JDK 18 (JEP 374) – Thin / lightweight Uncontended: CAS on the object header (JDK 21+ has a new "lightweight locking" mode) ~20 ns Inflated (fat) monitor Contended or wait() called: an ObjectMonitor with an entry list Parks threads in the OS

Virtual threads and synchronized:

  • JDK 21–23: a VT that blocks inside synchronized (on IO, sleep, wait, or contended monitor entry) pins its carrier. The carrier OS thread is blocked too.
  • JDK 24+ (JEP 491): monitors are owned by the virtual thread, not the carrier. The VT unmounts when it blocks in synchronized or in Object.wait(). Pinning remains only for native frames (JNI, Unsafe upcalls) and class initializers. See Pinning.

docs.title: wait / notify: guarded blocks
docs.text:
public class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object[] items;
    private int head, tail, count;

    public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) { items = new Object[capacity]; }

    public synchronized void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        while (count == items.length) wait();     // ALWAYS a while loop (spurious wakeups)
        items[tail] = item; tail = (tail + 1) % items.length; count++;
        notifyAll();                              // notifyAll: producers and consumers share one wait set
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public synchronized T take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (count == 0) wait();
        T item = (T) items[head]; items[head] = null; head = (head + 1) % items.length; count--;
        notifyAll();
        return item;
    }
}

Rules:

  1. Call wait/notify only while holding the monitor. Otherwise you get IllegalMonitorStateException.
  2. Always wait in a while loop that re-checks the condition.
  3. Prefer notifyAll() unless you can prove every waiter waits for the same condition.
  4. In new code, prefer BlockingQueue or Lock + Condition (Locks), which gives separate wait sets.

docs.title: Old vs new: a thread-safe counter
Process vs thread
docs.text: Process Platform thread Virtual thread (21+) Memory Own address space Shares heap; own stack (~1 MB reserved by default, -Xss) Shares heap; stack is a heap object that grows as needed (bytes to KB) Scheduled by OS OS kernel JVM (ForkJoinPool of carriers) Creation cost ms ~50–100 µs, plus a syscall ~1 µs, no syscall Practical max per JVM – Thousands Millions Context switch Expensive ~1–10 µs (kernel) Cheap (stack copy in user space)

docs.title: Creating threads: then and now
Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> NEW: new Thread() NEW --> RUNNABLE: start() RUNNABLE --> BLOCKED: waiting for monitor (synchronized) BLOCKED --> RUNNABLE: monitor acquired RUNNABLE --> WAITING: wait() / join() / park() WAITING --> RUNNABLE: notify() / unpark() / target ends RUNNABLE --> TIMED_WAITING: sleep(ms) / wait(ms) / parkNanos TIMED_WAITING --> RUNNABLE: timeout / notify RUNNABLE --> TERMINATED: run() returns or throws TERMINATED --> [*]

RUNNABLE ≠ running

RUNNABLE means eligible to run. The thread may be on a CPU or waiting for one. A thread blocked in a socket read also shows as RUNNABLE in Java, because the JVM can't see kernel waits. For a virtual thread blocked on a socket, the VT is unmounted and shows as WAITING, and no carrier is blocked.

docs.title: Interruption: the cooperative cancellation protocol
docs.text:
Thread worker = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        try {
            var job = queue.take();           // blocking call: throws InterruptedException
            process(job);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore the flag, then exit
            return;
        }
    }
});
worker.interrupt();   // request cancellation

Rules:

  • Never swallow InterruptedException. Restore the flag or rethrow it.
  • Thread.stop() is gone (it throws UnsupportedOperationException since Java 20). Cancellation is always cooperative.
  • Future.cancel(true) interrupts the thread running the task. StructuredTaskScope interrupts sibling subtasks for you.

docs.title: Daemon vs user threads
docs.text: The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain. Virtual threads are always daemon threads, so a main method that starts virtual threads and returns lets the JVM exit immediately. Call join() on them, or close an executor.

docs.title: Uncaught exceptions
docs.text:
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) ->
        log.error("Thread {} died", t.getName(), e));
// With executors: exceptions from submit() are captured in the Future. Call get() or you will never see them.
// execute() lets them reach the handler.

docs.title: Example: the classic race condition
docs.text:
class Counter { int value; void inc() { value++; } } // read → add → write: 3 steps

var c = new Counter();
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) ex.submit(c::inc);
}
System.out.println(c.value); // often < 10000: lost updates

Three ways to fix it: synchronized void inc(), AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), or LongAdder.increment(). See Atomics for when each is right.

docs.title: Decision tree: which tool?
docs.text: flowchart TD     Q{What kind of work?}     Q -->|Blocking IO: HTTP, JDBC, files| VT[Virtual threads<br/>newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor]     Q -->|CPU-bound, divisible| FJ[ForkJoinPool / parallel stream<br/>size ≈ #cores]     Q -->|CPU-bound, independent tasks| FP[Fixed platform pool<br/>size ≈ #cores]     Q -->|Periodic / delayed| SCH[ScheduledExecutorService<br/>or Spring @Scheduled]     Q -->|Streaming with backpressure| RX[Reactive / Flow API<br/>or VT + BlockingQueue]     VT --> L{Need to limit calls to a downstream?}     L -->|Yes| SEM[Semaphore bulkhead]     L -->|No| OK[Done]     VT --> F{Fan-out to N calls?}     F -->|Yes| SC[StructuredTaskScope<br/>or invokeAll]

docs.title: Sharing state: choose in this order
docs.text:
1. Don't share. Use confinement or immutable records.
  2. Use a thread-safe class (ConcurrentHashMap, LongAdder, BlockingQueue).
  3. Use atomics for single-variable state.
  4. Use synchronized for simple compound state (pinning-free from Java 24).
  5. Use ReentrantLock / StampedLock when you need tryLock, timeouts, fairness, interruptible waits, or optimistic reads.

docs.title: Ten rules
docs.text:
1. Never pool virtual threads. Create one per task.
  2. Limit resources (connections, rate) with semaphores or pools of resources, not pools of threads.
  3. Always set timeouts on IO. A virtual thread that blocks forever is still a leak.
  4. On Java 21–23, do not block (IO or sleep) inside synchronized on a hot path. Use ReentrantLock.
  5. Don't cache expensive objects in ThreadLocal when running on virtual threads. There are millions of threads, so you get millions of copies.
  6. Keep CPU-heavy work on a bounded platform pool. Virtual threads don't make CPU faster.
  7. Prefer try (var executor = ...) so executors are always closed.
  8. Handle InterruptedException: restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() or propagate it.
  9. Name your threads (Thread.ofVirtual().name("order-", 0)). Thread dumps are unreadable otherwise.
  10. Measure with JFR (jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed) before and after.

docs.title: Key JVM flags
docs.text: Flag Purpose -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=N Number of carrier threads (default: #cores) -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize=N Max carriers when compensating for pinning (default 256) -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full Print stack when a VT pins (JDK 21–23 only, removed in 24) -XX:+UseZGC (-XX:+ZGenerational on 21) Low-pause GC, a good fit for many VT stacks --enable-preview Required for structured concurrency (all versions), scoped values (21–24) jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json out.json Thread dump that includes virtual threads jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr Start a flight recording

docs.title: Spring Boot (3.2+ / 4.x)
docs.text:
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true      # Tomcat/Jetty request threads, @Async, @Scheduled, Kafka/Rabbit listeners
  main:
    keep-alive: true     # virtual threads are daemon threads; keep the JVM alive for schedulers

docs.title: Java 8 → 25: Concurrency Feature Evolution
docs.text:
L2 L3

This is the complete list of concurrency-relevant changes between the Java 8 baseline and today. Bold marks the ones that change how you design code; the rest are tuning or convenience.

docs.title: Release-by-release
docs.text:
Release Type Concurrency feature Why it matters 8 (2014) LTS CompletableFuture / CompletionStage Composable async pipelines with no callback hell 8 Parallel streams (on the common ForkJoinPool) Data parallelism in one call; easy to misuse 8 StampedLock Optimistic reads, faster than ReentrantReadWriteLock for read-mostly data 8 LongAdder, LongAccumulator, DoubleAdder Striped counters with no CAS contention under heavy writes 8 ConcurrentHashMap rewrite (no segments, tree bins), computeIfAbsent, forEach/reduce/search bulk ops Atomic compound ops on maps 8 ForkJoinPool.commonPool() Shared default pool, used by parallel streams and *Async methods 8 @sun.misc.Contended (internal) Prevents false sharing in JDK classes 9 Feature java.util.concurrent.Flow (Reactive Streams interfaces), SubmissionPublisher Standard backpressure contract 9 VarHandle (JEP 193) Supported replacement for sun.misc.Unsafe CAS and fences 9 CompletableFuture.orTimeout, completeOnTimeout, delayedExecutor, copy, failedFuture Timeouts without extra schedulers 9 Thread.onSpinWait() CPU hint for spin loops 10 Feature Thread-local handshakes (JEP 312) Stops individual threads without a global safepoint 11 LTS HttpClient (async, CompletableFuture-based) Standard non-blocking HTTP 14 Feature Helpful NPEs, records preview Indirect: immutable data carriers are good for concurrency 15 Feature Biased locking disabled and deprecated (JEP 374); removed in 18 Uncontended synchronized costs slightly more, contended costs less 16 Feature Records final, Stream.toList() Immutable DTOs shared across threads safely 17 LTS Sealed classes; strong encapsulation of JDK internals Unsafe hacks discouraged 19 Feature Virtual threads preview (JEP 425); ExecutorService is now AutoCloseable; Future.resultNow/exceptionNow/state() try-with-resources executors 19 Structured concurrency incubator (JEP 428) 20 Feature VT 2nd preview (JEP 436); Scoped values incubator (JEP 429) 21 (2023) LTS Virtual threads FINAL (JEP 444); Thread.ofVirtual(), Thread.Builder, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() Thread-per-request scales to millions 21 Structured concurrency preview (JEP 453), Scoped values preview (JEP 446) --enable-preview 21 Generational ZGC (JEP 439) Lower GC overhead with millions of short-lived VT stacks 22 Feature SC 2nd preview (JEP 462), SV 2nd preview (JEP 464) 23 Feature SC 3rd preview (JEP 480), SV 3rd preview (JEP 481); ZGC generational by default 24 (2025) Feature Synchronize virtual threads without pinning (JEP 491) synchronized blocks/methods unmount; jdk.tracePinnedThreads removed 24 SC 4th preview (JEP 499), SV 4th preview (JEP 487) 25 (2025) LTS Scoped values FINAL (JEP 506) Production-safe ThreadLocal replacement 25 SC 5th preview (JEP 505): new StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner) API API reshaped; still preview 25 Stable values preview (JEP 502) Thread-safe lazy initialization without double-checked locking 26 Feature SC 6th preview (JEP 525) Still evolving

Which version should I target?

  • Java 21 LTS is the minimum for virtual threads in production. Audit synchronized around blocking IO, because it pins carriers.
  • Java 24 is the first release where synchronized is VT-friendly. It is a non-LTS release, so most enterprises move from 21 → 25 LTS and get JEP 491 plus final scoped values.
  • Treat structured concurrency as preview in every release up to and including 26. Wrap it behind your own small abstraction if you adopt it (see Structured Concurrency).

docs.title: Old way vs new way: the API map
docs.text: Need Java 8 way Java 21/24/25 way Run one task per request Fixed ThreadPoolExecutor(200) Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() Start a thread new Thread(r).start() Thread.ofVirtual().name("worker-", 0).start(r) or Thread.startVirtualThread(r) Shut down an executor shutdown() + awaitTermination() in a finally block try (var ex = ...) { } (AutoCloseable since 19) Fan-out to N services CompletableFuture.allOf(...) + thenCombine chains Plain blocking calls inside StructuredTaskScope (preview), or VT executor + invokeAll Timeout an async call ScheduledExecutorService + cancel cf.orTimeout(2, SECONDS) (9+) or scope.joinUntil (21–24) / Joiner + config timeout (25) Per-request context ThreadLocal + try/finally remove() ScopedValue.where(KEY, v).run(...) (final in 25) Limit concurrency to a downstream Size of thread pool Semaphore (threads are no longer the scarce resource) Lazy singleton Double-checked locking with volatile Holder idiom, or StableValue (25 preview) Read-mostly cache lock ReentrantReadWriteLock StampedLock optimistic read, or ConcurrentHashMap Hot counter AtomicLong LongAdder Low-level CAS sun.misc.Unsafe VarHandle Pinning-safe locking around IO ReentrantLock (21–23) synchronized is fine again (24+) Get a result from a done Future try { f.get() } catch (...) f.resultNow() / f.state() (19+)

docs.title: Learning Path: 0 → 15 Years
docs.text:
Concurrency skill grows in four distinct stages. Each stage changes what question you ask.

Level Experience The question you ask Must master L1 0–2 yrs "How do I run this in the background safely?" Thread lifecycle, synchronized, volatile, ExecutorService, race conditions, virtual-thread basics L2 3–5 yrs "Which tool fits this problem?" JMM/happens-before, locks, atomics, concurrent collections, CompletableFuture, pool sizing, VT migration L3 6–9 yrs "Why is production slow or stuck?" Thread dumps, JFR, pinning, contention profiling, structured concurrency, backpressure, JMH L4 10–15 yrs "What concurrency model should the platform use?" docs.title: Skill checklist
docs.text:
• I can explain why count++ is not atomic.
  • I can explain happens-before without saying "it flushes the cache".
  • I know when to choose ReentrantLock over synchronized, and why that choice changed in Java 24.
  • I can size a platform thread pool for CPU-bound and IO-bound work.
  • I know why you never pool virtual threads.
  • I can find a pinned virtual thread with JFR.
  • I can limit concurrency to a downstream with a Semaphore instead of pool size.
  • I can explain structured concurrency's cancellation semantics.
  • I can say when reactive is still the better choice than virtual threads.
  • I can apply Little's Law to size connection pools, threads, and rate limits.

docs.title: How interviewers grade concurrency answers
docs.text:
Signal Junior Senior Staff/Architect Correctness vocabulary Race, deadlock Happens-before, linearizability Consistency models across services Tool choice Knows the APIs Explains trade-offs Sets platform defaults and guardrails Failure thinking "Add try/catch" Timeouts, cancellation, backpressure Blast radius, isolation, capacity models Evidence – "I'd profile with JFR" "Here's how we measured and rolled it out" Virtual threads What they are Pinning, limits, migration When not to use them; org-wide adoption

The answer structure that works

Definition → mechanism → example → trade-off → what changed in Java 21/24. For example: "volatile gives visibility and ordering through a happens-before edge between a write and later reads, which is why the stop-flag example works. It doesn't give atomicity, so count++ still races. Nothing about it changed with VTs."

docs.title: Coding Problems
docs.text: Quick-reference versions of classic whiteboard problems. For 21 problems with runnable, tested solutions, diagrams, and line-by-line explanations, see the Coding Interview tab.

docs.title: 1. Print odd/even numbers alternately with two threads
docs.text:
public class OddEven {
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private int n = 1;
    private final int max;
    OddEven(int max) { this.max = max; }

    void print(boolean odd) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (n <= max) {
                if ((n % 2 == 1) == odd) {
                    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": " + n++);
                    lock.notifyAll();
                } else {
                    try { lock.wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; }
                }
            }
            lock.notifyAll();
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] a) throws InterruptedException {
        var p = new OddEven(10);
        Thread t1 = Thread.ofPlatform().name("odd").start(() -> p.print(true));
        Thread t2 = Thread.ofPlatform().name("even").start(() -> p.print(false));
        t1.join(); t2.join();
    }
}
Follow-up: generalize to N threads printing in round-robin. Use n % N == id, or one Semaphore per thread and release the next one.

docs.title: 4. Implement a simple thread pool
docs.text:
public final class SimplePool implements AutoCloseable {
    private final BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue;
    private final List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>();
    private volatile boolean shutdown;

    public SimplePool(int threads, int capacity) {
        queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(capacity);
        for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) {
            workers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().name("pool-", i).start(() -> {
                while (!shutdown || !queue.isEmpty()) {
                    try {
                        Runnable r = queue.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
                        if (r != null) r.run();
                    } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; }
                    catch (RuntimeException e) { /* log, keep worker alive */ }
                }
            }));
        }
    }
    public void submit(Runnable r) throws InterruptedException {
        if (shutdown) throw new RejectedExecutionException();
        queue.put(r);                                     // blocks when full = backpressure
    }
    @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        shutdown = true;
        for (Thread w : workers) w.join();
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Deadlock: write one, then fix it
docs.text:
Object a = new Object(), b = new Object();
Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { synchronized (a) { sleep(50); synchronized (b) {} } });
Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { synchronized (b) { sleep(50); synchronized (a) {} } });  // deadlock
// Fix: both threads lock a then b (global order), or use tryLock with a timeout

docs.title: 7. Concurrent LRU cache
docs.text:
public final class LruCache<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    private final LinkedHashMap<K, V> map;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {     // access order
            @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> e) { return size() > LruCache.this.capacity; }
        };
    }
    public V get(K k) { lock.lock(); try { return map.get(k); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }  // get mutates order → needs the lock
    public void put(K k, V v) { lock.lock(); try { map.put(k, v); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
}
// Production: Caffeine (lock-amortized, W-TinyLFU) beats this by far.

docs.title: 9. Fetch N URLs concurrently with a max of K in flight and an overall timeout
10. Dining philosophers
docs.text:
Fix with resource ordering: each philosopher picks up the lower-numbered fork first. Alternatives are a Semaphore(N-1) "waiter", or tryLock on both forks with backoff.

void dine(int i, ReentrantLock[] forks) {
    ReentrantLock first = forks[Math.min(i, (i + 1) % forks.length)];
    ReentrantLock second = forks[Math.max(i, (i + 1) % forks.length)];
    first.lock(); try { second.lock(); try { eat(i); } finally { second.unlock(); } } finally { first.unlock(); }
}

docs.title: 11. Count words in 1,000 files in parallel
docs.text:
ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); var paths = Files.list(dir)) {
    paths.forEach(p -> ex.submit(() -> {
        try (var lines = Files.lines(p)) {
            lines.flatMap(l -> Arrays.stream(l.split("\\W+"))).filter(w -> !w.isEmpty())
                 .forEach(w -> counts.computeIfAbsent(w.toLowerCase(), k -> new LongAdder()).increment());
        }
        return null;
    }));
}

docs.title: 12. Implement CountDownLatch using wait/notify
docs.text:
final class MyLatch {
    private int count;
    MyLatch(int count) { this.count = count; }
    synchronized void countDown() { if (count > 0 && --count == 0) notifyAll(); }
    synchronized void await() throws InterruptedException { while (count > 0) wait(); }
}

docs.title: 13. Implement a read-write lock
docs.text:
final class SimpleRwLock {
    private int readers, writersWaiting; private boolean writing;
    synchronized void lockRead() throws InterruptedException { while (writing || writersWaiting > 0) wait(); readers++; }
    synchronized void unlockRead() { if (--readers == 0) notifyAll(); }
    synchronized void lockWrite() throws InterruptedException {
        writersWaiting++;
        try { while (writing || readers > 0) wait(); } finally { writersWaiting--; }
        writing = true;
    }
    synchronized void unlockWrite() { writing = false; notifyAll(); }
}
Writer preference (writersWaiting) prevents writer starvation.

docs.title: 14. Parallel merge sort with Fork/Join
docs.text:
class MergeSort extends RecursiveAction {
    final int[] a, tmp; final int lo, hi;
    MergeSort(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) { this.a = a; this.tmp = tmp; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi; }
    @Override protected void compute() {
        if (hi - lo < 4096) { Arrays.sort(a, lo, hi); return; }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        invokeAll(new MergeSort(a, tmp, lo, mid), new MergeSort(a, tmp, mid, hi));
        merge(lo, mid, hi);
    }
    void merge(int lo, int mid, int hi) {
        System.arraycopy(a, lo, tmp, lo, hi - lo);
        for (int i = lo, j = mid, k = lo; k < hi; k++)
            a[k] = (j >= hi || (i < mid && tmp[i] <= tmp[j])) ? tmp[i++] : tmp[j++];
    }
}

docs.title: Threads basics
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a process and a thread?

A process has its own address space. Threads in a process share the heap but each has its own stack and program counter. Threads are cheaper to create and to switch between, and they communicate through shared memory, which is why they need synchronization.

2. What are the ways to create a thread in Java?

Extend Thread; implement Runnable (or Callable for a result) and pass it to a Thread or executor; and, since Java 21, Thread.ofPlatform()/ofVirtual() builders, Thread.startVirtualThread, and Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().

3. Runnable vs Callable?

Runnable.run() returns nothing and can't throw checked exceptions. Callable.call() returns a value and can throw Exception. Submitting a Callable gives you a Future<T>.

4. What happens if you call run() instead of start()?

run() executes on the current thread like a normal method call. No new thread is created.

5. Can you start a thread twice?

No. The second start() throws IllegalThreadStateException.

6. Name the thread states.

NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.

7. Difference between BLOCKED and WAITING?

BLOCKED = waiting to enter a synchronized monitor. WAITING = waiting indefinitely for another thread's action (wait(), join(), LockSupport.park()).

8. What does join() do?

It makes the caller wait until the target thread terminates, and it creates a happens-before edge from the thread's actions to the return of join().

9. sleep() vs wait()?

sleep is a static Thread method. It pauses without releasing locks. wait is an Object method that must be called while holding the monitor, and it releases the monitor until it's notified.

10. What is a daemon thread?

A background thread that doesn't keep the JVM alive. The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain. Virtual threads are always daemons.

11. What is thread priority, and should you rely on it?

A hint (1–10) to the OS scheduler. Don't rely on it: it's platform-dependent, and it's ignored for virtual threads.

12. How do you stop a thread?

Cooperatively: interrupt() it, and have the thread check isInterrupted() or handle InterruptedException. Thread.stop() is unsupported.

docs.title: Synchronization
docs.text:
13. What is a race condition?

When correctness depends on the timing or interleaving of threads, such as two threads doing count++ and losing an update.

14. Why is count++ not thread-safe?

It's three steps: read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value, and one increment is lost.

15. What does synchronized guarantee?

Mutual exclusion on a monitor, plus visibility: an unlock happens-before the next lock of the same monitor.

16. Synchronized method vs synchronized block?

A method locks this (or the Class for static methods) for the whole body. A block lets you choose the lock object and narrow the scope, which is usually better.

17. What is volatile?

A field modifier that guarantees visibility (reads see the latest write) and ordering (no reordering across it). It doesn't make compound actions atomic.

18. Is synchronized reentrant?

Yes. A thread holding a monitor can enter other blocks synchronized on the same monitor.

19. What is a deadlock? Give an example.

Two or more threads each wait for a lock the other holds. T1 holds A and wants B, while T2 holds B and wants A.

20. How do you prevent deadlock?

Acquire locks in a consistent global order, use tryLock with timeouts, hold fewer locks, or avoid shared mutable state.

21. What is wait()/notify() used for? Why call wait in a loop?

Guarded waiting for a condition. Use a loop because of spurious wakeups, and because the condition may change again before the thread reacquires the lock.

22. notify() vs notifyAll()?

notify wakes one arbitrary waiter. notifyAll wakes all of them. Prefer notifyAll unless every waiter waits for the same condition.

23. What is thread safety?

A class is thread-safe if it behaves correctly when accessed from multiple threads with no extra synchronization by callers.

24. Why are immutable objects thread-safe?

Their state can't change after construction (with final fields and no escaping this), so there's nothing to race on.

docs.title: Executors and collections
docs.text:
25. Why use an ExecutorService instead of creating threads?

It separates task submission from execution policy, lets you reuse platform threads, bounds concurrency, manages lifecycle, and returns Futures.

26. submit() vs execute()?

execute(Runnable) returns nothing, and exceptions go to the uncaught exception handler. submit returns a Future, and exceptions are captured in it.

27. shutdown() vs shutdownNow()?

shutdown stops accepting tasks and lets queued tasks finish. shutdownNow also interrupts running tasks and returns the queued ones.

28. What does Future.get() do?

It blocks until the task completes, then returns the result or throws ExecutionException (failure), CancellationException, or InterruptedException. There's also a timeout overload.

29. HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap?

HashMap isn't thread-safe. Hashtable synchronizes every method (slow, legacy). ConcurrentHashMap uses fine-grained locking and CAS, has lock-free reads, and provides atomic compute*/merge.

30. What is CopyOnWriteArrayList good for?

Read-mostly lists such as listeners. Every write copies the array, and iterators see a snapshot.

31. What is a BlockingQueue?

A queue whose put blocks when it's full and whose take blocks when it's empty. It's the building block for producer–consumer designs.

32. What is AtomicInteger?

A lock-free integer that uses CAS for atomic operations like incrementAndGet.

33. What does CountDownLatch do?

It lets threads wait until a count reaches zero. It's one-shot. Use it, for example, to wait for N tasks to finish.

docs.title: Virtual threads (Java 21)
docs.text:
34. What is a virtual thread?

A lightweight Thread that the JVM schedules onto a small pool of OS carrier threads. Blocking unmounts it, so millions can exist.

35. How do you create one?

Thread.ofVirtual().start(r), Thread.startVirtualThread(r), or Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().

36. Are virtual threads faster?

Not per task. They raise throughput for IO-bound concurrent work. CPU-bound work gets no speed-up.

37. Should you pool virtual threads?

No. They're cheap to create, so you create one per task. Limit concurrency with semaphores instead.

38. How do you enable virtual threads in Spring Boot?

Use Spring Boot 3.2+ on Java 21+ and set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.

39. How do you check whether code runs on a virtual thread?

Thread.currentThread().isVirtual().

40. What does try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {...} do at the end of the block?

close() shuts down the executor and waits for all submitted tasks to complete. ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since Java 19.

docs.title: Java Memory Model
docs.text:
1. Explain happens-before.

A partial order of actions. If A happens-before B, A's effects are visible to B and A is ordered before it. Edges come from program order, monitor unlock→lock, volatile write→read, start(), join(), j.u.c handoffs, and transitivity.

2. Why does the JMM exist?

Compilers and CPUs reorder and cache memory operations. The JMM defines which results are legal, so code that is correctly synchronized behaves as if it were sequentially consistent (the DRF-SC guarantee).

3. What is safe publication? List idioms.

Making an object and its state visible to other threads correctly: a static initializer, a volatile/AtomicReference field, a final field, a lock-guarded field, or a concurrent collection.

4. Why must the DCL singleton field be volatile?

Without it, another thread may see the reference before the constructor's writes (reordering) and get a partially built object.

5. What guarantees do final fields give?

If this doesn't escape during construction, any thread that sees the reference sees the final fields fully initialized, with no synchronization.

6. Does volatile long matter on 64-bit JVMs?

The spec allows tearing of non-volatile long/double values, and volatile forbids it. HotSpot on 64-bit doesn't tear in practice, but use volatile to rely on the spec rather than on implementation behaviour.

docs.title: Locks and atomics
docs.text:
7. ReentrantLock vs synchronized?

ReentrantLock adds tryLock, timeouts, interruptible acquisition, fairness, and multiple Conditions, but it needs a finally unlock. On JDK 21–23, it also avoids VT pinning. On 24+, synchronized is fine for VTs too.

8. What is a fair lock, and what does it cost?

A fair lock grants access in FIFO order. That prevents starvation but lowers throughput, because it disables barging.

9. When would you use ReadWriteLock?

For read-heavy data with long reads and rare writes. Beware of writer starvation, and note that upgrading from a read lock to a write lock deadlocks.

10. Explain StampedLock optimistic reads.

tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp without locking. You read the fields, then validate(stamp). If a writer intervened, you fall back to a read lock. It isn't reentrant.

11. What is CAS? What is the ABA problem?

Compare-and-swap is an atomic conditional update. ABA: a value changes A→B→A, so a CAS succeeds wrongly. Fix it with stamped references or by not reusing nodes.

12. AtomicLong vs LongAdder?

LongAdder stripes updates across cells, so it scales under contention. Its sum() isn't an atomic snapshot. Use it for metrics, and use AtomicLong when you need an exact value per read, such as IDs.

13. What is VarHandle?

The Java 9 API for atomic and ordered access to fields and array elements, with access modes (plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile, CAS). It's the supported replacement for Unsafe.

14. What is a Condition?

A wait set tied to a Lock. Multiple conditions (notFull, notEmpty) allow targeted signal() calls.

15. What is lock striping?

Using several locks for different parts of the data (hash buckets), as the old segmented ConcurrentHashMap and LongAdder cells do.

docs.title: Executors and pools
docs.text:
16. Explain ThreadPoolExecutor parameters and growth behaviour.

Core size, max size, keep-alive, work queue, thread factory, and rejection handler. The pool fills core threads, then the queue, then grows to max only when the queue is full, then rejects.

17. Why is Executors.newFixedThreadPool risky in production?

It uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so it can run out of memory under overload, and maxPoolSize is never used.

18. How do you size a pool for CPU-bound vs IO-bound work?

CPU: about the core count. IO: cores × util × (1 + wait/compute). Better still, use Little's Law and measure. With VTs, IO work needs no pool.

19. Name the rejection policies and when to use each.

Abort (signal overload to the caller), CallerRuns (natural backpressure), Discard (best-effort), DiscardOldest (only the latest matters).

20. What is thread-pool-induced deadlock?

Tasks in a bounded pool waiting on other tasks queued in the same pool. All threads wait, and the queued tasks never run.

21. How does a ScheduledExecutorService handle exceptions?

An exception thrown by a periodic task cancels all later runs silently. Catch everything inside the task.

22. What is ForkJoinPool work stealing?

Each worker has a deque. It pushes and pops its own tasks LIFO, while idle workers steal from the other end FIFO. That gives good locality and load balancing.

23. Problems with parallel streams?

They share the common pool, so blocking calls starve the whole JVM. They're inefficient on small or poorly splittable sources, and stateful lambdas cause races.

docs.title: CompletableFuture
docs.text:
24. thenApply vs thenCompose?

thenApply maps a value (like map). thenCompose chains a function that returns another CompletionStage (like flatMap).

25. Which thread runs a thenApply callback?

The thread that completes the previous stage, or the caller if the stage is already complete. The *Async variants run on the given (or common) executor.

26. How do you handle errors in a CF chain?

exceptionally (recover), handle (value or error), whenComplete (side effect), and exceptionallyCompose (Java 12).

27. How do you add timeouts to a CF?

orTimeout (fails with TimeoutException) or completeOnTimeout(default), both added in Java 9. Neither cancels the underlying work.

28. Does cancel(true) interrupt a CF's task?

No. CompletableFuture isn't connected to the thread running it, so the flag is ignored.

29. allOf vs anyOf?

allOf completes when all complete (and returns Void). anyOf completes with the first completion, even an exceptional one.

docs.title: ThreadLocal and context
docs.text:
30. What are the risks of ThreadLocal in thread pools?

Values leak into the next task on the same pooled thread, and you get memory leaks (especially classloader leaks in app servers). Always remove().

31. How does MDC work with async code?

It's ThreadLocal-based, so you copy the context map into tasks with a TaskDecorator or context-propagation wrappers.

docs.title: Virtual threads (mid-level)
docs.text:
32. How do virtual threads differ internally from platform threads?

A VT is a continuation scheduled on a ForkJoinPool of carriers, and its stack lives on the heap. A platform thread maps 1:1 to an OS thread.

33. What is pinning?

A VT that can't unmount while blocked, so it holds its carrier. On JDK 21–23 this happens inside synchronized and native frames. On 24+, only in native code and class initializers.

34. How do you detect pinning?

The JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned. On 21–23 you can also use -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full.

35. Once threads are virtual, how do you limit concurrency to a database?

Through the connection pool size (HikariCP) plus connectionTimeout, and with a Semaphore for other resources.

36. What does spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true change?

Tomcat/Jetty request handling, the @Async executor, @Scheduled, and messaging listeners all run on virtual threads.

37. Are ThreadLocals supported on VTs?

Yes, but don't use them as caches (no reuse, one copy per VT). For context, prefer ScopedValue.

38. What happens with @Transactional when you fork work to another VT?

The forked work isn't in the transaction, because the connection and transaction are bound to the original thread.

39. Why do VTs need explicit backpressure?

The thread pool used to cap concurrency implicitly. With unlimited VTs, downstreams can be flooded unless you add semaphores or rate limits.

40. What's the risk of CPU-heavy work on VTs?

VTs aren't time-sliced. CPU-bound VTs occupy the carriers and starve the IO-bound ones. Use a bounded platform pool for CPU work.

docs.title: Collections and synchronizers
docs.text:
41. Why does ConcurrentHashMap disallow null keys and values?

get() returning null would be ambiguous (absent vs a null value), and you can't resolve that atomically with containsKey in concurrent code.

42. Is ConcurrentHashMap.size() exact?

It's an estimate during concurrent updates (summed counter cells). Use mappingCount() for a long.

43. CyclicBarrier vs CountDownLatch?

A barrier is reusable, and N parties wait for each other. A latch is one-shot, and waiters wait for N events from anyone.

44. What is a Semaphore used for?

Limiting concurrent access to N permits, as in bulkheads, connection caps, and rate limiting.

45. What is Phaser?

A reusable barrier with dynamic registration and multiple phases. Parties can join and leave.

docs.title: Internals
docs.text:
1. How does HotSpot implement synchronized today?

Lightweight locking (CAS on the header, or the newer lightweight mode in 21+) when uncontended. It inflates to an ObjectMonitor under contention or wait(). Biased locking was removed in JDK 18.

2. What is a memory barrier, and which ones does volatile emit on x86?

A barrier is an ordering constraint. x86 is TSO, so only store→load reordering needs a barrier: a volatile write emits a lock-prefixed instruction (or mfence), and volatile reads are plain loads.

3. Explain store buffering and why 0,0 is possible in Dekker's test.

Each core's write sits in its store buffer while it reads the other variable from cache, so both reads see 0. Making the fields volatile forbids that outcome.

4. What is false sharing, and how do you fix it?

Independent variables on one cache line cause invalidation ping-pong. Fix it with padding, @Contended, or JDK classes like LongAdder.

5. How does ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+) work?

An array of bins. Empty bins are filled with a CAS, and non-empty bins are locked by synchronizing on the head node. Long bins turn into red-black trees (TreeBins). Resizing is cooperative (threads help transfer), the counter is LongAdder-style, and reads are lock-free with volatile semantics.

6. How does AbstractQueuedSynchronizer work?

A volatile int state plus a CLH-style FIFO queue of waiting nodes. Acquire tries a CAS on state, and on failure it enqueues and LockSupport.park()s. Release updates state and unparks the successor. ReentrantLock, Semaphore, and CountDownLatch are built on it.

7. What is LockSupport.park/unpark?

A per-thread permit primitive. unpark before park makes the park return immediately. VTs implement park by unmounting.

docs.title: Virtual threads in depth
docs.text:
8. Describe mount and unmount.

When it's scheduled, the VT's continuation runs on a carrier (frames are thawed from heap stack chunks). When it blocks, Continuation.yield freezes the changed frames to the heap, and the carrier is released. The VT may resume on another carrier.

9. How does a blocking socket read avoid blocking the carrier?

The JDK's socket implementation uses non-blocking IO. On EAGAIN it registers the fd with a poller (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) and parks the VT. The poller unparks the VT when the fd is ready.

10. Which operations capture the carrier instead of unmounting?

File IO and DNS lookups (the scheduler compensates with extra carriers), native code or JNI, and class initialization. On 21–23 also synchronized blocking and Object.wait().

11. What exactly did JEP 491 change?

Monitors are now associated with the virtual thread, not the carrier. VTs can unmount while holding, contending for, or wait()ing on monitors. jdk.tracePinnedThreads was removed.

12. What are the scheduler tuning knobs, and when would you touch them?

jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism and maxPoolSize (plus minRunnable). Touch them rarely, for example when container CPU detection is off or when compensation hits the cap.

13. Are virtual threads preemptive?

No time-slicing. A VT runs until it blocks, yields, or finishes. CPU-bound loops monopolize their carriers.

14. How do you get a thread dump that includes VTs?

jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file. jstack shows only platform threads (the carriers).

15. Why is ThreadLocal caching harmful with VTs, while context is acceptable?

Caching relies on thread reuse, which VTs don't have, so you get one copy per task and millions of objects. Context is per request anyway, so it costs only the value.

docs.title: Modern APIs
docs.text:
16. What problem does structured concurrency solve?

Unstructured Futures leak tasks on failure, don't propagate cancellation, and lose the parent–child relation. SC bounds subtask lifetimes to a scope, cancels siblings, propagates errors, and makes task trees observable.

17. Compare ShutdownOnFailure and ShutdownOnSuccess (21–24).

The first shuts the scope down on the first failure (all results required). The second shuts it down on the first success (any result is enough).

18. How did the SC API change in Java 25?

StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner, config) replaced the subclasses: Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(), allSuccessfulOrThrow(), and custom Joiners. Timeouts are set in config, and join() throws FailedException.

19. Why are scoped values better than ThreadLocal?

They're immutable per binding, bounded in lifetime, inherited cheaply by SC subtasks, and JIT-friendly. They're final in Java 25.

20. Do executor tasks inherit scoped values?

No. Only StructuredTaskScope.fork does. For other executors, capture the value and rebind it explicitly.

docs.title: Performance and debugging
docs.text:
21. A service's p99 latency doubled after enabling VTs on JDK 21. How do you investigate?

Check jdk.VirtualThreadPinned in JFR. Look at JSON thread dumps for VTs piling up in one frame (DB pool, synchronized). Check CPU-bound work on VTs, downstream saturation from the extra concurrency, and GC.

22. Throughput didn't improve after enabling VTs. Why?

The service is CPU-bound, or limited by the DB or connection pools, a bottleneck in a lock or rate limiter, or a downstream. VTs only remove the thread bottleneck.

23. How do you find lock contention in production?

JFR JavaMonitorEnter/ThreadPark events, async-profiler -e lock, or several thread dumps showing many threads BLOCKED on one address.

24. How do you benchmark concurrent code correctly?

JMH with forks, warm-up, @Param concurrency levels, blackholes or returned values, and -prof gc. Then load-test the service at a constant rate (wrk2/k6) to avoid coordinated omission.

25. What is coordinated omission?

A closed-loop load generator waits for slow responses before sending more, which hides queueing delay. Use constant-rate tools.

26. How do you test memory-model correctness?

jcstress: it runs the actors many times across interleavings and classifies the outcomes.

docs.title: Design and trade-offs
docs.text:
27. Design a bounded producer/consumer pipeline with backpressure, without reactive libraries.

Stages connected by bounded BlockingQueues, with N VT workers per stage and poison pills for shutdown. A full queue blocks producers (backpressure). Add metrics on queue depth.

28. How do you implement a bulkhead with VTs?

A semaphore per dependency with tryAcquire(timeout). Fail fast with 503 and track usage and rejections. Avoid thread-pool bulkheads.

29. How do you propagate deadlines across a fan-out?

Compute a deadline at the edge. Each call uses the remaining time as its timeout, the fan-out scope enforces the overall deadline, and you propagate it via a header.

30. When is reactive still the better choice than VTs?

Streaming with end-to-end backpressure, very high fan-out with tiny CPU per request where the last few percent of efficiency matter, and existing healthy reactive stacks.

31. How do you keep per-key ordering while processing in parallel?

Per-key lanes, where a single consumer per key drains a queue, using CHM compute for atomic lane lifecycle, plus contiguous offset commits.

32. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking in a DB-backed service?

Optimistic (@Version) for low-contention updates, retrying on conflict. Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE) for hot rows, with tiny transactions, or redesign with atomic SQL updates.

33. How would you implement a rate limiter?

A token bucket or sliding window. In-process: a lock-protected bucket that sleeps outside the lock (cheap on VTs). Distributed: Redis Lua script or a gateway.

34. What's wrong with synchronized (this) { httpClient.send(...) }?

The lock is held across IO, which serializes all callers. It pins VTs on 21–23, and the lock is public. Narrow the critical section to state changes only.

35. How do you make a cache refresh non-blocking for readers?

Use an immutable snapshot in an AtomicReference. One thread refreshes it (balking with compareAndSet on a flag) while readers keep reading the old snapshot.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
36. Your Kafka consumer lags. Would VTs help?

Only if processing is IO-bound and you parallelize within a partition (per-key lanes). VTs alone don't add parallelism beyond the number of consumers, which is capped by partitions.

37. 10k scheduled reminders: timers or VTs?

Sleeping VTs are fine for short horizons within one process lifetime. For durability, use a persistent scheduler (Quartz, DB polling with SKIP LOCKED).

38. How do you shut down a service gracefully with in-flight VTs?

Graceful server shutdown, a readiness probe that goes down, closing executors (shutdown + awaitTermination + shutdownNow), and an aligned K8s grace period.

39. How do you avoid connection storms after enabling VTs?

Small fixed DB pools, PgBouncer, admission control, and per-dependency semaphores. Raise limits only after load tests.

40. A parallelStream() in a request handler makes the whole JVM slow. Why?

It uses the common FJ pool shared by every request (and by CompletableFuture async defaults). Concurrent requests contend for it, and blocking starves it.

41. How do you propagate tracing context into tasks you fork yourself?

OpenTelemetry Context.taskWrapping(executor) or Micrometer ContextExecutorService.wrap. Structured scopes plus scoped values in the future.

42. Explain the difference between linearizability and sequential consistency.

Both give a single total order. Linearizability also respects real-time order: an operation takes effect between its invocation and its response. Atomic* operations are linearizable.

43. What is the single-writer principle?

Only one thread mutates a given piece of state, and others send it messages. This avoids contention and locks (Disruptor, actors, partitions).

44. invokeAny vs anyOf?

invokeAny returns the first successful result and cancels the others. anyOf completes with the first completion, success or failure, and cancels nothing.

45. How do VTs change the way you write retries and timeouts?

Write them as plain loops with Thread.sleep and blocking calls with timeouts. There's no need for schedulers and CF chains, and deadline budgets stay explicit.

docs.title: Interview: 10–15 Years (Staff / Principal / Architect)
docs.text:
L4

At this level, interviewers want judgement backed by numbers, failure analysis, and organizational impact.

docs.title: Platform strategy
docs.text:
1. Your org has 80 Java 11 services, some on WebFlux. What's your concurrency strategy for the next two years?

Standardize on JDK 25 LTS and Spring Boot 3.5+/4.x. Make MVC + virtual threads the golden path for request/response services, and keep WebFlux for streaming, the gateway, and healthy reactive services. Give the platform template admission control, bulkheads, JFR pinning alerts, and lint rules. Migrate by tiers (IO-heavy aggregators first), toggle by configuration, and use canaries and dashboards. Measure the effect on cost and latency, and roll back on regressions.

2. How do you decide between virtual threads and reactive for a new service?

Ask: is there streaming or backpressure across boundaries? Is there an existing reactive ecosystem? What's the team's skill set? What do the drivers support? What's CPU per request? Default to VTs. Choose reactive for streams, SSE/WebSocket fan-out, and the gateway tier, and justify it with a prototype benchmark.

3. What guardrails would you put in a service template for VTs?

An admission filter, a semaphore bulkhead library with metrics, mandatory timeouts in HTTP/DB client factories, a CPU executor for heavy work, a JFR pinning monitor, a context-propagation wrapper, ArchUnit rules (no VT pooling, no ThreadLocal fields outside the allow-list, no parallelStream in IO code), and load-test gates.

4. How do you justify the migration cost to leadership?

A capacity model: thread-bound vs CPU-bound ceilings per service, pods saved, and incident classes removed (pool exhaustion). Add developer productivity (less code, simpler debugging, onboarding) and a pilot with before/after metrics. Present ranges, not promises.

5. Which services gain the least from VTs?

CPU-bound services (ML scoring, image processing), services already at their DB limits, and low-concurrency batch jobs. The gain is roughly the ratio of the thread ceiling to the other ceilings.

docs.title: Capacity and performance
docs.text:
6. Walk through capacity planning for a 5k-rps checkout service using Little's Law.

In-flight = λ × latency. DB connections = λ × DB time per request (with headroom), checked against the DB's max_connections across pods. Downstream permits = λ × latency. CPU = λ × CPU time / target utilization, which sets the pod count. Then validate with load tests and add headroom for retries and failover.

7. A downstream slows from 100 ms to 5 s. Compare the platform-thread and VT services' behaviour.

Platform: thread exhaustion makes the entire service fail (cascade). VT without limits: in-flight work grows 50×, along with heap, sockets, and connection pool exhaustion, which can also cascade. VT with bulkheads and timeouts: only that path fails fast, so the blast radius is contained.

8. How do you set timeout values across a call chain?

Budget from the edge SLO downward: each hop's timeout is smaller than its caller's, account for retries (budget ≥ attempts × timeout + backoff), and propagate deadlines so downstreams stop working on requests that have already been abandoned.

9. How do retries interact with overload?

Retries amplify load (retry storms). Use retry budgets (a percentage of traffic), jittered backoff, circuit breakers, idempotency keys, and only retry idempotent operations.

10. When would you use hedged requests, and what are the risks?

For tail-latency-sensitive idempotent reads with variable latency. The risks are extra load (cap it at a few percent), non-idempotent side effects, and making things worse during an overload (disable hedging when error rates rise).

docs.title: Failure isolation and resilience
docs.text:
11. Design the resilience layers for a service calling five dependencies.

Edge admission control → per-dependency bulkhead + timeout + circuit breaker + retry budget → resource pools. Add fallbacks for optional data, plus degraded flags in the response, and dashboards and alerts per layer.

12. How do you prevent one tenant from starving others in a multi-tenant service?

Per-tenant semaphores and rate limits (weighted), fair queuing, separate pools or cells for big tenants, and quotas at the gateway. Make it observable per tenant.

13. What's a cell-based architecture, and how does it relate to concurrency limits?

Partition users into independent stacks (cells), each with bounded capacity. Limits and failures stay within a cell, which reduces the blast radius. Concurrency limits are then sized per cell.

14. How do you handle backpressure end to end, from mobile client to database?

Client rate limits and retries with jitter, the gateway's rate limiting, service admission control (429/503 with Retry-After), bounded queues and semaphores inside, DB pool limits, and bounded queue consumers with lag-based autoscaling.

docs.title: Distributed concurrency
docs.text:
15. How do you guarantee no double charge in payments?

Idempotency keys stored with a unique constraint, a state machine with conditional updates, an outbox for events, reconciliation jobs, and provider-side idempotency keys.

16. Distributed lock with Redis: is it safe?

It's fine for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work). For correctness, it isn't safe on its own, because of GC pauses, clock drift, and lease expiry. Use fencing tokens verified by the storage layer, or a consensus system (ZooKeeper or etcd) plus fencing.

17. Saga vs 2PC?

2PC blocks while holding locks, the coordinator is a single point of failure, and many systems don't support it. A saga is a sequence of local transactions with compensations. It's eventually consistent, needs idempotent steps and careful design of the compensation semantics, and is usually orchestrated for complex flows.

18. How do you keep an aggregate consistent under concurrent commands across pods?

Optimistic concurrency on the aggregate version, a single writer per aggregate (partition by key), or DB constraints. Avoid in-JVM locks.

19. Explain exactly-once in Kafka, and its limits.

Idempotent producer + transactions + read_committed consumers give exactly-once within Kafka. Side effects outside Kafka need idempotent consumers or the outbox/inbox pattern.

20. How do you process a work queue in PostgreSQL across many workers?

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT n within a short transaction, a visibility timeout or lease, retries with a dead-letter table, and an index on status/run_at.

docs.title: Leadership and migration
docs.text:
21. Describe a concurrency incident you'd expect, and how you'd run the postmortem.

For example, a pool exhaustion cascade. Build a timeline from metrics and thread dumps, find the root cause (missing timeout or bulkhead), determine contributing factors (retry storm), and take actions (template change, alert, load test), all blameless.

22. How do you roll out JDK 21 → 25 across the fleet safely?

Upgrade the build first (compile at the new release), update dependencies, canary by tier, compare GC and latency, keep the toggles, and set a deadline policy for laggards. Use the JEP 491 benefit to drop ReentrantLock workarounds gradually.

23. Would you adopt structured concurrency (preview) in production?

Only behind an internal facade, with --enable-preview managed centrally and an awareness that the API changes between releases (it did between 24 and 25). A non-preview VT fallback inside the facade is pragmatic.

24. How do you train 200 engineers on concurrency?

A leveled curriculum (this playbook), golden-path code, code review checklists, internal talks with real incidents, and katas (race, deadlock, pinning).

25. What metrics define 'concurrency health' for a service?

In-flight vs limit, bulkhead saturation and rejections, pool waiters, pinned events, p99 vs SLO, retry rate, timeouts per dependency, and heap trend.

docs.title: Deep technical (architect still expected to know)
docs.text:
26. Why might a VT service have higher memory usage than expected?

Missing timeouts (parked VTs accumulate), large per-request object graphs, ThreadLocal caches, deep stacks (big frames), and unbounded fan-out.

27. What happens when the VT scheduler's maxPoolSize is reached?

No more compensating carriers are added. Further capturing operations reduce effective parallelism, and VTs queue. JFR may show VirtualThreadSubmitFailed in extreme cases.

28. Can VTs cause a deadlock that platform threads wouldn't?

The same lock-ordering deadlocks occur. On JDK 21–23, pinning can starve carriers: all carriers are pinned, waiting for a lock held by an unmounted VT that can't get a carrier. That's carrier-starvation deadlock, which JEP 491 largely fixes.

29. How does GC interact with millions of VTs?

Stack chunks are heap objects, so they're scanned and moved by GC. Parked VTs' stacks are roots only if the VT is reachable. Generational ZGC handles many short-lived chunks well.

30. What's next for Java concurrency beyond 25?

Structured concurrency finalization, possibly custom schedulers, better observability (scheduler MXBean in 24), and continued work on removing pinning from native and class-init paths.

docs.title: Open-ended design prompts
docs.text:
31. Design a notification platform sending 50M messages/day over multiple channels.

See System Design Rounds.

32. Design a rate limiter service for a public API.

See System Design Rounds.

33. Design the inventory reservation for a flash sale.

See Case Studies.

34. Design a job scheduler with exactly-once execution semantics.

Use durable job rows with a unique (job, schedule) key, workers claiming with SKIP LOCKED and leases plus fencing, idempotent handlers, and a dead-letter table. "Exactly-once" really means at-least-once execution with idempotent handlers.

35. Design a real-time order-tracking feed for 1M concurrent app users.

WebSocket/SSE gateway (reactive or VT-per-connection), a pub/sub fan-out (Redis Streams or Kafka) partitioned by order, backpressure that drops intermediate location updates, connection-draining on deploys, and autoscaling on connection count.

36. How would you design a thread-safe, in-memory cache with refresh-ahead for 100k rps?

Caffeine (W-TinyLFU, async refresh) with refreshAfterWrite, bounded size, stampede protection (one loader per key), metrics, and a snapshot for config.

37. Your team proposes moving a reactive gateway to VTs. How do you evaluate it?

Benchmark at production RPS and connection counts with both. Compare p99, CPU, and memory, check feature parity (filters, streaming), weigh the operational familiarity, and decide on evidence.

38. How do you prevent thundering herds after a cache flush or restart?

Request coalescing (single-flight per key), jittered TTLs, warm-up before taking traffic, and serving stale data while revalidating.

39. What's the role of immutability in your platform's concurrency strategy?

Records and immutable DTOs by default, copy-on-write snapshots for config, and events as immutable facts. That removes most shared-mutable-state bugs.

40. Summarize what changed in Java concurrency from 8 to 25 in one minute.

8: composable async (CF), better primitives (StampedLock, LongAdder). 9: Flow, VarHandle, CF timeouts. 19–21: virtual threads (final in 21) and AutoCloseable executors. 24: no pinning on synchronized. 25: scoped values final, structured concurrency reshaped (preview). Net effect: simple blocking code is scalable again, and limits move from thread pools to explicit resource bulkheads.

docs.title: System Design Rounds (Concurrency-heavy)
docs.text: Each prompt includes the clarifying questions to ask, a model design, a diagram, and the concurrency talking points interviewers listen for.

docs.title: 1. Product page aggregator (BFF)
docs.text:
Ask: QPS? Latency SLO? Which parts are optional? Personalization?

flowchart LR App --> BFF[BFF: MVC + VTs] BFF -->|required| Cat[Catalog] BFF -->|optional| Price[Pricing] BFF -->|optional| Inv[Inventory] BFF -->|optional| Rec[Recommendations] BFF --> Cache[(Caffeine + Redis)]

Talking points: fan-out with a deadline (structured scope), required vs optional parts with fallbacks and a degraded flag, a bulkhead per dependency, a cache with stampede protection, hedging the recommendations call, and capacity via Little's Law. See the Fan-out service.

docs.title: 2. Notification platform
docs.text:
Ask: Volume (50M/day ≈ 600/s average, 10k/s peak)? Channels? Priority? Delivery guarantees? Provider quotas?

flowchart LR Producers -->|events| K[(Kafka: notifications.v1<br/>partition by user)] K --> W[Workers: VT per message<br/>per-channel semaphores + token buckets] W --> SMS[SMS provider] & Push[FCM/APNs] & Email[Email provider] W --> DB[(Status store)] W -->|failures| DLQ[(Retry topics + DLQ)]

Talking points: per-provider quotas as token buckets plus semaphores, retry topics with backoff, idempotency (a message id with a unique constraint), priority via separate topics, per-user ordering through partitioning, lag-based autoscaling, and VTs keeping the provider IO cheap.

docs.title: 3. Flash sale / inventory reservation
docs.text: See Case Study 2. Key points: an atomic decrement in Redis or a conditional SQL update, a waiting room with admission control, no hot-row FOR UPDATE convoys, async order creation, and a reservation TTL with compensation.

docs.title: 4. Distributed rate limiter
docs.text:
Ask: Per user, per API key, or global? Accuracy vs latency? Limit scale (100 rps or 100k rps)?

Option Pros Cons Local token bucket per pod No network hop Inaccurate (limit ÷ pods) Redis + Lua sliding window Accurate, atomic A network hop. Redis becomes a hot spot Local buckets + periodic sync Fast, approximately accurate Complexity

Talking points: Lua for atomicity, key sharding, failing open vs closed, Retry-After headers, and in-process limiting with VTs (sleeping is cheap, but don't let waiters pile up unbounded).

docs.title: 5. Job scheduler
docs.text:
Ask: Cron vs one-off? Exactly-once? Duration? Multi-tenant?

sequenceDiagram participant S as Scheduler pods participant DB as jobs table participant W as Worker VT loop every 1s S->>DB: claim N due jobs (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, lease 60s) DB-->>S: jobs S->>W: run each on a VT (bulkhead per job type) W->>DB: complete (if lease token matches) / retry with backoff end

Talking points: leases with fencing tokens, idempotent handlers, heartbeats for long jobs, a dead-letter table, and per-type concurrency limits.

docs.title: 6. Chat / real-time messaging
docs.text: Talking points: WebSocket connection handling (Netty/reactive, or VT-per-connection read/write loops), per-conversation ordering (partition by conversation), fan-out to online members over pub/sub, backpressure for slow clients (bounded outbound queue, then drop or disconnect), presence with TTL heartbeats, and connection-aware deploys.

docs.title: 7. Payment processing service
docs.text: Talking points: idempotency keys, a state machine (CREATED → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED / FAILED) with optimistic locking, the outbox, provider timeouts with reconciliation (an unknown outcome is not a failure), bulkhead and circuit breaker per provider, and no retries on non-idempotent calls without a key.

docs.title: 8. Web crawler
docs.text: Talking points: a frontier queue (priority + politeness), per-host semaphores and crawl delay, a global concurrency limit, dedup (Bloom filter plus a store), VT per fetch, robots.txt caching, and checkpointing for restart. See example 21 in Worked Examples.

docs.title: Virtual Threads Deep-Dive Q&A (50 questions)
docs.text: From basic to architect, all about virtual threads.

docs.title: Basics (L1)
docs.text:
1. In one sentence, what is a virtual thread?

A java.lang.Thread that the JVM, not the OS, schedules onto a small pool of carrier threads, so blocking it is cheap.

2. Which JEP made virtual threads final, and in which release?

JEP 444, in Java 21 (LTS). They were previewed in 19 (JEP 425) and 20 (JEP 436).

3. Why does main exit immediately after Thread.startVirtualThread(...)?

Virtual threads are daemon threads. Call join() on the thread, or use an executor's close().

4. Will a CPU-bound loop run faster on 1,000 VTs than on 8 platform threads (8 cores)?

No. Only 8 carriers can run at once, and the extra VTs add scheduling overhead.

5. Why is newFixedThreadPool(100, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) an anti-pattern?

It pools cheap threads and brings back queueing. Use a VT-per-task executor plus a Semaphore(100) to limit concurrency.

6. Do existing libraries need changes to run on VTs?

Mostly no. Blocking JDK APIs were retrofitted. Libraries that held synchronized around IO pinned on 21–23 (fixed in 24), and native/JNI code still pins.

7. Can you set priority or daemon status on a VT?

No. Daemon is always true, and priority is fixed at NORM_PRIORITY (setPriority has no effect).

8. What does Thread.currentThread() return inside a VT?

The virtual thread itself, never the carrier.

9. How many VTs can you create?

Millions. The limit is heap memory for their stacks and the objects they reference.

10. Does a VT have a thread ID and a name?

Yes. It has an ID, and an optional name (empty by default). Name them for debugging.

docs.title: Mechanics (L2)
docs.text:
11. What is a carrier thread?

A platform thread in the VT scheduler's ForkJoinPool that runs (mounts) virtual threads.

12. What is a continuation?

A resumable sequence of frames. yield saves its stack to the heap, and run restores it. It's the internal building block of VTs.
