13. What is the default scheduler, and how big is it?

A FIFO-mode ForkJoinPool with parallelism equal to available processors, growing up to 256 threads to compensate for captured carriers.

14. Where does a parked VT's stack live?

In heap StackChunk objects, which hold only the frames in use.

15. What happens when a VT calls Thread.sleep?

It schedules a timed unpark and yields. The carrier is freed for other VTs.

16. What happens when a VT reads from a socket with no data?

The JDK registers the socket with the poller, parks the VT, and unmounts it. When data arrives the poller unparks it, and it resumes on some carrier.

17. What happens when a VT does file IO?

File IO can't use the poller on most OSes, so the VT captures the carrier and the scheduler temporarily adds a compensating carrier.

18. What's the cost of creating a VT?

Around a microsecond: an object allocation with no OS call. Creating a platform thread costs tens to hundreds of microseconds plus memory reservation.

19. Can a VT resume on a different carrier?

Yes. Never rely on carrier identity or carrier-local state.

20. Are VTs time-sliced?

No. A VT runs until it blocks, yields, or terminates.

docs.title: Pinning and compatibility (L3)
docs.text:
21. Define pinning.

A VT that can't unmount when it blocks, so it holds the carrier OS thread for the whole wait.

22. What pinned on JDK 21–23?

Blocking inside synchronized (including contended entry), Object.wait(), native/JNI frames, and class initializers.

23. What still pins on JDK 24+?

Native frames (JNI, or foreign upcalls on the stack) and class initializers that block.

24. How do you find pinning?

JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (20 ms threshold by default). On 21–23 you can also use -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full.

25. On JDK 21, you find synchronized around a JDBC call. What are your options?

Replace it with ReentrantLock, move the IO outside the lock, upgrade the library, or upgrade to JDK 24+.

26. Should you replace every synchronized with ReentrantLock?

No. Short, CPU-only critical sections never block, so their pinning is harmless. Fix only the hot paths that block, based on JFR evidence. On 24+, keep synchronized.

27. Do ThreadLocals work on VTs?

Yes, including inheritable ones. Avoid using them as caches. Use ScopedValue for context (final in 25).

28. Are VTs visible in ThreadMXBean and jstack?

No, those show platform threads only. Use jcmd Thread.dump_to_file (and JSON format) for VTs.

29. What's the JDK 24 MXBean for the scheduler?

jdk.management.VirtualThreadSchedulerMXBean: parallelism, pool size, mounted count, queued count.

30. Can a VT be interrupted while blocked in IO?

Yes. Interruptible socket operations abort with an exception (the channel is closed for NIO channels), so cancellation works.

docs.title: Production (L3–L4)
docs.text:
31. What becomes the concurrency limit once threads are virtual?

Resources: CPU, DB connections, downstream capacity, memory, file descriptors. Limit them explicitly.

32. How do you implement load shedding with VTs?

An admission semaphore at the edge with tryAcquire, returning 503 or 429 with Retry-After when it's full.

33. How do you size the Hikari pool when VTs are on?

The same way as before: λ × DB time with headroom, kept small and checked against the DB's limits. Don't enlarge it just because there are more threads.

34. What's the effect of VTs on downstream load?

It usually rises at the same incoming traffic, because the service no longer queues internally. Coordinate with downstream owners and add bulkheads.

35. How do you do CPU-heavy work in a VT-based service?

Submit it to a bounded platform executor (size ≈ cores) and block the VT on its result.

36. How do you ensure context (MDC, security, tracing) flows into VTs you create?

Wrap executors (DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService, OTel Context.taskWrapping, Micrometer ContextExecutorService), or use ScopedValue with structured concurrency.

37. Does @Async with VTs need a queue capacity?

No queue. Use spring.task.execution.simple.concurrency-limit to bound it if needed.

38. What's the impact on GC?

More, smaller allocations (stack chunks). Generational ZGC or G1 handles it well. Watch the allocation rate and heap after GC.

39. How do you measure the benefit before rolling out?

Load-test at production-like concurrency with VTs on and off (configuration toggle), comparing max sustainable RPS at the SLO, p99, CPU, memory, and pool waiters.

40. What is the main architectural risk of VTs?

Removing the accidental bulkhead (pool size) without adding explicit limits. Overload then propagates to downstreams and memory.

docs.title: Architect (L4)
docs.text:
41. VT vs reactive: give three cases for each.

VT: CRUD/aggregator microservices, JDBC/JPA-heavy services, teams without reactive skills. Reactive: SSE/WebSocket streaming at scale, end-to-end backpressured pipelines, existing healthy reactive codebases or gateways.

42. How do VTs affect your microservice timeout strategy?

They make it more important. Blocking forever is cheap for the thread but costly for resources. Use deadline propagation, per-call timeouts, and scope deadlines.

43. How would you roll VTs out across 100 services?

Tier by IO-heaviness. Ship the platform template with guardrails, toggle by configuration, run canaries with pinning and latency dashboards, track a fleet scorecard, and keep a rollback plan.

44. Could a VT-based service run out of memory where a platform-thread service wouldn't?

Yes. Unbounded in-flight work (no admission control, no timeouts) accumulates parked VTs and their request state, where a pool would have rejected or queued it at the edge.

45. How do structured concurrency and VTs complement each other?

VTs make forking cheap. SC makes forking safe: bounded lifetimes, cancellation, error propagation, observability, and scoped value inheritance.

46. What does a JSON thread dump give you that jstack doesn't?

Every VT, grouped by thread container (executor or scope), showing the parent–child structure and making mass analysis (jq grouping) easy.

47. How do VTs change the way you size Kubernetes pods?

Size by CPU and memory demand, not thread count. Make sure cpu limits give at least 2 carriers, and watch CFS throttling.

48. When would you set jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism manually?

When container CPU detection is wrong, or to deliberately limit carrier parallelism (for isolation or benchmarks). It's rare.

49. What did Netflix-style 'VT deadlock' incidents on JDK 21 teach the industry?

With few carriers, pinned VTs waiting on a lock held by an unmounted VT can starve all carriers. The lessons were to audit synchronized+blocking on 21–23, upgrade libraries, and move to JDK 24+ (JEP 491).

50. What would you still not do with VTs today?

Pool them, run long CPU-bound work on them, rely on them for fairness or priority, keep large ThreadLocal caches, or skip explicit limits and timeouts.

docs.title: Java 8 Toolkit
docs.text:
L2

java.util.concurrent (Java 5) plus the Java 8 additions are still the backbone of every Java service. Virtual threads don't replace this toolkit. They change which pieces you use for what:

Tool Role before Java 21 Role with virtual threads ThreadPoolExecutor Run all IO and CPU work CPU-bound work only, plus legacy code CompletableFuture Avoid blocking threads during IO Still useful for composition. Plain blocking code is often simpler ForkJoinPool Divide-and-conquer CPU work Same. Also the default VT scheduler Concurrent collections Shared state Same, and even more important with millions of threads Synchronizers Coordination Same. Semaphore becomes the main way to limit concurrency ThreadLocal Per-thread cache and context Context only, ideally replaced by ScopedValue

docs.title: Why it existed
docs.text: Before Java 21, a blocked platform thread was expensive, so you avoided blocking. CompletableFuture (CF) lets you describe a pipeline whose stages run when data arrives, so no thread sits waiting.

docs.title: Core API map
docs.text:
Category Methods Create supplyAsync, runAsync, completedFuture, failedFuture (9), new CompletableFuture<>() + complete Transform thenApply (map), thenCompose (flatMap), thenAccept, thenRun Combine thenCombine, thenAcceptBoth, applyToEither, allOf, anyOf Errors exceptionally, handle, whenComplete, exceptionallyCompose (12) Timeouts (9) orTimeout, completeOnTimeout Get join (unchecked), get (checked), getNow, resultNow (19), state (19)

Every xxx stage method has xxxAsync variants: xxxAsync(fn) runs on the common pool, and xxxAsync(fn, executor) runs on your executor. Always pass your own executor in servers.

docs.title: Fan-out: then (CF) and now (VT)
docs.text:
The scenario is a product page that needs product, price, and stock from three services, each with a timeout and a fallback.

Java 8 / 11 — CompletableFutureJava 21 — virtual threads, blocking styleJava 21–24 — structured concurrency (preview) 
private final ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64);

public CompletableFuture<ProductPage> page(String id) {
    CompletableFuture<Product> product = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> catalog.get(id), io)
            .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);                      // Java 9+
    CompletableFuture<Price> price = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(id), io)
            .completeOnTimeout(Price.UNKNOWN, 200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    CompletableFuture<Stock> stock = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> inventory.get(id), io)
            .exceptionally(ex -> Stock.UNKNOWN);

    return product.thenCombine(price, (p, pr) -> new Object[]{p, pr})
                  .thenCombine(stock, (arr, s) -> new ProductPage((Product) arr[0], (Price) arr[1], s));
}

Problems: the Object[] combination is clumsy, stack traces show ForkJoinPool frames instead of your call site, a failure in product does not cancel price or stock, and the 64-thread pool still blocks 64 OS threads.

private final ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();

public ProductPage page(String id) throws Exception {
    Future<Product> product = vt.submit(() -> catalog.get(id));     // each call: plain blocking code
    Future<Price>   price   = vt.submit(() -> pricing.get(id));
    Future<Stock>   stock   = vt.submit(() -> inventory.get(id));
    return new ProductPage(
            product.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS),
            orDefault(price, Price.UNKNOWN, 200),
            orDefault(stock, Stock.UNKNOWN, 200));
}

public ProductPage page(String id) throws Exception {
    try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
        var product = scope.fork(() -> catalog.get(id));
        var price   = scope.fork(() -> pricing.getOr(id, Price.UNKNOWN));
        var stock   = scope.fork(() -> inventory.getOr(id, Stock.UNKNOWN));
        scope.joinUntil(Instant.now().plusMillis(300));   // deadline for the whole fan-out
        scope.throwIfFailed();                            // first failure cancels the siblings
        return new ProductPage(product.get(), price.get(), stock.get());
    }
}

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Using the common pool for blocking IO. It has Ncpu - 1 threads, and blocking starves parallel streams across the whole JVM.
  2. Forgetting that thenApply may run on the completing thread, which can be a Netty IO thread.
  3. Swallowed exceptions. A CF that nobody join()s or handle()s loses its exception.
  4. cancel(true) doesn't interrupt the running task (CompletableFuture ignores mayInterruptIfRunning).
  5. allOf returns Void. You re-join() every future afterwards.

docs.title: When CompletableFuture is still the right tool (even on Java 21+)
docs.text:
• You are in a reactive/async stack (WebFlux, Vert.x, the async HttpClient) and must return a CompletionStage.
  • You need an async API contract (a library method returning CompletionStage<T>).
  • You want to complete a value from a callback (new CompletableFuture<>(), then complete() from a listener).
  • For internal fan-out inside a service, plain blocking code on VTs is simpler.

docs.title: Concurrent Collections
docs.text:
L2

Need Class Notes Hash map ConcurrentHashMap Lock-free reads, per-bin locking on write, atomic compute*/merge Sorted map/set ConcurrentSkipListMap/Set Lock-free, O(log n) Read-mostly list/set CopyOnWriteArrayList/Set Every write copies the array. Listener lists, configs Bounded FIFO handoff ArrayBlockingQueue One lock, fixed array, predictable memory Optionally bounded FIFO LinkedBlockingQueue Two locks (put/take), higher throughput. Always pass a capacity Direct handoff SynchronousQueue Capacity 0. Producer waits for a consumer Handoff or queue LinkedTransferQueue (7) transfer() waits for a consumer Priority PriorityBlockingQueue Unbounded Delayed DelayQueue Elements become available after a delay Deque LinkedBlockingDeque, ConcurrentLinkedDeque Work stealing, LIFO Non-blocking queue ConcurrentLinkedQueue Michael-Scott lock-free queue

docs.title: ConcurrentHashMap: atomic compound operations
Iteration semantics
docs.text:
• ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentSkipListMap: weakly consistent iterators. They never throw ConcurrentModificationException and may or may not reflect concurrent updates.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList: snapshot iterators that see the array as it was when iteration started.
  • Collections.synchronizedList: you must hold the list's lock while iterating, or you risk a ConcurrentModificationException.

docs.title: Producer–consumer with virtual threads
docs.text:
BlockingQueue<Order> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10_000);       // bounded = backpressure

try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    ex.submit(() -> { for (Order o : source) queue.put(o); queue.put(Order.POISON); return null; });
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {                                   // 100 cheap consumers
        ex.submit(() -> {
            for (Order o; (o = queue.take()) != Order.POISON; ) process(o);
            queue.put(Order.POISON);                                  // pass the poison pill on
            return null;
        });
    }
}

Blocking on put/take is free with virtual threads. The VT simply unmounts.

docs.title: Anatomy of ThreadPoolExecutor
docs.text:
flowchart TD S[submit task] --> A{running threads < corePoolSize?} A -->|yes| N1[start new core thread] A -->|no| B{queue.offer succeeds?} B -->|yes| Q[(work queue)] B -->|no| C{threads < maxPoolSize?} C -->|yes| N2[start non-core thread] C -->|no| R[RejectedExecutionHandler] Q --> W[worker threads poll the queue]

The #1 misconception

The pool grows beyond corePoolSize only when the queue is full. With an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue (which newFixedThreadPool uses), maximumPoolSize is never used, and the queue can grow until you hit an OutOfMemoryError.

docs.title: Production-grade platform pool (Java 8 style, still valid for CPU work)
docs.text:
public final class Pools {
    public static ThreadPoolExecutor cpuPool(String name) {
        int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
        ThreadFactory tf = new ThreadFactory() {
            private final AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger();
            @Override public Thread newThread(Runnable r) {
                Thread t = new Thread(r, name + "-" + n.incrementAndGet());
                t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.error("uncaught in {}", th.getName(), e));
                return t;
            }
        };
        ThreadPoolExecutor ex = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                cores, cores,                                 // fixed size for CPU work
                60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000),              // BOUNDED queue = backpressure
                tf,
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());   // slow the producer down instead of dropping
        ex.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(false);
        ex.prestartAllCoreThreads();
        return ex;
    }
}

The same pool on Java 21+ is shorter:

ThreadFactory tf = Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 0)
        .uncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) -> log.error("uncaught in {}", t.getName(), e))
        .factory();

docs.title: Rejection policies
docs.text: Policy Behaviour Use when AbortPolicy (default) Throws RejectedExecutionException Caller can return 503 / retry CallerRunsPolicy Runs the task on the submitting thread Natural backpressure for internal producers DiscardPolicy Silently drops Best-effort telemetry only DiscardOldestPolicy Drops the head of the queue Latest value matters (e.g., UI refresh)

docs.title: Executors factory methods: what they really do
docs.text: Factory Core / max Queue Risk newFixedThreadPool(n) n / n Unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue Unbounded queue → OOM newCachedThreadPool() 0 / ∞ SynchronousQueue Unbounded threads → OOM / thrashing newSingleThreadExecutor() 1 / 1 Unbounded Queue growth newScheduledThreadPool(n) n / ∞ DelayedWorkQueue – newWorkStealingPool() (8) ForkJoinPool Per-worker deques Async mode, not for blocking work newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() (21) One new VT per task None Unbounded concurrency. Add semaphores for downstreams newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory) (21) One thread per task None Same, with a custom factory (e.g., named VTs)

docs.title: Lifecycle: then and now
Scheduling
docs.text:
ScheduledExecutorService ses = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("sched-", 0).factory());
ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::refreshCache, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);   // fixed RATE: may run late but never overlaps
ses.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::poll, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);         // fixed DELAY between end and next start

An exception kills a periodic task silently

If the Runnable throws, every later run is suppressed. Wrap the body in try/catch(Throwable).

Pattern with VTs: keep the scheduler tiny (one platform thread) and have each tick hand the real (blocking) work to a virtual thread, so a slow tick never delays the next one: ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> Thread.startVirtualThread(this::refreshCache), 0, 30, SECONDS);

docs.title: Work stealing
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph W1[Worker 1] D1[deque: t1 t2 t3 t4] end subgraph W2[Worker 2 — idle] D2[deque: empty] end W1 -- push/pop at HEAD (LIFO) --> D1 W2 -- steal from TAIL (FIFO) --> D1

Each worker owns a deque. It pushes and pops its own tasks at the head (cache-friendly), and idle workers steal large, old tasks from the tail. This same pool type is the default scheduler for virtual threads, running in FIFO async mode.

docs.title: RecursiveTask
docs.text:
class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    private final long[] a; private final int lo, hi;
    SumTask(long[] a, int lo, int hi) { this.a = a; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi; }

    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            long s = 0; for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) s += a[i]; return s;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        SumTask left = new SumTask(a, lo, mid);
        left.fork();                                   // push to own deque
        long right = new SumTask(a, mid, hi).compute(); // compute right half directly
        return right + left.join();                    // join may help by running other tasks
    }
}
long total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(data, 0, data.length));

docs.title: Parallel streams
docs.text:
long primes = LongStream.rangeClosed(2, 5_000_000).parallel().filter(Primes::isPrime).count();

Rules for parallel streams:

Do Don't CPU-heavy, stateless, large N (>10k elements × non-trivial work) Blocking IO (HTTP, JDBC) inside map Splittable sources: arrays, ArrayList, IntStream.range LinkedList, Stream.iterate, IO-backed streams Associative reductions (sum, reduce with identity) Shared mutable accumulators (list.add inside forEach) Measure with JMH Assume it's faster. It often isn't for N < 10k

Run parallel streams in a custom pool to isolate them from the common pool:

ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
try {
    long n = pool.submit(() -> list.parallelStream().filter(this::expensive).count()).get();
} finally { pool.shutdown(); }

docs.title: ManagedBlocker: telling Fork/Join you're about to block
docs.text: If you must block inside a FJ task, ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(blocker) lets the pool spawn a compensating thread. The JDK itself uses this mechanism to compensate for pinned virtual threads on JDK 21–23 (up to maxPoolSize, default 256).

docs.title: Java 21+: CPU work vs IO work
docs.text:
// IO fan-out → virtual threads
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { ... }

// CPU crunch → parallel stream / FJ (platform threads = #cores)
var scores = candidates.parallelStream().map(this::score).toList();

Virtual threads give no speed-up for CPU-bound work, because there are still only Ncpu carriers.

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text:
CPU-bound: threads ≈ Ncpu (or Ncpu + 1 to cover the occasional page fault).

Mixed / IO-bound (Goetz, JCIP):

threads = Ncpu × Utarget × (1 + W/C)

where W/C is the ratio of wait time to compute time.

Example: 8 cores, target 80% CPU, each request waits 95 ms on IO and computes 5 ms → 8 × 0.8 × (1 + 19) = 128 threads.

docs.title: Little's Law (the formula an L4 engineer reaches for first)
docs.text:
L = λ × W
concurrency in system = arrival rate × time in system

Example: 2,000 req/s, p99 latency 250 ms → 500 requests in flight. On Java 8 that means 500 platform threads (~500 MB of reserved stack, plus context-switch overhead). With virtual threads, 500 VTs cost a few MB.

Little's Law sizes every resource:

Resource Formula Example Request threads λ × request latency 2000 × 0.25 s = 500 DB connections λ_db × query time 2000 × 0.010 s = 20 (+ headroom → 30) Downstream permits λ_down × downstream latency 2000 × 0.08 s = 160

Virtual threads change which number you tune

With platform threads you tuned thread count, and that indirectly limited DB connections, sockets, and memory. With virtual threads, the thread count is effectively unlimited, so you must tune the resources directly: HikariCP maximumPoolSize, Semaphore permits per downstream, and rate limiters. See Resilience.

docs.title: Measuring instead of guessing
docs.text:
1. Expose ThreadPoolExecutor metrics: getActiveCount, getQueue().size(), getCompletedTaskCount (Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics does this).
  2. Load test, then increase the size until throughput plateaus or p99 latency rises.
  3. The right size lands at the knee of the throughput/latency curve.
xychart-beta title "Throughput vs pool size (IO-bound service, illustrative)" x-axis "Threads" [8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512] y-axis "Requests/s" 0 --> 2200 line [150, 300, 600, 1150, 1900, 2050, 1800]

Past the knee, context switching, lock contention, and GC pressure make throughput drop. Virtual threads move the knee far to the right for IO-bound work, but CPU-bound work still has the same knee.

docs.title: Synchronizers
docs.text:
L2

Synchronizer Mental model Reusable Typical use CountDownLatch A gate that opens after N events No Wait for N services to start, or N tasks to finish CyclicBarrier N threads meet, then all proceed Yes Iterative simulations, phased computations Semaphore N permits Yes Limit concurrency (bulkheads, connection caps). Essential with VTs Phaser (7) Dynamic barrier with registration Yes Variable parties, multi-phase work Exchanger Two threads swap objects Yes Double-buffering pipelines

docs.title: CountDownLatch
docs.text:
CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(3);
for (String svc : List.of("db", "cache", "broker")) {
    Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> { connect(svc); ready.countDown(); });
}
if (!ready.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) throw new IllegalStateException("startup timed out");

docs.title: CyclicBarrier
docs.text:
CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(4, () -> log.info("phase done"));  // barrier action
for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) {
    int id = w;
    Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
        for (int step = 0; step < 10; step++) {
            simulate(id, step);
            try { barrier.await(); } catch (Exception e) { return; }      // BrokenBarrierException if a party fails
        }
    });
}

docs.title: Semaphore: the virtual-thread-era rate limiter
docs.text:
public final class Bulkhead {
    private final Semaphore permits;
    private final Duration maxWait;
    public Bulkhead(int maxConcurrent, Duration maxWait) {
        this.permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent, true);
        this.maxWait = maxWait;
    }
    public <T> T call(Callable<T> c) throws Exception {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire(maxWait.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))
            throw new BulkheadFullException();                 // shed load instead of queuing forever
        try { return c.call(); } finally { permits.release(); }
    }
}

docs.title: Phaser
docs.text:
Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1);                        // register self
for (Task t : tasks) {
    phaser.register();
    Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> {
        t.stage1(); phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();
        t.stage2(); phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
    });
}
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();                      // wait for stage 1 of all tasks
phaser.arriveAndDeregister();

docs.title: Old vs new: wait for N tasks
Two different jobs
docs.text: Use Example Virtual-thread verdict Per-thread cache of an expensive, non-thread-safe object SimpleDateFormat, MessageDigest, Kryo, byte buffers ❌ Bad. One copy per VT means millions of copies and no reuse Implicit context passing MDC request id, security context, transaction ⚠️ Works, but mutable, leak-prone, and inheritance is expensive → use ScopedValue

docs.title: Classic usage and its leak
docs.text:
private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FMT =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));

// In a pooled-thread server, ALWAYS clean up context-style ThreadLocals:
try {
    CURRENT_USER.set(user);
    chain.doFilter(req, res);
} finally {
    CURRENT_USER.remove();            // otherwise the next request on this pooled thread sees the old user
}

docs.title: Replacements
docs.text: Old New ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> DateTimeFormatter (immutable, thread-safe, Java 8) ThreadLocal<MessageDigest> Create one per use (cheap), or use a small object pool ThreadLocal<byte[]> buffer Allocate per call (TLAB allocation is cheap), or use a bounded pool ThreadLocal<RequestContext> ScopedValue<RequestContext> (final in Java 25) — see Scoped Values InheritableThreadLocal ScopedValue + StructuredTaskScope (bindings are inherited by forked subtasks at no copying cost)

docs.title: Virtual-thread specifics
docs.text:
• VTs support ThreadLocal and InheritableThreadLocal (JEP 444 kept them for compatibility).
  • There is no reuse: a VT runs one task and dies, so caching in a ThreadLocal gives zero benefit and costs memory.
  • jdk.internal.misc.CarrierThreadLocal is JDK-internal. Don't depend on carrier identity.
  • Find heavy ThreadLocal users with a heap dump, by grouping ThreadLocalMap$Entry by referent class.

docs.title: Modern Concurrency (Java 21 → 25)
docs.text:
L3 L4

Virtual threads make threads cheap. The following two APIs make using many threads safe:

API Status Replaces Gives you Structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope) Preview 21–26 ExecutorService + Future for fan-out Subtask lifetimes bounded by a lexical scope, automatic cancellation, error propagation, observable task trees Scoped values (ScopedValue) Preview 21–24, final 25 ThreadLocal for context Immutable, bounded-lifetime, cheaply inherited context

Also on this tab: Virtual Threads vs Reactive and the Flow API.

docs.title: Enabling preview features
docs.text:
# Compile & run (JDK 21 example)
javac --release 21 --enable-preview Main.java
java --enable-preview Main
# Single-file launch
java --enable-preview --source 21 Main.java

// Gradle Kotlin DSL
tasks.withType<JavaCompile>().configureEach { options.compilerArgs.add("--enable-preview") }
tasks.withType<Test>().configureEach { jvmArgs("--enable-preview") }
tasks.withType<JavaExec>().configureEach { jvmArgs("--enable-preview") }

Preview means the API can change

Code written against the 21–24 StructuredTaskScope API (ShutdownOnFailure) does not compile on 25, where the API became StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner). Isolate preview APIs behind one internal class.

docs.title: Flow API & Reactive Streams (Java 9+)
docs.text:
L3

java.util.concurrent.Flow contains the four Reactive Streams interfaces, so libraries (Reactor, RxJava, Akka, the JDK HttpClient) can interoperate:

sequenceDiagram participant P as Publisher participant S as Subscriber S->>P: subscribe(subscriber) P->>S: onSubscribe(subscription) S->>P: subscription.request(n) — demand = backpressure P->>S: onNext(item) × ≤ n S->>P: request(m) P->>S: onNext ... P->>S: onComplete() / onError(t)

docs.title: SubmissionPublisher example
docs.text:
try (var publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<String>(
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), 256)) {    // per-subscriber buffer = 256

    publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<>() {
        private Flow.Subscription sub;
        public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { sub = s; s.request(10); }
        public void onNext(String item)              { process(item); sub.request(1); }
        public void onError(Throwable t)             { log.error("stream failed", t); }
        public void onComplete()                     { log.info("done"); }
    });

    for (String line : lines) publisher.submit(line);   // blocks when the buffer is full → backpressure
}

With virtual threads, a blocking submit() is cheap, which makes SubmissionPublisher a convenient in-process backpressured pipeline that needs no external library.

docs.title: Scoped Values
docs.text: L3 — final in Java 25 (JEP 506), preview in 21–24.

docs.title: Why replace ThreadLocal?
docs.text: Problem with ThreadLocal ScopedValue answer Mutable: any callee can set() Immutable within a binding Unbounded lifetime: leaks if you forget remove() Lifetime = the run/call block InheritableThreadLocal copies maps on every child thread Children of a StructuredTaskScope share the parent's bindings for free Hard to reason about data flow Data flow is visible: where(K, v).run(...) Slow lookups with many entries JIT-friendly lookups with a per-thread cache

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
public final class RequestContext {
    public static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance();
    public static final ScopedValue<Principal> USER    = ScopedValue.newInstance();
}

// At the edge (filter / controller advice)
ScopedValue.where(RequestContext.REQUEST_ID, requestId)
           .where(RequestContext.USER, principal)
           .run(() -> orderService.placeOrder(cmd));

// Anywhere deeper — no parameter threading needed
String rid = RequestContext.REQUEST_ID.get();                 // NoSuchElementException if unbound
String rid2 = RequestContext.REQUEST_ID.orElse("unknown");
boolean bound = RequestContext.REQUEST_ID.isBound();

Returning a value:

Receipt r = ScopedValue.where(USER, principal).call(() -> checkout.run(cart));   // call() for a result

docs.title: Rebinding for a nested scope
docs.text:
ScopedValue.where(USER, admin).run(() -> {
    audit();                                            // sees admin
    ScopedValue.where(USER, systemUser).run(this::job); // nested: sees systemUser
    audit();                                            // sees admin again
});

docs.title: Inheritance with structured concurrency
docs.text:
ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, "req-42").run(() -> {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
        scope.fork(() -> log("[{}] fetch user", REQUEST_ID.get()));   // "req-42", no copy cost
        scope.fork(() -> log("[{}] fetch cart", REQUEST_ID.get()));
        scope.join();
    } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
});

Plain executors do NOT inherit scoped values

executor.submit(...) runs in a new thread with no bindings. Only StructuredTaskScope.fork inherits them. Capture the value and re-bind it explicitly if you need it inside an executor task.

docs.title: Then and now: MDC / request id
The problem with unstructured concurrency
docs.text:
Future<User> u = executor.submit(() -> findUser(id));
Future<Order> o = executor.submit(() -> fetchOrder(id));
User user = u.get();     // if this throws...
Order order = o.get();   // ...fetchOrder keeps running: a LEAKED task
  • If findUser fails, fetchOrder keeps running and wastes resources.
  • If the caller thread is interrupted, the subtasks don't find out.
  • A thread dump shows no relationship between the request and its subtasks.

docs.title: The structured version
docs.text:
Structured concurrency says that subtasks started in a block must finish before the block exits, just as a method call returns before its caller continues. Errors and cancellation flow along that parent–child tree.

flowchart TD P[handle request — scope owner] --> A[fork: findUser] P --> B[fork: fetchOrder] P --> C[fork: fetchRecs] B -. fails .-> P P -. cancel/interrupt .-> A P -. cancel/interrupt .-> C P --> J[join → throw → scope closes<br/>no subtask outlives the block]

docs.title: API: Java 21–24 (JEP 453 / 462 / 480 / 499)
docs.text:
Response handle(long id) throws ExecutionException, InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
        Subtask<User>  user  = scope.fork(() -> findUser(id));
        Subtask<Order> order = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrder(id));

        scope.join()              // wait for both, or for the first failure
             .throwIfFailed();    // rethrows as ExecutionException

        return new Response(user.get(), order.get());
    }   // close(): guarantees every subtask is finished
}

Built-in policies (21–24):

Class Shuts down when Use ShutdownOnFailure First subtask fails All results required ("invoke all") ShutdownOnSuccess<T> First subtask succeeds Redundant calls ("invoke any"), scope.result() Custom subclass Your handleComplete override Quorum, "first N", collect all successes 
// First successful wins (21–24)
try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnSuccess<Quote>()) {
    scope.fork(() -> vendorA.quote(item));
    scope.fork(() -> vendorB.quote(item));
    scope.fork(() -> vendorC.quote(item));
    scope.joinUntil(Instant.now().plusMillis(400));
    return scope.result();             // losers are interrupted
}

docs.title: API: Java 25 (JEP 505, fifth preview) — reshaped
docs.text:
// All must succeed (the default joiner)
try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
    Subtask<User>  user  = scope.fork(() -> findUser(id));
    Subtask<Order> order = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrder(id));
    scope.join();                                  // throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException
    return new Response(user.get(), order.get());
}

// First success wins
try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Quote>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow())) {
    vendors.forEach(v -> scope.fork(() -> v.quote(item)));
    return scope.join();                           // join() returns the winning result
}

// Collect every result as a stream of subtasks (throws on the first failure)
try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Price>allSuccessfulOrThrow())) {
    stores.forEach(s -> scope.fork(() -> s.price(sku)));
    List<Price> prices = scope.join().map(Subtask::get).toList();
}

// Timeout via configuration
try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(),
        cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)).withName("checkout-fanout"))) { ... }
21–24 25 new ShutdownOnFailure() open() / open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow()) new ShutdownOnSuccess<T>() open(Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow()) joinUntil(Instant) open(joiner, cf -> cf.withTimeout(d)) throwIfFailed() join() throws FailedException Subclass + handleComplete Implement Joiner<T,R> (onFork, onComplete, result)

docs.title: Custom policy: quorum (Java 25 Joiner)
docs.text:
/** Succeeds when `quorum` subtasks succeed; cancels the rest. */
final class QuorumJoiner<T> implements StructuredTaskScope.Joiner<T, List<T>> {
    private final int quorum;
    private final Queue<T> ok = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
    private final AtomicInteger okCount = new AtomicInteger();
    QuorumJoiner(int quorum) { this.quorum = quorum; }

    @Override public boolean onComplete(Subtask<? extends T> st) {
        if (st.state() == Subtask.State.SUCCESS) {
            ok.add(st.get());
            return okCount.incrementAndGet() >= quorum;   // true → cancel the scope
        }
        return false;
    }
    @Override public List<T> result() {
        if (okCount.get() < quorum) throw new IllegalStateException("quorum not reached");
        return List.copyOf(ok).subList(0, quorum);
    }
}
// usage: List<Ack> acks = StructuredTaskScope.open(new QuorumJoiner<Ack>(2)) ... scope.join();

docs.title: Production advice: isolate the preview API
docs.text:
/** Stable internal facade. Only this class changes when the JDK API changes. */
public final class FanOut {
    public static <A, B, R> R both(Callable<A> a, Callable<B> b, BiFunction<A, B, R> combine, Duration timeout)
            throws Exception {
        try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {   // non-preview fallback
            Future<A> fa = ex.submit(a);
            Future<B> fb = ex.submit(b);
            try {
                long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos();
                A ra = fa.get(Math.max(0, deadline - System.nanoTime()), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
                B rb = fb.get(Math.max(0, deadline - System.nanoTime()), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
                return combine.apply(ra, rb);
            } catch (ExecutionException | TimeoutException | InterruptedException e) {
                fa.cancel(true); fb.cancel(true);                      // emulate structured cancellation
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}

When structured concurrency becomes final, swap the body of this class and leave the callers untouched.

docs.title: Same problem, two answers
docs.text:
Both solve "don't waste an OS thread while waiting":

  • Reactive (WebFlux / Reactor, RxJava, Vert.x): never block. Describe the pipeline as operators, and let a few event-loop threads run callbacks when data arrives.
  • Virtual threads: block freely. The JVM parks the cheap thread and reuses the carrier.
Reactive (WebFlux)Virtual threads (MVC) 
public Mono<OrderView> view(long id) {
    return orderRepo.findById(id)                                   // R2DBC
        .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new NotFound(id)))
        .flatMap(o -> Mono.zip(
                paymentClient.get().uri("/payments/{id}", id).retrieve().bodyToMono(Payment.class)
                             .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))
                             .onErrorReturn(Payment.UNKNOWN),
                shippingClient.get().uri("/shipments/{id}", id).retrieve().bodyToMono(Shipment.class))
            .map(t -> new OrderView(o, t.getT1(), t.getT2())));
}

public OrderView view(long id) throws Exception {
    Order o = orderRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new NotFound(id));  // JPA/JDBC
    try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        Future<Payment> p  = ex.submit(() -> paymentClient.get(id));       // RestClient
        Future<Shipment> s = ex.submit(() -> shippingClient.get(id));
        return new OrderView(o, orDefault(p, Payment.UNKNOWN, 300), s.get());
    }
}

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
• Default to virtual threads for request/response microservices.
  • Keep reactive where you need streaming, backpressure across network boundaries, or where an existing reactive codebase is healthy (don't rewrite just because of VTs).
  • Gateways (Spring Cloud Gateway) are reactive by design. That's fine. There's also a Spring Cloud Gateway Server MVC variant that runs on VTs.

docs.title: Why System.nanoTime() loops lie
docs.text: JIT warm-up, dead-code elimination, on-stack replacement, and GC all distort hand-rolled timings. The examples in this repo are good for orders of magnitude. Use JMH for decisions.

docs.title: JMH: platform pool vs virtual threads
docs.text:
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.Throughput)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 3, time = 5)
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 10)
@Fork(value = 2, jvmArgsAppend = {"-XX:+UseZGC"})
public class FanOutBenchmark {

    @Param({"100", "1000", "10000"})
    int concurrency;

    ExecutorService platform;

    @Setup public void setup() { platform = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200); }
    @TearDown public void tearDown() { platform.close(); }

    static int io() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(10); return 1; }

    @Benchmark
    public int platformPool() throws Exception { return run(platform); }

    @Benchmark
    public int virtualThreads() throws Exception {
        try (var vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { return run(vt); }
    }

    private int run(ExecutorService ex) throws Exception {
        List<Future<Integer>> fs = new ArrayList<>(concurrency);
        for (int i = 0; i < concurrency; i++) fs.add(ex.submit(FanOutBenchmark::io));
        int sum = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : fs) sum += f.get();
        return sum;                          // return the result → no dead-code elimination
    }
}

mvn archetype:generate -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jmh -DarchetypeArtifactId=jmh-java-benchmark-archetype
mvn package && java -jar target/benchmarks.jar FanOutBenchmark -prof gc

Read -prof gc too. VTs allocate stack chunks, so check gc.alloc.rate.norm per operation.

docs.title: jcstress: testing the memory model
docs.text:
@JCStressTest
@Outcome(id = "1, 1", expect = Expect.ACCEPTABLE, desc = "both see each other")
@Outcome(id = {"0, 1", "1, 0"}, expect = Expect.ACCEPTABLE, desc = "interleaved")
@Outcome(id = "0, 0", expect = Expect.ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING, desc = "store buffering: reordering!")
@State
public class StoreBufferingTest {
    int x, y;                                    // make these volatile and 0,0 disappears
    @Actor public void actor1(II_Result r) { x = 1; r.r1 = y; }
    @Actor public void actor2(II_Result r) { y = 1; r.r2 = x; }
}

On x86 this observes 0, 0 (store-buffer reordering) millions of times per run. That's proof that plain fields are not sequentially consistent.

docs.title: Load testing a service
docs.text:
Tool Strength k6 JS scripts, thresholds in CI, good for HTTP Gatling Scala/Java DSL, rich reports wrk2 / hey Quick, constant-rate (wrk2 avoids coordinated omission) JFR + async-profiler Where the time actually goes under load

Always compare at the same request rate: p50/p99, error rate, CPU, heap, DB pool waiters. Then find the max sustainable rate where p99 meets the SLO.

docs.title: Cache lines
docs.text:
CPUs move memory in 64-byte cache lines. If two threads write to different variables on the same line, the line ping-pongs between cores (MESI invalidations). This is false sharing.

flowchart LR subgraph Line["one 64-byte cache line"] A[counterA — written by core 1] --- B[counterB — written by core 2] end C1[Core 1 L1] <-->|invalidate / reload| Line C2[Core 2 L1] <-->|invalidate / reload| Line

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
// 1. Padding (manual, fragile: the JVM may reorder fields)
class PaddedCounter { long p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6,p7; volatile long value; long q1,q2,q3,q4,q5,q6,q7; }

// 2. @Contended (JDK-internal; needs -XX:-RestrictContended for user classes)
@jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended volatile long value;

// 3. Best: use JDK classes that already handle it
LongAdder adder = new LongAdder();     // Cells are @Contended internally

ConcurrentHashMap's counter cells, Exchanger, ForkJoinPool work queues, and Thread's random seeds all use @Contended internally.

docs.title: Time & Cost Savings: Java 8 → 21/24
docs.text:
L3 L4

This page answers "how much do we actually save?" in four currencies: wall-clock time, hardware, developer time, and incident time. The first table uses numbers measured with this repo's examples. The rest are models you can plug your own numbers into.

docs.title: 1. Measured in this repo (JDK 21, 4 vCPU container)
docs.text:
Scenario (example file) Java 8 approach Java 21 approach Speed-up 10,000 tasks × 100 ms IO (PlatformVsVirtualBenchmark) Fixed pool 200: 5,061 ms VT per task: 224 ms 22× Same, oversized pool 1000 1,261 ms (1000 OS threads) 224 ms 5.6× 2,000 requests × 3-way fan-out (FanOutComparison) 200 request threads + CF on 200-thread IO pool: 2,695 ms VT per request & subtask: 184 ms 14.6× 1,000,000 × 1 s sleeps (MillionThreads) Pool 200: ≈ 83 min (computed) 9.6 s ~500× Blocking in synchronized, 2 carriers (PinningDemo) n/a JDK 21: 1,014 ms (pinned) vs ReentrantLock 102 ms JDK 24 makes both ≈ 100 ms xychart-beta title "10k IO tasks (100 ms each) — wall time in ms, lower is better" x-axis ["Pool 200 (Java 8)", "Pool 1000 (Java 8)", "Virtual threads (Java 21)"] y-axis "ms" 0 --> 5500 bar [5061, 1261, 224]

Why such big numbers?

These are IO-bound workloads, and IO-bound is exactly what VTs fix. The win is throughput under concurrency: the platform pool caps concurrency at its size (time ≈ tasks / pool × latency), while VTs let all tasks wait at once. CPU-bound work gets no speed-up.

docs.title: 2. Throughput model for a real service
docs.text:
max_rps(platform) = threads / avg_latency          (thread-bound)
max_rps(virtual)  = min(cores × util / cpu_per_req,   (CPU-bound)
                        db_pool / db_time_per_req,     (pool-bound)
                        downstream limits)

Example A (CPU-heavy): an API with 200 Tomcat threads, avg latency 250 ms (240 ms IO, 10 ms CPU), on 4 cores at 70% target utilization:

Java 8 (200 threads) Java 21 (VTs) Thread-bound limit 200 / 0.25 = 800 rps none CPU-bound limit 4 × 0.7 / 0.010 = 280 rps 280 rps Result 280 rps 280 rps (no gain)

The CPU limit (280) is below the thread limit (800), so VTs don't help. Example B (IO-heavy aggregator): 250 ms latency, 2 ms CPU:

Java 8 Java 21 Thread-bound 800 rps – CPU-bound 1,400 rps 1,400 rps Result 800 rps 1,400 rps (+75%) with the same pods

Rule of thumb: VT gain ≈ min(CPU limit, other limits) / thread limit. It's largest for services with a low CPU per request and a high latency: aggregators, BFFs, gateways, and notification senders.

docs.title: 3. Hardware and cost
docs.text:
Item Java 8 (platform threads) Java 21 (VTs) Memory per waiting request ~0.5–1 MB stack reservation + thread structures ~1–10 KB of heap stack chunks 5,000 concurrent requests 2.5–5 GB of stacks; impractical ~50 MB Context switch Kernel, ~1–10 µs User-mode mount/unmount, ~100s of ns Pods for 10k concurrent slow requests (aggregator, illustrative) ~25 pods × 400 threads ~6–8 pods (CPU-bound)

Example cost model (illustrative, plug in your own prices): 25 → 8 pods at ~$70/pod-month (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is about $1,190 per month per service. Across 20 IO-heavy services, that's on the order of $285k per year. Measure your own services before quoting numbers to finance.

docs.title: 4. Developer time (code size and complexity)
docs.text:
Measured on the paired examples in this playbook:

Task Java 8 LOC Java 21 LOC Saving 3-way fan-out with fallbacks (FanOutComparison) 14 7 50% Fan-out service (fan-out-service.md) ~30 + pool config ~15 ~50% Executor lifecycle (invokeAll + shutdown) 14 10 ~30% Retry with backoff Scheduled executor + CF: ~25 Loop + sleep: 10 60% @Async executor config 12 lines of Java 1–3 properties ~80% Request context cleanup try/finally per entry point ScopedValue.where().run() No leak class of bugs

The bigger win is non-LOC: sequential stack traces, debugger stepping, normal profilers, and no reactive learning curve. Teams moving from WebFlux to MVC + VTs commonly report faster onboarding and fewer "lost context" or "swallowed error" bugs.

docs.text: Failure class Java 8 frequency Java 21+ Thread pool exhaustion cascades Common Gone. Replaced by explicit bulkheads Pool-induced deadlock (nested submit().get()) Occasional Gone ThreadLocal leaks across requests Occasional Rare (ScopedValue, bounded lifetime) Lost async exceptions Common with CF Rare (sequential code, structured scopes) Pinning n/a Possible on 21–23, mostly gone on 24+

docs.title: @Async and @Scheduled
Then vs now
Propagating context into @Async
docs.text:
@Bean
TaskDecorator contextPropagatingDecorator() {
    return runnable -> {
        Map<String, String> mdc = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
        SecurityContext security = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
        return () -> {
            if (mdc != null) MDC.setContextMap(mdc);
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(security);
            try { runnable.run(); }
            finally { MDC.clear(); SecurityContextHolder.clearContext(); }
        };
    };
}

Spring Boot applies a single TaskDecorator bean to the auto-configured executor. With Micrometer Context Propagation you can use ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator instead.

docs.title: Kafka listeners on virtual threads
docs.text:
@KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.order.order.placed.v1", groupId = "notification", concurrency = "6")
public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlaced event) {
    // blocking calls are fine: templates DB, SMS provider HTTP
    var template = templates.find(event.locale());
    smsClient.send(event.phone(), template.render(event));
}
  • concurrency is still the number of consumers (one per partition at most). VTs make each consumer's blocking work cheap, but they don't add parallelism within a partition.
  • For parallelism within a partition while keeping per-key order, dispatch each record to a per-key lane (see Case Studies) and commit offsets only after the lane finishes. Alternatively, use Confluent's Parallel Consumer.

docs.title: Scheduling patterns
The connection pool is now your real concurrency limit
docs.text: flowchart LR     subgraph Pod       V1[VT 1] & V2[VT 2] & V3[VT ...] & V4[VT 5000] --> H{HikariCP<br/>maximumPoolSize = 20<br/>connectionTimeout = 2s}     end     H --> DB[(PostgreSQL<br/>max_connections = 500)]

docs.title: Sizing (Little's Law)
docs.text:
connections_per_pod = peak_rps_per_pod × avg_db_time_per_request × safety(1.2–1.5)
Σ (pods × connections_per_pod) + admin/headroom ≤ DB max_connections

Example: 400 rps/pod × 12 ms DB time = 4.8 → pool 8–10. With 30 pods that's about 300 connections. A PostgreSQL instance often performs best at roughly cores × 2–4 active connections, so put PgBouncer (transaction pooling) in front of it if the pod count is high.

Don't grow the pool because 'VTs can handle it'

Bigger pools make the database slower: context switching, lock contention, and memory. Keep pools small, and let VTs queue cheaply on getConnection().

docs.title: HikariCP configuration
docs.text:
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      minimum-idle: 10              # fixed-size pool: no churn
      connection-timeout: 2000      # VTs waiting longer fail fast → 503 instead of piling up
      max-lifetime: 1800000
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false             # don't hold a connection for the whole request

Use HikariCP 5.1+. Earlier versions used synchronized in places that could pin on JDK 21.

docs.title: Transactions are thread-bound
docs.text:
@Transactional binds the connection to the current thread (with ThreadLocal). So:

  • Work forked to another VT inside a @Transactional method is not in the transaction.
  • Don't fan out DB writes inside one transaction. Fan out reads before opening the transaction, then write sequentially.
public OrderReceipt place(PlaceOrder cmd) throws Exception {
    // 1. Parallel reads, no TX, each uses its own pooled connection
    Cart cart; Address addr; Quote quote;
    try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        var c = ex.submit(() -> carts.load(cmd.cartId()));
        var a = ex.submit(() -> addresses.load(cmd.addressId()));
        cart = c.get(); addr = a.get();
        quote = pricing.quote(cart, addr);
    }
    // 2. Short write transaction
    return tx.execute(status -> orders.save(Order.from(cart, addr, quote)));
}

docs.title: Long-running queries
docs.text: Set statement_timeout on the DB side, and queryTimeout / jakarta.persistence.query.timeout on the client side. A VT blocked on a 10-minute report query holds a connection for 10 minutes. Route reports to a separate pool (and a read replica) so they can't starve OLTP.

docs.title: JDBC vs R2DBC in the VT era
docs.text: JDBC on VTs R2DBC Throughput Bounded by the pool, which is the same bound for both Same Programming model Plain / JPA / jOOQ / MyBatis Reactive only Transactions @Transactional Reactive transactions Ecosystem Everything Limited Recommendation Default Only inside an existing reactive stack

docs.title: Fan-out Aggregator Service
docs.text:
L2 L3

The most common microservice concurrency problem is: "build one response from N downstream calls, fast, and degrade gracefully."

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Catalog is required. If it fails, the request fails, and the other calls are cancelled.
  • Price and stock are optional. On failure or timeout, use a default and flag the response as degraded.
  • All calls run in parallel, under one deadline (800 ms).
  • No subtask may outlive the request.
  • Each downstream is protected by its own bulkhead.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     autonumber     participant C as Client     participant VT as Request VT (Tomcat)     participant S as FanOut scope (800 ms)     participant Cat as catalog VT     participant Pr as pricing VT     participant Inv as inventory VT     C->>VT: GET /api/products/p-1/page     VT->>S: open(deadline)     par fork       S->>Cat: catalog.get (bulkhead catalog)       S->>Pr: pricing.get (bulkhead pricing)       S->>Inv: inventory.get (bulkhead inventory)     end     Cat-->>S: Product (120 ms)     Inv-->>S: Stock (60 ms)     Note over Pr: slow-* ids take 5 s     S--xPr: deadline → cancel(true) → fallback Price.unknown     S->>VT: close(): every subtask finished     VT-->>C: 200 {..., degraded:["price"]}

docs.title: Java 8 version (for contrast)
docs.text:
@Service
public class ProductPageServiceJava8 {
    private final ExecutorService io = new ThreadPoolExecutor(64, 64, 0, SECONDS,
            new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000), new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());

    public ProductPage page(String id) {
        CompletableFuture<Product> product = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> catalog.get(id), io);
        CompletableFuture<Price> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(id), io)
                .completeOnTimeout(Price.unknown(id), 800, MILLISECONDS)
                .exceptionally(ex -> Price.unknown(id));
        CompletableFuture<Stock> stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventory.get(id), io)
                .completeOnTimeout(Stock.unknown(id), 800, MILLISECONDS)
                .exceptionally(ex -> Stock.unknown(id));
        try {
            return product.thenCombine(price, Pair::new)
                          .thenCombine(stock, (pp, s) -> new ProductPage(pp.a(), pp.b(), s, List.of(), ""))
                          .get(800, MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            throw new DeadlineExceededException("catalog");    // BUT pricing/inventory keep running: leak
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e.getCause());           // stack trace points into ForkJoinPool
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
        // Also: completeOnTimeout does NOT cancel the underlying call; the IO thread stays busy.
        // Also: we can't tell which parts degraded without extra flags.
        // Also: 64 OS threads cap the whole service at 64 concurrent downstream calls.
    }
}

docs.title: Java 21 version: the service
The FanOut facade (structured concurrency without preview)
Same service with StructuredTaskScope (Java 25 preview)
docs.text:
public ProductPage page(String id) throws InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAll(),
            cf -> cf.withTimeout(props.fanOutTimeout()))) {
        var product = scope.fork(() -> catalog.get(id));
        var price   = scope.fork(() -> pricing.get(id));
        var stock   = scope.fork(() -> inventory.get(id));
        try {
            scope.join();
        } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) {
            // unfinished subtasks were cancelled; fall through and inspect their state
        }
        if (product.state() != Subtask.State.SUCCESS) throw new DeadlineExceededException("catalog");
        var degraded = new ArrayList<String>();
        Price pr = price.state() == Subtask.State.SUCCESS ? price.get() : fallback(degraded, "price", Price.unknown(id));
        Stock st = stock.state() == Subtask.State.SUCCESS ? stock.get() : fallback(degraded, "stock", Stock.unknown(id));
        return new ProductPage(product.get(), pr, st, List.copyOf(degraded), Thread.currentThread().toString());
    }
}

docs.title: The sample's facade (Java 21, no preview)
Java 25 version (ScopedValue, final)
docs.text:
public final class RequestContext {
    private static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance();

    public static <T> T callWith(String id, Callable<T> body) throws Exception {
        return ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, id).call(body::call);
    }
    public static String requestId() { return REQUEST_ID.orElse("none"); }

    /** Plain executors don't inherit bindings. StructuredTaskScope.fork does, automatically. */
    public static <T> Callable<T> propagate(Callable<T> task) {
        if (!REQUEST_ID.isBound()) return task;
        String captured = REQUEST_ID.get();
        return () -> callWith(captured, task);
    }
}

docs.title: Bridging to logging (MDC)
docs.text:
The controller binds both the context and the MDC. Logback's %X{requestId} reads the MDC:

ProductPageController.java
package com.playbook.vt.api;

import com.playbook.vt.application.NotificationService;
import com.playbook.vt.application.ProductPageService;
import com.playbook.vt.concurrency.RequestContext;
import com.playbook.vt.domain.ProductPage;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestHeader;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.UUID;

@RestController
public class ProductPageController {

    private final ProductPageService productPages;
    private final NotificationService notifications;

    public ProductPageController(ProductPageService productPages, NotificationService notifications) {
        this.productPages = productPages;
        this.notifications = notifications;
    }

    @GetMapping("/api/products/{id}/page")
    public ProductPage page(@PathVariable String id,
                            @RequestHeader(value = "X-Request-Id", required = false) String requestId)
            throws Exception {
        String rid = requestId != null ? requestId : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        MDC.put("requestId", rid);
        try {
            return RequestContext.callWith(rid, () -> productPages.page(id));
        } finally {
            MDC.remove("requestId");
        }
    }

    @PostMapping("/api/orders/{id}/confirm")
    public Map<String, String> confirm(@PathVariable String id) throws Exception {
        return Map.of("result", notifications.sendOrderConfirmation(id).get());
    }

    /** Shows which kind of thread served the request. With virtual threads on: isVirtual=true. */
    @GetMapping("/api/debug/thread")
    public Map<String, Object> thread() {
        Thread t = Thread.currentThread();
        return Map.of("name", t.getName(), "isVirtual", t.isVirtual(), "toString", t.toString());
    }
}

Virtual threads remove the accidental bulkhead that the thread pool used to be. This page adds back the limits you need, explicitly and per resource.

Bulkhead with metrics
Using Resilience4j instead

resilience4j:
  bulkhead:            # SEMAPHORE bulkhead: VT-friendly
    instances:
      payments: { max-concurrent-calls: 50, max-wait-duration: 50ms }
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      payments: { timeout-duration: 800ms, cancel-running-future: true }
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payments: { sliding-window-size: 50, failure-rate-threshold: 50, wait-duration-in-open-state: 10s }

@Bulkhead(name = "payments")                        // type = SEMAPHORE (default). Avoid THREADPOOL with VTs
@CircuitBreaker(name = "payments", fallbackMethod = "queued")
public PaymentResult charge(Payment p) { return paymentsClient.charge(p); }

docs.title: Retry budgets
docs.text: Retries multiply load during an outage. Limit them with deadline budgets (example 17 in Worked Examples) and with a global retry ratio (for example, retries ≤ 10% of requests). Sleeping between retries is free on a VT, but the load you add to the downstream isn't.

docs.title: Overload test result (from the sample)
docs.text: The integration test fires 300 concurrent page requests at a 4-vCPU container, where the self-hosted downstreams compete for the same CPU. The pass criteria are no 500s, no hang: every response is a 200, a 503 (shed by a bulkhead or admission control), or a 504 (deadline). That's graceful degradation, and it's exactly what the limits are for.

docs.title: Compare virtual vs platform threads yourself
docs.text:
# Terminal 1: virtual threads ON (default)
mvn spring-boot:run
# Terminal 2: load
hey -z 30s -c 2000 http://localhost:8080/api/products/p-1/page      # or: k6, wrk, Gatling

# Then: virtual threads OFF (Tomcat's 200 platform threads)
mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments="--spring.threads.virtual.enabled=false"

Expect the platform-thread run to plateau at roughly 200 threads / 0.13 s ≈ 1,500 rps, with latency growing as the Tomcat queue fills. The VT run keeps scaling until CPU or bulkhead limits kick in.

docs.title: Shutdown sequence in Kubernetes
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram participant K as Kubelet participant P as Pod (Spring Boot) participant LB as Service / Ingress K->>P: preStop hook (sleep 5s: let endpoints update) K->>LB: remove pod from endpoints K->>P: SIGTERM P->>P: readiness → OUT_OF_SERVICE P->>P: server.shutdown=graceful: stop accepting, finish in-flight VTs P->>P: @PreDestroy: close executors (interrupt stragglers) P-->>K: exit 0 (before terminationGracePeriodSeconds) 
server.shutdown: graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s

# deployment.yaml
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 35
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] }

Executors you create yourself must be closed. The sample registers cpuExecutor with destroyMethod = "close", and FanOut scopes are closed per request by try-with-resources.

docs.title: Container CPU and the VT scheduler
docs.text:
• availableProcessors() follows the cgroup CPU limit, so a pod limited to cpu: 2 gets 2 carriers.
  • Fractional limits round up (1.5 → 2).
  • Very low limits (≤ 1 CPU) mean one carrier. A single CPU-heavy request then blocks all VTs. Give VT services at least 2 CPUs, or set -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism.

docs.title: Recommended JVM flags (Java 21/25 service)
docs.text:
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75
  -XX:+UseZGC                          # add -XX:+ZGenerational on JDK 21; generational is the default from 23
  -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
  -XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxage=1h,maxsize=200m,dumponexit=true,filename=/tmp/app.jfr
  -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=<cpu limit, only if you need to override>
"

G1 is also fine. ZGC shines when the heap is large and there are many VT stack chunks.

docs.title: Runbook: "the service is slow"
docs.text: Check Command / metric If… Is it pinning? jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned Events present on JDK 21–23 → fix synchronized+IO Is a pool exhausted? hikaricp_connections_pending, bulkhead_in_use At the limit → the downstream is slow, or the limit is too low What are VTs waiting on? JSON thread dump + jq grouping Thousands parked in one frame → that's the bottleneck CPU saturated? Pod CPU, executor_active{name=cpu} CPU work on VTs, or under-provisioned pods GC? GC pause / heap after GC Rising heap → stuck VTs (missing timeouts)

docs.text:
application.yml (from examples/spring-boot-vt)
spring:
  application:
    name: product-page-service
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true            # Tomcat request threads, @Async, @Scheduled run on virtual threads
  main:
    keep-alive: true           # virtual threads are daemons; keep the JVM alive

server:
  port: 8080
  shutdown: graceful           # finish in-flight requests on SIGTERM
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200                 # ignored for request handling when virtual threads are on
    accept-count: 1000

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,prometheus,threaddump
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true

playbook:
  concurrency:
    admission:
      max-in-flight: 5000              # Little's Law: peak RPS x p99 latency x headroom
    fan-out-timeout: 800ms             # deadline for the whole product-page fan-out
    cpu-pool-size: 0                   # 0 = availableProcessors()
    bulkheads:
      catalog:   { max-concurrent: 200, max-wait: 50ms }
      pricing:   { max-concurrent: 100, max-wait: 50ms }
      inventory: { max-concurrent: 100, max-wait: 50ms }
  downstream:
    base-url: http://localhost:8080/sim
    self-hosted: true                  # call our own /sim endpoints on whatever port we bound
    connect-timeout: 500ms
    read-timeout: 1s
  simulation:
    catalog-latency: 120ms
    pricing-latency: 80ms
    inventory-latency: 60ms

logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [%X{requestId:-}]"

With spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, Spring Boot configures:

Component What runs on virtual threads Tomcat / Jetty Every HTTP request handler applicationTaskExecutor @Async methods and AsyncTaskExecutor injection. A SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor that starts a new VT per task Task scheduler @Scheduled methods (SimpleAsyncTaskScheduler) Kafka / RabbitMQ / JMS / Pulsar listener containers Listener invocations Spring Data Redis Cluster command executor Spring for GraphQL / Spring WebMVC async Async request processing

With VTs on, Tomcat doesn't use its worker pool for requests. Limit concurrency with an admission filter (Resilience) and with server.tomcat.max-connections (default 8192).

docs.title: Bulkhead test: an invariant under 2,000 VTs
Fan-out tests: parallelism, cancellation, deadlines
Integration and overload tests
Tips for deterministic concurrency tests
docs.text:
1. Coordinate with latches, not sleeps. started.await() before triggering a failure makes the test deterministic.
  2. Assert ranges for timing (< 800 ms parallel vs 900 ms sequential) and leave CI headroom.
  3. Hammer the code: 1,000+ VTs are cheap and expose races far more often than 4 platform threads.
  4. Check cleanup: bulkhead.inUse() == 0 after the run proves permits are always released.
  5. jcstress for anything lock-free (Benchmarking).

docs.title: Case 1: grocery checkout API (fan-out + saga)
docs.text:
Requirements: p99 < 400 ms, 2k rps peak, 5 downstreams, no double charging.

Decision Choice Why Concurrency model MVC + virtual threads Blocking JDBC/JPA, readable saga code Parallel reads Fan-out scope with an 800 ms deadline Cart, address, and quote in parallel Payments Bulkhead 50 + timeout 2 s + idempotency key Isolate the slowest, riskiest dependency Writes One short TX + transactional outbox Atomic state + event, no dual writes Inventory Reservation with TTL + compensation Saga instead of distributed TX

Capacity: 2,000 rps × 0.3 s = 600 in-flight VTs (trivial). DB: 2,000 × 3 queries × 4 ms = 24 connections across pods.

docs.title: Case 2: flash sale (inventory contention)
docs.text:
10,000 users try to buy 100 units within seconds.

flowchart LR U[10k requests] --> AC{Admission<br/>token bucket} AC -->|excess| W[429 + waiting room] AC --> R[Redis DECR stock:sku<br/>atomic, single-threaded] R -->|>= 0| O[Create order async via queue] R -->|< 0| SO[Sold out]
  • Don't do SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on one hot row from 10k VTs. Lock convoys form, and the pool exhausts.
  • Do use an atomic counter (Redis DECR or UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku=? AND qty > 0, then check the row count).
  • In-JVM: AtomicInteger with a CAS loop for a single-node demo. It doesn't work across pods.

docs.title: Case 3: ordered parallel event processing
docs.text:
Process Kafka events in parallel while keeping per-key order. This is the hardened version of example 22.

/**
 * Per-key ordering, cross-key parallelism. All lane state is mutated ONLY inside ConcurrentHashMap.compute,
 * which is atomic per key, so "is a drainer running?" and "remove the idle lane" can never race.
 */
public final class KeyedLanes<K, E> implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final class Lane<E> {
        final ArrayDeque<E> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        boolean running;
    }

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, Lane<E>> lanes = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final ExecutorService vts = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    private final Consumer<E> handler;

    public KeyedLanes(Consumer<E> handler) { this.handler = handler; }

    public void submit(K key, E event) {
        var startDrainer = new boolean[1];
        lanes.compute(key, (k, lane) -> {
            if (lane == null) lane = new Lane<>();
            lane.queue.add(event);
            if (!lane.running) { lane.running = true; startDrainer[0] = true; }
            return lane;
        });
        if (startDrainer[0]) vts.submit(() -> drain(key));
    }

    private void drain(K key) {
        while (true) {
            var next = new ArrayList<E>(1);
            lanes.compute(key, (k, lane) -> {
                E e = lane.queue.poll();
                if (e == null) return null;    // idle: remove the lane atomically; next submit starts a new drainer
                next.add(e);
                return lane;
            });
            if (next.isEmpty()) return;
            handler.accept(next.get(0));       // blocking work OUTSIDE the map's bin lock
        }
    }

    @Override public void close() { vts.close(); }
}

Why this is race-free

The lane's queue and running flag are only touched inside compute for that key, which ConcurrentHashMap executes atomically per key (and with a happens-before edge between calls). A drainer that finds the queue empty removes the lane in the same atomic step, so a concurrent submit either sees the old lane (and its event is drained) or creates a fresh lane and starts a new drainer. The handler runs outside compute, because blocking inside it would block other keys in the same bin. For Kafka, track completed offsets per partition and commit only the highest contiguous one.

docs.title: Optimistic locking
docs.text:
@Entity
class Wallet {
    @Id Long id;
    long balanceMinor;
    @Version long version;          // UPDATE ... SET balance=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?
}

@Retryable(retryFor = ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class, maxAttempts = 3)
@Transactional
public void debit(long walletId, long amountMinor) {
    Wallet w = repo.findById(walletId).orElseThrow();
    if (w.balanceMinor < amountMinor) throw new InsufficientFunds();
    w.balanceMinor -= amountMinor;
}

docs.title: Distributed locks need fencing tokens
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram participant A as Worker A participant L as Lock service participant B as Worker B participant S as Storage A->>L: acquire → token 33 Note over A: long GC pause, lease expires B->>L: acquire → token 34 B->>S: write (token 34) ✔ A->>S: write (token 33) ✘ rejected: 33 < 34

Without the token check in storage, A's stale write corrupts data. Redis SET NX alone is not safe for correctness-critical work. Use it only for efficiency, such as avoiding duplicate work.

docs.text: sequenceDiagram     participant C as Client     participant API     participant DB     C->>API: POST /payments (Idempotency-Key: k1)     API->>DB: INSERT idem(k1, IN_PROGRESS) — unique     alt inserted       API->>API: process       API->>DB: UPDATE idem(k1) = {status, response}       API-->>C: 201     else duplicate key       API->>DB: SELECT response for k1       API-->>C: same 201 (or 409 if still IN_PROGRESS)     end

docs.title: Job queues on PostgreSQL with SKIP LOCKED
docs.text:
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'READY' AND run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY run_at
  LIMIT 10
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'RUNNING', locked_by = :worker, locked_at = now()
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM next)
RETURNING *;

Each pod polls the queue, and each claimed job runs on its own VT. Multiple pods never claim the same row.
