Production safety

jcmd Thread.print, jstack, and JSON thread dumps pause the JVM briefly (a safepoint): milliseconds for hundreds of threads, more with huge stacks. JFR with the default settings costs about 1% overhead. Async-profiler in CPU mode costs a few percent. jmap -dump and heap dumps can pause for seconds, so avoid them on a hot pod without draining traffic first.

docs.title: The practice target: TroubledService
docs.text:
Most pages on this tab attach tools to one deliberately broken program. It contains a deadlock, a contended lock, pinned virtual threads, 10,000 virtual threads starving on a 5-permit "connection pool", and a CPU hog. That way every tool has something real to find.

examples/tools-lab/diagnostics/TroubledService.java
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

/**
 * A deliberately misbehaving process to practise every concurrency tool on. It runs until killed and contains:
 *   1. a DEADLOCK between two platform threads ("payment-worker" / "refund-worker")
 *   2. LOCK CONTENTION: 8 platform threads fighting over one monitor ("hot-lock-N")
 *   3. PINNED virtual threads: blocking sleep inside synchronized (JDK 21-23 pins; JDK 24+ doesn't).
 *      Default 2. Pass a number >= #cores (e.g. "4" on 4 cores) to reproduce CARRIER STARVATION on JDK 21:
 *      every carrier is pinned and the other 10,000 virtual threads never get to run.
 *   4. 10,000 PARKED virtual threads waiting on a tiny "connection pool" (Semaphore(5)) -> pool exhaustion
 *   5. a CPU hog ("cpu-burner") for CPU profiling
 * Run: java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints TroubledService.java [pinnedThreads]
 */
public class TroubledService {

    static final Object ACCOUNTS = new Object();
    static final Object LEDGER = new Object();
    static final Object HOT_LOCK = new Object();
    static final Semaphore CONNECTION_POOL = new Semaphore(5);
    static final AtomicLong hotCounter = new AtomicLong();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int pinned = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 2;
        System.out.println("pid=" + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " pinnedThreads=" + pinned
                + " carriers=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());

        // 1. deadlock
        CountDownLatch both = new CountDownLatch(2);
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("payment-worker").start(() -> {
            synchronized (ACCOUNTS) { both.countDown(); await(both); synchronized (LEDGER) { } }
        });
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("refund-worker").start(() -> {
            synchronized (LEDGER) { both.countDown(); await(both); synchronized (ACCOUNTS) { } }
        });

        // 2. contention
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
            Thread.ofPlatform().name("hot-lock-" + i).start(() -> {
                while (true) {
                    synchronized (HOT_LOCK) {
                        long x = 0;
                        for (int k = 0; k < 20_000; k++) x += k;   // hold the lock doing work
                        hotCounter.addAndGet(x);
                    }
                }
            });
        }

        // 3. pinned virtual threads (sleep while holding a monitor)
        var vts = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
        for (int i = 0; i < pinned; i++) {
            Object lock = new Object();
            vts.submit(() -> {
                while (true) {
                    synchronized (lock) { Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(50)); }   // pins on JDK 21-23
                }
            });
        }

        // 4. pool exhaustion: 10k VTs, 5 permits, each holder "queries the DB" for 2 s
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
            vts.submit(() -> {
                CONNECTION_POOL.acquire();
                try { slowQuery(); } finally { CONNECTION_POOL.release(); }
                return null;
            });
        }

        // 5. CPU hog
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-burner").start(() -> {
            double d = 0;
            while (true) d += Math.sqrt(System.nanoTime() % 1000);
        });

        Thread.sleep(Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    static void slowQuery() throws InterruptedException { TimeUnit.SECONDS.sleep(2); }

    static void await(CountDownLatch l) {
        try { l.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    }
}

cd examples/tools-lab/diagnostics
java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints TroubledService.java      # prints pid=...

-XX:+DebugNonSafepoints makes profilers attribute samples to the exact line, not only the nearest safepoint.

docs.title: jcstress: Testing the Java Memory Model
docs.text:
L3 L4 · ✅ the project below was built and run on JDK 21 (x86-64, 4 vCPU); the numbers are real

Normal unit tests can't prove the absence of a race: the bad interleaving might happen once in a billion runs. jcstress (OpenJDK's concurrency stress harness) runs tiny "actor" methods concurrently hundreds of millions of times across JVM configurations, records every outcome, and classifies each one as acceptable, interesting, or forbidden.

Project: examples/tools-lab/jcstress

cd examples/tools-lab/jcstress
mvn package                                         # target/jcstress.jar
java -jar target/jcstress.jar -m quick              # all tests, quick mode (~ minutes)
java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t StoreBuffering     # tests matching a regex
java -jar target/jcstress.jar -m default            # longer, more samples
# HTML report: results/index.html

docs.title: How a jcstress test works
docs.text: sequenceDiagram     participant H as jcstress harness     participant S as fresh @State object     participant A1 as @Actor 1 (thread 1)     participant A2 as @Actor 2 (thread 2)     participant R as Result (e.g. II_Result)     loop hundreds of millions of times       H->>S: new State()       par concurrently         A1->>S: x = 1, then read y into r1         A2->>S: y = 1, then read x into r2       end       H->>R: record (r1, r2), e.g. "0, 0"     end     H->>H: histogram vs @Outcome rules → OK / FAILED

docs.title: Test 1: store buffering (can both threads miss each other's write?)
Test 2: lost update (volatile is not atomic)
Test 3: unsafe publication (plain vs final fields)
Overall run
docs.text:
(Results: 84 planned; 84 passed, 0 failed, 0 soft errs, 0 hard errs)
  Interesting tests: 2 matching test results.

84 runs = 6 tests × several JVM flag configurations (jcstress varies JIT modes and heap settings to provoke different code shapes).

docs.title: Outcome annotations cheat sheet
docs.text:
Expect Meaning Use for ACCEPTABLE Allowed and expected Normal interleavings ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING Allowed by the JMM, but surprising Documenting reorderings you want to see ACCEPTABLE_SPEC Allowed by the spec, rarely seen in practice Edge cases FORBIDDEN The test fails if it's ever seen Asserting your synchronization works

Result types: I_Result, II_Result, JJ_Result, Z_Result, L_Result, … (field r1, r2, … of the given types). Other annotations: @Arbiter (runs after the actors), and @JCStressTest(Mode.Termination) with a @Signal method (to test that a spinning thread can be stopped, e.g. that a stop flag needs volatile).

docs.title: jstack -l: deadlock detection
docs.text:
$ jstack -l 717
...
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"payment-worker":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f7380001170 (object 0x000000073745c258, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "refund-worker"
"refund-worker":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f7374000fe0 (object 0x000000073745c248, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "payment-worker"
Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================
"payment-worker":
    at TroubledService.lambda$main$0(TroubledService.java:35)
    - waiting to lock <0x000000073745c258> (a java.lang.Object)
    - locked <0x000000073745c248> (a java.lang.Object)
"refund-worker":
    at TroubledService.lambda$main$1(TroubledService.java:38)
    - waiting to lock <0x000000073745c248> (a java.lang.Object)
    - locked <0x000000073745c258> (a java.lang.Object)

How to read it: each thread holds (- locked) the object the other is waiting for (- waiting to lock). That's a cycle, so it's a deadlock. Lines 35 and 38 point straight at the opposite-order synchronized blocks. The JVM finds this cycle for you (monitors and java.util.concurrent locks). Fix it with lock ordering.

docs.title: Lock contention in the same dump
docs.text:
"hot-lock-1" #25 [743] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=954.38ms elapsed=7.49s ... waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
    at TroubledService.lambda$main$2(TroubledService.java:45)
    - waiting to lock <0x000000073745c268> (a java.lang.Object)

Seven threads are BLOCKED on the same address 0x…c268, while one holds it (- locked <0x…c268>). That's a hot lock. Take three dumps, five seconds apart: if the same address shows up in all of them, it's systematic, not bad luck.

Field Meaning #25 / [743] / nid=743 Java thread id / OS thread id (match nid with top -H to find the hot thread) cpu=954.38ms elapsed=7.49s CPU used so far. A BLOCKED thread with rising CPU means it keeps getting the lock briefly State: BLOCKED (on object monitor) Waiting to enter synchronized WAITING (parking) LockSupport.park: j.u.c locks, queues, semaphores RUNNABLE in socketRead0 Waiting on IO (the JVM can't see kernel waits)

docs.title: JSON thread dump: the only way to see virtual threads
docs.text:
jstack and Thread.print show platform threads only. With 10,000 virtual threads in TroubledService, jstack printed ~370 lines. The JSON dump contains all 10,000+:

$ jcmd 770 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json
Created /tmp/threads.json                                      (1.0 MB)

docs.title: jq recipes
docs.text:
1. Threads per container (executor / scope):

jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | "\(.threads|length)\t\(.container)"' threads.json | sort -nr | head

10004   java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@257fe2f5
18  <root>
4   ForkJoinPool-1/jdk.internal.vm.SharedThreadContainer@3379e3b3     ← the carrier threads

2. Group all threads by their first application frame. This is the most useful query of all:

jq -r '[.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[]
        | (.stack | map(select(test("^(java\\.base/|jdk\\.)")|not)) | .[0] // "(jdk frames only)")]
       | group_by(.) | map({count: length, frame: .[0]}) | sort_by(-.count) | .[:6][]
       | "\(.count)\t\(.frame)"' threads.json

9920    TroubledService.lambda$main$4(TroubledService.java:68)     ← CONNECTION_POOL.acquire()
11  (jdk frames only)
6   TroubledService.lambda$main$2(TroubledService.java:45)     ← hot lock
5   TroubledService.slowQuery(TroubledService.java:83)          ← the 5 permit holders
2   TroubledService.lambda$main$3(TroubledService.java:60)     ← pinned VTs
1   TroubledService.lambda$main$0(TroubledService.java:35)     ← deadlock

Diagnosis in one line: 9,920 requests wait for 5 "connections", which is pool exhaustion. The JVM isn't slow; the bottleneck is the resource. (This is the virtual-thread version of a "Tomcat threads all busy" incident.)

3. Count threads waiting in a specific call:

jq '[.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[] | select(any(.stack[]; test("Semaphore.acquire")))] | length' threads.json

9920

docs.title: A real finding: carrier starvation (JDK 21)
docs.text:
Run the target with as many pinning threads as there are cores (java TroubledService.java 4 on a 4-core machine) and the same dump looks completely different:

10000 threads with 0 frames        ← virtual threads that have NEVER been mounted
4 threads with 8 frames            ← the 4 pinned ones, each sleeping inside synchronized
flowchart LR V1[VT: sleep in synchronized] -->|pins| C1[carrier 1] V2[VT: sleep in synchronized] -->|pins| C2[carrier 2] V3[VT: sleep in synchronized] -->|pins| C3[carrier 3] V4[VT: sleep in synchronized] -->|pins| C4[carrier 4] Q[10,000 runnable VTs<br/>empty stacks] -. no free carrier .-> X((never run))

Thread.sleep inside synchronized pins the carrier on JDK 21–23, and sleeping doesn't trigger the scheduler's compensation. With every carrier pinned, the other 10,000 virtual threads never start. An empty stack in the JSON dump is the tell-tale sign. JDK 24+ (JEP 491) unmounts in this case. On 21, use ReentrantLock (Pinning).

JDK 21 JSON format

In JDK 21 each thread entry has only tid, name, and stack. There's no virtual flag or thread state. Later JDKs add more fields. The recipes above use only stack, so they work everywhere.

docs.title: jstat: rule out GC first
docs.text:
$ jstat -gcutil 271 1000 3
  S0     S1     E      O      M     CCS    YGC     YGCT     FGC    FGCT     CGC    CGCT       GCT
     -  83.36  68.75   2.22  98.03  94.34      2     0.022     0     0.000     0     0.000     0.022

YGC and GCT barely move, so GC isn't the problem, and you can look at threads and locks instead.

docs.title: Programmatic: ThreadMXBean
docs.text:
ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads();           // monitors + ownable synchronizers; platform threads only
ThreadInfo[] infos = mx.dumpAllThreads(true, true); // locked monitors + synchronizers

The deadlock coding problem uses this to detect and report the cycle at runtime.

docs.title: In Kubernetes
docs.text:
kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.print -l > dump-$(date +%s).txt
kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/t.json && kubectl cp <pod>:/tmp/t.json ./t.json

docs.title: Java Flight Recorder & Mission Control
docs.text:
L3 · ✅ JFR output on this page is real (JDK 21, TroubledService) · JMC is a GUI, described but not run here

JFR is a recorder built into the JVM, with about 1% overhead in its default configuration and safe for production. It records events: lock waits, parks, virtual-thread pinning, CPU samples, GC, IO. JMC is the desktop GUI for exploring .jfr files. Since JDK 21, the jfr view command gives you most of JMC's summary tables in the terminal.

docs.title: Starting a recording
docs.text:
How Command At JVM start java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar Continuous ring buffer (production) -XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxage=1h,maxsize=250m,dumponexit=true,filename=/dumps/app.jfr On a running JVM jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=lab settings=profile duration=20s filename=lab.jfr Dump the ring buffer now jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=1 filename=now.jfr Stop jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=lab

settings=default costs about 1% and is suitable for always-on. settings=profile gives more detail (lower thresholds, more stack traces) at about 2%.

$ jcmd 717 JFR.start name=s settings=profile duration=15s filename=s.jfr
Started recording 1. The result will be written to: s.jfr

docs.title: Concurrency events
docs.text: Event Fires when Default threshold jdk.JavaMonitorEnter A thread waited to enter synchronized 20 ms (10 ms in profile) jdk.JavaMonitorWait Object.wait() 20 ms jdk.ThreadPark LockSupport.park (j.u.c locks, queues, semaphores) 20 ms jdk.VirtualThreadPinned A virtual thread blocked while pinned 20 ms jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed The scheduler couldn't start/unpark a VT Always jdk.VirtualThreadStart/End VT lifecycle Off by default (high volume) jdk.ExecutionSample CPU sample of a running thread 10–20 ms period jdk.ThreadCPULoad Per-thread CPU 10 s period jdk.ThreadDump Periodic thread dump Off by default

docs.title: jfr summary: what's in the file
docs.text:
$ jfr summary s.jfr        (concurrency lines)
 jdk.JavaMonitorEnter                     4678        110167
 jdk.ThreadPark                           1581         48709
 jdk.VirtualThreadPinned                  1190         17310
 jdk.ExecutionSample                      1131         12281

Columns: event type, count, size in bytes. 4,678 monitor waits and 1,190 pinning events in 15 seconds are both red flags.

jfr view --help lists about 50 views. These four answer most concurrency questions:

Method                                                         Pinned Count Longest Pinning Total Time Pinned
-------------------------------------------------------------- ------------ --------------- -----------------
TroubledService.lambda$main$3(Object)                                 1,190         66.5 ms            59.7 s

$ jfr view contention-by-site s.jfr
                                              Contention by Site
StackTrace                                                                              Count    Avg.    Max.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----- ------- -------
TroubledService.lambda$main$2()                                                         4,677 15.7 ms 60.0 ms

$ jfr view hot-methods s.jfr
                                     Java Methods that Executes the Most
Method                                                                                        Samples Percent
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------- -------
TroubledService.lambda$main$2()                                                                   767  67.82%
TroubledService.lambda$main$5()                                                                   364  32.18%

$ jfr view thread-cpu-load lab.jfr
Thread                         System   User
------------------------------ ------ ------
cpu-burner                      0.18% 24.41%
C2 CompilerThread1              0.68%  8.78%
hot-lock-0                      1.30%  2.52%
hot-lock-5                      1.51%  2.47%
...

Reading them together: lambda$main$3 (sleep inside synchronized) pinned virtual threads for a total of 59.7 s in a 15 s window. lambda$main$2 is both the most contended site and the hottest method, which is typical when work is done inside a lock. cpu-burner uses a quarter of the machine.

Other useful views: contention-by-thread, contention-by-class, thread-count, latencies-by-type, allocation-by-thread.

docs.title: Live views without a file: jcmd JFR.view
docs.text:
$ jcmd 770 JFR.view thread-count
                              Java Thread Statistics
Time         Active Threads   Daemon Threads   Accumulated Threads   Peak Threads
---------- ---------------- ---------------- --------------------- --------------
07:38:11                 26               14                    27             27

Thread counts don't include virtual threads

This process had 10,000+ virtual threads, but thread-count (like jvm.threads.live in Micrometer) reports 26: platform threads only. Count virtual threads with a JSON thread dump, or with your own gauge (for example, ThreadPerTaskExecutor sizes, or in-flight semaphore permits).

docs.title: jfr print: raw events with stacks
docs.text:
$ jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned --stack-depth 6 lab.jfr
jdk.VirtualThreadPinned {
  startTime = 07:36:19.831 (2026-11-02)
  duration = 50.0 ms
  eventThread = "" (javaThreadId = 32, virtual)
  stackTrace = [
    java.lang.VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread(boolean, long) line: 689
    java.lang.VirtualThread.parkNanos(long) line: 648
    java.lang.VirtualThread.sleepNanos(long) line: 807
    java.lang.Thread.sleep(Duration) line: 590
    TroubledService.lambda$main$3(Object) line: 56
    java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.run() line: 317
  ]
}

parkOnCarrierThread is the giveaway: the virtual thread parked on its carrier instead of unmounting. The first application frame (TroubledService…line 56, which is line 60 in the current file) is what you fix.

Other flags: --json (machine-readable), --categories 'Java Application', and jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter --stack-depth 10.

docs.title: In-process streaming (Java 14+)
docs.text:
Turn events into metrics and alerts without files, as the Spring sample's PinningMonitor does:

try (var rs = new RecordingStream()) {
    rs.enable("jdk.VirtualThreadPinned").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(10)).withStackTrace();
    rs.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(50));
    rs.onEvent("jdk.VirtualThreadPinned", e -> pinnedCounter.increment());
    rs.onEvent("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter", e -> log.warn("lock wait {} ms on {}", e.getDuration().toMillis(),
            e.getClass("monitorClass").getName()));
    rs.startAsync();
}

docs.title: JMH: Java Microbenchmark Harness
docs.text:
L3 · ✅ the project below was built and run on JDK 21 (4 vCPU); the numbers are real

Hand-written timing loops lie, because of JIT warm-up, dead-code elimination, constant folding, and GC noise. JMH (from the OpenJDK team) handles all of that: separate forked JVMs, warm-up iterations, blackholes, and statistics with error bars.

Project: examples/tools-lab/jmh

cd examples/tools-lab/jmh
mvn package                                   # builds target/benchmarks.jar (shaded, main = org.openjdk.jmh.Main)
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar -l            # list benchmarks
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar CounterBenchmark
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar ExecutorBenchmark -prof gc
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar -h            # all options

docs.title: Benchmark 1: contended counters
docs.text:
Four threads increment one shared counter. @State(Scope.Group) plus @Group/@GroupThreads(4) is the JMH way of saying "these 4 threads share this state".

CounterBenchmark.java
package com.playbook.jmh;

import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Group;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.GroupThreads;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup;

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

/**
 * Four threads increment ONE shared counter as fast as they can. Which counter scales under contention?
 * Run: java -jar target/benchmarks.jar CounterBenchmark
 */
@State(Scope.Group)                                  // one counter instance shared by the 4 threads of a group
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.Throughput)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 3, time = 1)
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Fork(1)
public class CounterBenchmark {

    private long syncCounter;
    private final Object monitor = new Object();
    private long lockCounter;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong();
    private final LongAdder adder = new LongAdder();

    @Benchmark @Group("synchronized") @GroupThreads(4)
    public long synchronizedIncrement() {
        synchronized (monitor) { return ++syncCounter; }
    }

    @Benchmark @Group("reentrantLock") @GroupThreads(4)
    public long reentrantLockIncrement() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return ++lockCounter; } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    @Benchmark @Group("atomicLong") @GroupThreads(4)
    public long atomicIncrement() {
        return atomic.incrementAndGet();               // returned → JMH consumes it, no dead-code elimination
    }

    @Benchmark @Group("longAdder") @GroupThreads(4)
    public void adderIncrement() {
        adder.increment();                              // side effect on shared state is enough
    }
}

Result (real):

Benchmark                        Mode  Cnt    Score    Error   Units
CounterBenchmark.atomicLong     thrpt    5   52.478 ±  9.634  ops/us
CounterBenchmark.longAdder      thrpt    5  365.815 ± 17.587  ops/us
CounterBenchmark.reentrantLock  thrpt    5   20.521 ±  1.747  ops/us
CounterBenchmark.synchronized   thrpt    5    9.759 ±  2.024  ops/us
xychart-beta title "4 threads, one shared counter (ops per microsecond, higher is better)" x-axis ["synchronized", "ReentrantLock", "AtomicLong", "LongAdder"] y-axis "ops/us" 0 --> 400 bar [9.8, 20.5, 52.5, 365.8]

What it teaches:

  • LongAdder is 7× faster than AtomicLong and 37× faster than synchronized under contention. Each thread mostly updates its own striped cell, while AtomicLong makes every CAS fight over one cache line.
  • Locks pay for parking and waking threads. ReentrantLock beat synchronized here, but that varies with JDK version and contention. Measure your case; don't quote a rule.
  • LongAdder.sum() isn't an atomic snapshot, so for IDs or sequence numbers you still need AtomicLong.

docs.title: Benchmark 2: platform pool vs virtual threads
docs.text:
One "request" fans out N blocking 10 ms calls and waits for all of them. @Param runs the benchmark for each fan-out size.

ExecutorBenchmark.java
package com.playbook.jmh;

import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Level;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Param;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.TearDown;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

/**
 * One "request" = fan out N blocking IO calls (10 ms each) and wait for all. Average time per request.
 * Platform pool of 200 vs a new virtual thread per call.
 * Run: java -jar target/benchmarks.jar ExecutorBenchmark
 */
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 2)
@Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 2)
@Fork(1)
public class ExecutorBenchmark {

    @Param({"100", "1000"})
    int fanOut;

    ExecutorService platformPool;

    @Setup(Level.Trial)
    public void setUp() { platformPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200); }

    @TearDown(Level.Trial)
    public void tearDown() { platformPool.close(); }

    static int blockingIo() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(10);
        return 1;
    }

    @Benchmark
    public int platformPool200() throws Exception {
        return fanOut(platformPool);
    }

    @Benchmark
    public int virtualThreads() throws Exception {
        try (var vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            return fanOut(vt);
        }
    }

    private int fanOut(ExecutorService ex) throws Exception {
        List<Future<Integer>> fs = new ArrayList<>(fanOut);
        for (int i = 0; i < fanOut; i++) fs.add(ex.submit(ExecutorBenchmark::blockingIo));
        int sum = 0;
        for (Future<Integer> f : fs) sum += f.get();
        return sum;
    }
}

Result (real, -prof gc):

Benchmark                                             (fanOut)  Mode  Cnt       Score        Error   Units
ExecutorBenchmark.platformPool200                          100  avgt    3      12.573 ±      7.813   ms/op
ExecutorBenchmark.platformPool200:gc.alloc.rate.norm       100  avgt    3   10410.562 ±  10895.122    B/op
ExecutorBenchmark.platformPool200                         1000  avgt    3      54.354 ±      6.576   ms/op
ExecutorBenchmark.platformPool200:gc.alloc.rate.norm      1000  avgt    3   74973.388 ±  41761.902    B/op
ExecutorBenchmark.virtualThreads                           100  avgt    3      10.548 ±      0.915   ms/op
ExecutorBenchmark.virtualThreads:gc.alloc.rate.norm        100  avgt    3   79290.425 ±    181.851    B/op
ExecutorBenchmark.virtualThreads                          1000  avgt    3      11.099 ±      1.063   ms/op
ExecutorBenchmark.virtualThreads:gc.alloc.rate.norm       1000  avgt    3  855716.386 ± 511178.041    B/op
Fan-out Pool(200) Virtual threads Why 100 12.6 ms 10.5 ms Both fit: 100 < 200 threads, so the time ≈ one 10 ms call 1,000 54.4 ms 11.1 ms The pool runs 1000/200 = 5 waves × 10 ms. VTs all wait at once

-prof gc shows the cost: virtual threads allocate about 79 KB per 100 tasks, or ~800 bytes per virtual thread (thread object + continuation + stack chunks). The pool reuses threads and allocates far less. That's the honest trade-off: VTs swap threads (an OS-limited resource) for heap allocation (which the GC handles cheaply). It's the reason you don't create VTs for nanosecond-sized CPU tasks.

docs.title: The rules that make benchmarks correct
docs.text: Rule In the code Return the result or use a Blackhole, or the JIT deletes the work Methods return long/int Use @State for inputs (not constants), or the JIT folds them Counters live in the state object Fork at least once (@Fork(1)) so profiles from other benchmarks don't leak in @Fork(1) Warm up @Warmup(iterations = 3) Read the error column: overlapping intervals mean "no proven difference" ± Test contention explicitly @GroupThreads(4), @Threads(n), or -t 4 Look at allocation, not only time -prof gc Check what was actually compiled -prof perfasm (Linux, needs hsdis)

docs.title: Useful command-line options
docs.text:
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar CounterBenchmark -f 3 -wi 5 -i 10      # 3 forks, 5 warmups, 10 measurements
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar ExecutorBenchmark -p fanOut=10000      # override a @Param
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar -t 8 SomeBenchmark                     # 8 threads
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar -rf json -rff results.json             # machine-readable (jmh.morethan.io visualizes it)
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar -prof stack                            # where benchmark threads spend time (incl. waiting)

docs.title: Concurrency Libraries
docs.text:
L2 → L4

Before hand-writing a cache, rate limiter, or lock-free queue, check this list. These libraries are battle-tested and well-benchmarked. (Coordinates are indicative. Check Maven Central for current versions.)

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Library Use Concurrency highlights Caffeine (com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine) In-process cache W-TinyLFU eviction, lock-amortized reads, AsyncLoadingCache = single-flight loading, refreshAfterWrite Guava Cache Legacy cache Superseded by Caffeine 
AsyncLoadingCache<String, Product> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(10_000)
        .refreshAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(5))     // serve stale while ONE thread refreshes
        .buildAsync(id -> productClient.get(id));     // concurrent misses for one key → one load

docs.title: Resilience: bulkheads, rate limits, retries
docs.text: Library Use Notes Resilience4j CircuitBreaker, Bulkhead (semaphore), RateLimiter, Retry, TimeLimiter Prefer the semaphore bulkhead with virtual threads Failsafe Retry, circuit breaker, timeout, bulkhead, fallback Small, composable policies Bucket4j Token-bucket rate limiting, local or distributed (Redis/Hazelcast/JCache) Production version of problem 17

docs.title: High-performance queues and data structures
docs.text: Library Use JCTools Lock-free SPSC/MPSC/MPMC queues (used by Netty and others), faster than j.u.c queues for specific producer/consumer shapes LMAX Disruptor Ring-buffer, single-writer event processing with very low latency (Log4j 2 async loggers use it) Agrona Low-level buffers, ring buffers, and agents (used by Aeron) Eclipse Collections, fastutil Primitive collections. Fewer objects means less GC pressure under load

docs.title: Asynchronous and reactive programming
docs.text: Library Model Project Reactor Mono/Flux, backpressure (Spring WebFlux) RxJava 3 Observable/Flowable Vert.x Event loop + verticles (also supports virtual threads) Apache Pekko (fork of Akka) Actors, streams, clustering Kotlin coroutines Suspend functions, structured concurrency on the JVM

docs.title: Distributed coordination
docs.text: Library Use ShedLock "Run this @Scheduled job on only one node" using a DB/Redis lock row Redisson Redis-backed locks, semaphores, rate limiters (add fencing for correctness-critical work, see Distributed Concurrency) Apache Curator ZooKeeper recipes: leader election, locks, barriers Hazelcast Distributed maps, locks (CP subsystem), executors Quartz, JobRunr, db-scheduler Durable, clustered job scheduling Confluent Parallel Consumer Kafka consumption parallel within a partition, with per-key ordering

docs.title: Context propagation and observability
docs.text: Library Use Micrometer + Context Propagation Metrics, and carrying ThreadLocal context (MDC, tracing) across executors OpenTelemetry Java Traces; Context.taskWrapping(executor) jdk.jfr (built in) Custom JFR events for your own concurrency hotspots

docs.title: When to hand-roll anyway
docs.text:
• Interviews (see the Coding Interview tab).
  • Something tiny and domain-specific, where pulling in a dependency isn't worth it. Even then, test it with Lincheck/jcstress.

docs.title: Load Testing
docs.text:
L3 · Tools are described with ready-to-use scripts. No load-test numbers were measured for this page.

Micro-benchmarks (JMH) tell you which code is faster. Load tests tell you how the whole service behaves under concurrency: throughput, tail latency, where it saturates, and how it fails.

Tool Language Strengths Watch out k6 JavaScript Constant-arrival-rate executor, thresholds as CI gates, good docs Not a JVM tool (that's fine) Gatling Java/Kotlin/Scala DSL Rich HTML reports, open/closed workload models Heavier setup wrk2 CLI + Lua Constant rate, accurate HDR latency histograms Linux build, HTTP only hey / oha CLI Quick smoke load Closed-loop: suffers from coordinated omission JMeter GUI/XML Protocol variety, many teams know it Verbose, closed-loop by default vegeta CLI Constant rate, attack/report pipeline HTTP only

docs.title: Coordinated omission: why the tool's model matters
docs.text:
A closed-loop tool (N virtual users, each sending the next request after the previous one returns) automatically slows down when your service slows down, so it never measures the queueing your real users would experience. Open-model / constant-rate tools (k6 constant-arrival-rate, wrk2 -R, Gatling constantUsersPerSec) keep sending at the target rate, so latency includes queueing delay.

sequenceDiagram participant C as Closed-loop client participant S as Service (stalls 2 s) C->>S: request 1 Note over S: stall S-->>C: 2 s later Note over C: requests that "should" have been sent<br/>during the stall were never sent → hidden latency

docs.title: k6: constant arrival rate against the sample
docs.text:
// load/product-page.js — run: k6 run load/product-page.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    steady: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 1000, timeUnit: '1s',        // 1000 req/s regardless of response time
      duration: '2m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 500, maxVUs: 5000,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],      // < 1% errors (503 sheds count as errors here)
    http_req_duration: ['p(99)<400'],    // p99 under 400 ms or the run fails (CI gate)
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`http://localhost:8080/api/products/p-${__ITER % 1000}/page`);
  check(res, { 'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

docs.title: wrk2: quick constant-rate test
docs.text: wrk -t4 -c400 -d60s -R2000 --latency http://localhost:8080/api/products/p-1/page

docs.title: Experiment recipe: virtual vs platform threads
docs.text:
# A: virtual threads (default in the sample)
java -jar target/spring-boot-vt-1.0.0.jar
k6 run load/product-page.js

# B: platform threads (Tomcat's 200-thread pool)
java -jar target/spring-boot-vt-1.0.0.jar --spring.threads.virtual.enabled=false
k6 run load/product-page.js

Compare at the same request rate: p50/p99, error rate (503s from admission control are good failures), CPU, heap after GC, and the bulkhead and Hikari metrics. Then raise the rate until p99 breaks the SLO; that rate is your capacity. Repeat on hardware like production, because a laptop's numbers don't transfer.

$ curl -H 'Accept: text/plain' localhost:8091/actuator/threaddump | head
2026-11-02 07:49:48
Full thread dump OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (21.0.12.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu mixed mode, sharing):

"Reference Handler" - Thread t@9

    at java.base@21.0.12.1/java.lang.ref.Reference.waitForReferencePendingList(Native Method)
    ...

$ curl localhost:8091/actuator/threaddump | jq -c '.threads | length, (group_by(.threadState) | map({state: .[0].threadState, n: length}))'
25
[{"state":"RUNNABLE","n":8},{"state":"TIMED_WAITING","n":10},{"state":"WAITING","n":7}]

Actuator, jvm.threads.live, and ThreadMXBean don't see virtual threads

The sample serves every request on a virtual thread, yet the dump lists 25 platform threads. For virtual threads, use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json (JDK tools). Protect /actuator/threaddump (it exposes internals) and never make it public.

docs.title: Tracing across threads
docs.text:
OpenTelemetry's Java agent and Micrometer Tracing keep trace context in ThreadLocals. Work you hand to your own executors must be wrapped, or the trace breaks at the thread boundary:

ExecutorService traced = io.opentelemetry.context.Context.taskWrapping(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
// or Micrometer: ContextExecutorService.wrap(executor, () -> ContextSnapshotFactory.builder().build().captureAll())

docs.title: Profilers
docs.text: L3 · async-profiler CPU mode was run for this page. Its other modes and the GUI profilers are documented, not run here.

docs.title: Why sampling profilers, and why async-profiler
docs.text:
Classic JVMTI profilers only sample at safepoints, so they show where threads stopped, not where time was spent (safepoint bias). async-profiler uses perf_events and AsyncGetCallTrace to sample anywhere, including native and kernel frames, with a few percent overhead. That makes it the standard tool for CPU and lock analysis, and it's what IntelliJ's profiler uses internally.

Mode Flag Answers CPU -e cpu Where is CPU time spent? Wall clock -e wall (use -t for per-thread) Where is elapsed time spent, including waiting, sleeping, and blocking? Best for "slow but CPU is idle" Lock -e lock Which monitors/locks do threads wait on, and for how long? Allocation -e alloc Who allocates (TLAB-sampled)? Interval -i 1ms Sampling rate Output -f out.html (flame graph), -o flat=10, -o collapsed, -f out.jfr Report format

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
curl -LO https://github.com/async-profiler/async-profiler/releases/download/v4.1/async-profiler-4.1-linux-x64.tar.gz
tar xzf async-profiler-4.1-linux-x64.tar.gz
./async-profiler-4.1-linux-x64/bin/asprof --version

On Linux, allow perf events for non-root users (sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1) or run as the JVM's user. In containers, -e cpu may fall back to itimer, which is fine for most work.

docs.title: CPU profile of TroubledService (real output)
docs.text:
$ asprof -e cpu -d 8 -o flat=8 <pid>
Profiling for 8 seconds
Done
--- Execution profile ---
Total samples       : 1753
unknown_Java        : 14 (0.80%)
not_walkable_Java   : 526 (30.01%)

          ns  percent  samples  top
  ----------  -------  -------  ---
  5451300111   30.22%      545  [vdso]
  4053414665   22.47%      391  TroubledService.lambda$main$2
  2414299849   13.39%      232  _raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore_[k]
  2218522807   12.30%      204  finish_task_switch.isra.0_[k]
  2019718127   11.20%      202  TroubledService.lambda$main$5
   169945687    0.94%       17  os::javaTimeNanos

How to read it:

  • lambda$main$2 (the hot-lock loop, 22%) and lambda$main$5 (the CPU burner, 11%) are the application's CPU consumers, which matches jfr view hot-methods.
  • [vdso] (30%) is System.nanoTime() in the burner's loop (a fast kernel clock call).
  • _raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore_[k] and finish_task_switch_[k] are kernel frames for context switching and futex wake-ups. That's the cost of 8 threads fighting over one monitor: the OS keeps parking and waking them. JVMTI profilers can't show this at all.
  • not_walkable_Java (30%) are samples where the Java stack couldn't be walked (often in the middle of a transition). Adding -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints and running longer reduces the noise.

For a visual answer, write a flame graph:

asprof -e cpu -d 30 -f cpu.html <pid>       # open cpu.html: width = time, hover for details

docs.title: Lock and wall-clock profiling (commands to use)
docs.text:
These modes weren't run for this page, so there's no output to show. Here is what you'd use them for on the same target:

# Which locks do threads wait on? Expect TroubledService.lambda$main$2 / java.lang.Object (HOT_LOCK) to dominate.
asprof -e lock -d 30 -f lock.html <pid>

# Where does elapsed time go per thread? Expect the deadlocked threads at 100% in monitor enter,
# and the pinned virtual threads' carriers in Thread.sleep.
asprof -e wall -t -d 30 -f wall.html <pid>

# Start profiling at JVM launch as an agent
java -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=startup.html -jar app.jar

Wall clock is the concurrency profiler

CPU profiles hide waiting. If latency is high but CPU is low, -e wall -t shows which threads spend their time in park, Object.wait, socket reads, or getConnection. The flame graph is then split per thread.

docs.title: Annotate your intent
docs.text:
import com.google.errorprone.annotations.concurrent.GuardedBy;   // or javax.annotation.concurrent / jcip
import com.google.errorprone.annotations.ThreadSafe;
import com.google.errorprone.annotations.Immutable;

@ThreadSafe

Even without tooling, @GuardedBy documents which lock protects which field, and that's the first thing a reviewer needs to know.

docs.title: Error Prone: @GuardedBy checked at compile time
SpotBugs: inconsistent synchronization
ArchUnit: your team's concurrency rules as tests
docs.text:
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.acme")
class ConcurrencyRulesTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule noThreadLocalFields = fields().that().haveRawType(ThreadLocal.class)
            .should().bePrivate().andShould().beStatic()
            .because("ThreadLocal caches multiply per virtual thread; use ScopedValue or a shared instance");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule noRawThreads = noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..application..")
            .should().callConstructor(Thread.class, Runnable.class)
            .because("use an injected executor or Thread.ofVirtual() via the platform's helpers");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule noParallelStreamsInServices = noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..application..")
            .should().callMethod(java.util.Collection.class, "parallelStream")
            .because("parallel streams share the common pool; blocking IO there starves the JVM");
}

docs.title: Awaitility: assert asynchronous outcomes
docs.text:
Thread.sleep(500) in tests is either too short (flaky on a slow CI machine) or too long (slow on every machine). Awaitility polls a condition until it's true or a timeout expires.

AwaitilityTest.java
package com.playbook.tools;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.time.Duration;

import static org.awaitility.Awaitility.await;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

/**
 * Testing asynchronous code WITHOUT Thread.sleep: Awaitility polls a condition until it holds or a timeout expires.
 * Fast when the system is fast, tolerant when CI is slow, and the failure message says what never became true.
 */
class AwaitilityTest {

    @Test
    void orderIsEventuallyProcessed() {
        try (var processor = new OrderProcessor()) {
            processor.submit("order-1");
            processor.submit("order-2");

            await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
                   .pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(10))
                   .until(() -> processor.isProcessed("order-2"));

            await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
                   .untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(processor.processedCount()).isEqualTo(2));
        }
    }

    @Test
    void stateStaysStableDuringAWindow() {
        try (var processor = new OrderProcessor()) {
            // nothing submitted: assert the count STAYS 0 for 200 ms (Awaitility "during")
            await().during(Duration.ofMillis(200)).atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
                   .until(() -> processor.processedCount() == 0);
        }
    }
}

The class under test is a plain asynchronous worker:

OrderProcessor.java
package com.playbook.tools;

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue;

/** Asynchronous worker: callers submit and return immediately; a virtual thread processes in the background. */
public class OrderProcessor implements AutoCloseable {
    private final BlockingQueue<String> inbox = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();
    private final Set<String> processed = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
    private final Thread worker = Thread.ofVirtual().name("order-processor").start(this::loop);

    public void submit(String orderId) { inbox.add(orderId); }

    public boolean isProcessed(String orderId) { return processed.contains(orderId); }

    public int processedCount() { return processed.size(); }

    private void loop() {
        try {
            while (true) {
                String id = inbox.take();
                Thread.sleep(20);                 // simulated work
                processed.add(id);
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    @Override public void close() { worker.interrupt(); }
}
API Meaning await().atMost(d).until(callable) Poll until true, or fail after d with a ConditionTimeoutException untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(...)) Retry an AssertJ/JUnit assertion. The failure shows the last assertion message pollInterval(d), pollDelay(d) How often, and how long before the first check during(d) The condition must stay true for the whole window ("nothing happens") ignoreExceptions() Treat exceptions thrown while polling as "not yet"

docs.title: Lincheck: checking linearizability automatically
docs.text:
You declare the operations. Lincheck generates concurrent scenarios, runs them (stress mode), or systematically explores interleavings (model checking mode). It then checks that every result matches some sequential order. On failure it prints the exact interleaving.

LincheckTest.java
package com.playbook.tools;

import org.jetbrains.kotlinx.lincheck.LinChecker;
import org.jetbrains.kotlinx.lincheck.annotations.Operation;
import org.jetbrains.kotlinx.lincheck.strategy.managed.modelchecking.ModelCheckingOptions;
import org.jetbrains.kotlinx.lincheck.strategy.stress.StressOptions;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;

/**
 * Lincheck generates concurrent scenarios from the @Operation methods, runs them, and checks every result against
 * some SEQUENTIAL execution (linearizability). Model checking explores interleavings systematically and prints the
 * exact interleaving that breaks your code.
 */
class LincheckTest {

    /** Lincheck test for the BROKEN counter: we EXPECT it to find a bug. */
    public static class BrokenCounterTest {
        private final BrokenCounter counter = new BrokenCounter();
        @Operation public int incrementAndGet() { return counter.incrementAndGet(); }
        @Operation public int get() { return counter.get(); }
    }

    /** Same operations on a correct implementation. */
    public static class AtomicCounterTest {
        private final AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
        @Operation public int incrementAndGet() { return counter.incrementAndGet(); }
        @Operation public int get() { return counter.get(); }
    }

    @Test
    void modelCheckingFindsTheLostUpdate() {
        Throwable failure = assertThrows(Throwable.class,
                () -> LinChecker.check(BrokenCounterTest.class, new ModelCheckingOptions()));
        System.out.println("=== Lincheck report for BrokenCounter ===\n" + failure.getMessage());
    }

    @Test
    void atomicCounterIsLinearizable() {
        LinChecker.check(AtomicCounterTest.class, new ModelCheckingOptions());
        LinChecker.check(AtomicCounterTest.class, new StressOptions());
    }
}
BrokenCounter.java (the bug)
package com.playbook.tools;

/** Deliberately NOT thread-safe: Lincheck finds the interleaving that loses an update. */
public class BrokenCounter {
    private volatile int value;                   // volatile gives visibility, NOT atomicity

    public int incrementAndGet() { return ++value; }

    public int get() { return value; }
}

Real Lincheck report for BrokenCounter (columns trimmed for width. The read-arrow printed as ? in this console's encoding and is shown here as ➜):

= Invalid execution results =
| ------------------------------------------- |
|       Thread 1       |       Thread 2       |
| ------------------------------------------- |
| incrementAndGet(): 1 | incrementAndGet(): 1 |
| ------------------------------------------- |

The following interleaving leads to the error:
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|       Thread 1       |                                Thread 2                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|                      | incrementAndGet(): 1                                                  |
|                      |   counter.incrementAndGet(): 1 at LincheckTest$BrokenCounterTest...   |
|                      |     value ➜ 0 at BrokenCounter.incrementAndGet(BrokenCounter.java:7)  |
|                      |     switch                                                            |
| incrementAndGet(): 1 |                                                                       |
|                      |     value = 1 at BrokenCounter.incrementAndGet(BrokenCounter.java:7)  |
|                      |   result: 1                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

How to read it: both increments returned 1, which no sequential order can produce (one of them must return 2). The trace shows Thread 2 read value (0), then a context switch let Thread 1 do its whole increment, and then Thread 2 wrote its stale 0 + 1. That's the lost update, found by systematic exploration rather than luck, and pointed at the exact line. AtomicCounterTest passes both model checking and stress mode.

sequenceDiagram participant T1 as Thread 1 participant V as value participant T2 as Thread 2 T2->>V: read value → 0 Note over T2: context switch (found by model checking) T1->>V: read 0, write 1, return 1 T2->>V: write 0 + 1 = 1, return 1 ← lost update

Maven coordinates: org.jetbrains.kotlinx:lincheck-jvm (not lincheck, which is only the Kotlin-multiplatform root). Surefire needs -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading on JDK 21+ to avoid the dynamic-agent warning.

docs.title: Plain JUnit: the "hammer" pattern
docs.text:
Every solution in this playbook is tested this way: thousands of virtual threads, then assert an invariant:

@Test
void transfersConserveMoney() throws Exception {
    try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) ex.submit(() -> bank.transfer(randomFrom(), randomTo(), randomAmount()));
    }
    assertThat(bank.total()).isEqualTo(INITIAL_TOTAL);
}

Tips: assert invariants (sum, count, no negatives), not specific interleavings. Coordinate with latches, not sleeps. And repeat the test (@RepeatedTest(50)) for code that can fail intermittently.
