docs.title: The idea in one diagram
docs.text: flowchart TB     subgraph Before["Java 8–20: thread-per-request with platform threads"]       R1[Request] --> PT1[OS thread 1 — blocked on DB 95% of the time]       R2[Request] --> PT2[OS thread 2 — blocked on HTTP]       R3[Request ...] --> PTN[OS thread 200 — pool exhausted → requests queue]     end     subgraph After["Java 21+: thread-per-request with virtual threads"]       Q1[Request 1] --> V1[VT 1]       Q2[Request 2] --> V2[VT 2]       Q3[Request 100 000] --> VN[VT 100 000]       V1 & V2 & VN -. mounted only while running CPU work .-> C[8 carrier OS threads]     end

docs.title: Three sentences to remember
docs.text:
1. A virtual thread is a java.lang.Thread that the JVM schedules onto a small pool of OS carrier threads.
  2. When it blocks (socket, sleep, lock, queue), it unmounts: its stack is saved to the heap and the carrier runs another VT.
  3. So blocking becomes cheap, and the simple thread-per-request style scales like async code. That helps throughput, not the latency of a single request.

docs.title: What problem do they solve?
docs.text:
A typical web request spends ~5% of its time on CPU and ~95% waiting on databases, HTTP, or caches. With platform threads, every waiting request holds an OS thread with about 1 MB of reserved stack. A server tops out at a few thousand concurrent requests, long before CPU is saturated.

Virtual threads make waiting free, so you can have one thread per concurrent task, even a million of them.

docs.title: Five ways to create a virtual thread
docs.text:
// 1. Fire and forget
Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> System.out.println("hello from " + Thread.currentThread()));

// 2. Builder: named, started
Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().name("worker-1").start(() -> doWork());
t.join();

// 3. Builder: unstarted
Thread u = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> doWork());
u.start();

// 4. Factory: names get a counter: io-0, io-1, ...
ThreadFactory f = Thread.ofVirtual().name("io-", 0).factory();

// 5. Executor: the one you will use 90% of the time
try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    ex.submit(() -> doWork());
}

docs.title: Hello, one million threads
docs.text:
public class MillionThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000).forEach(i ->
                ex.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); return i; }));
        }
        System.out.printf("1M tasks, each sleeping 1s, finished in %d ms%n",
                (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000);
    }
}

Measured (examples/plain-java/MillionThreads.java, JDK 21, 4-vCPU container): 200,000 tasks in 2.5 s, and 1,000,000 tasks in 9.6 s (most of that is creating and scheduling a million objects on 4 cores). With Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200) it takes 1_000_000 / 200 × 1 s ≈ 83 minutes. Try newCachedThreadPool() and you get OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread.

Runnable version: examples/plain-java/MillionThreads.java.

docs.title: Platform vs virtual: side by side
docs.text: Platform thread Virtual thread Created by new Thread(), Thread.ofPlatform() Thread.ofVirtual(), Thread.startVirtualThread() Backed by 1 OS thread for its whole life Any carrier, only while running Stack Fixed reservation (default 512 KB–1 MB) Growable stack chunks on the heap Creation ~µs to 100 µs (syscall) ~sub-µs (object allocation) Daemon Configurable Always daemon Priority Configurable Always NORM_PRIORITY (setPriority is ignored) Thread group Configurable A fixed "VirtualThreads" group isVirtual() false true Pool it? Yes Never

docs.title: What virtual threads are NOT
docs.text:
• Not faster threads. A single request's latency stays the same. You gain throughput: more concurrent requests on the same hardware.
  • Not for CPU-bound work. With 8 cores you get 8 units of compute, whether 8 or 8 million threads are runnable.
  • Not green threads from Java 1.1. Those were M:1 (all on one OS thread). VTs are M:N, with multi-core work stealing.
  • Not coroutines you must mark. No async/await keywords and no colored functions. Existing blocking code just works.

docs.title: Example: an echo server, old vs new
Quiz (answers in Interview → VT Q&A)
docs.text:
1. Why does main exit immediately after Thread.startVirtualThread(...) unless you join()?
  2. Will a CPU-bound loop run faster on 1,000 virtual threads than on 8 platform threads?
  3. Why is Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) an anti-pattern?

docs.title: The three pieces
docs.text:
classDiagram class VirtualThread { +Continuation cont +Executor scheduler +volatile int state +Thread carrierThread +run() +park() +unpark() } class Continuation { +StackChunk tail +run() "mount + resume" +yield() "unmount + freeze stack" } class ForkJoinPool { +parallelism = #cores +asyncMode = FIFO +maxPoolSize = 256 } class CarrierThread { platform thread } VirtualThread --> Continuation : runs inside VirtualThread --> ForkJoinPool : scheduled on ForkJoinPool --> CarrierThread : owns N
  1. Continuation (jdk.internal.vm.Continuation): a resumable unit of execution. yield() freezes the frames into heap StackChunk objects. run() thaws them back onto the carrier stack.
  2. Scheduler: a dedicated FIFO ForkJoinPool. parallelism defaults to availableProcessors().
  3. Carrier thread: a platform thread in that pool that mounts VTs.

docs.title: Mount / unmount lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram autonumber participant VT as Virtual Thread participant S as Scheduler (FJP) participant C as Carrier (OS thread) participant OS as Kernel / Poller VT->>S: start() → submit continuation S->>C: worker picks task C->>VT: mount (thaw frames) VT->>VT: run user code VT->>OS: socket.read() would block Note over VT,OS: JDK registers the fd with the Poller (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) VT->>C: yield → freeze frames to heap C->>S: carrier free → runs other VTs OS-->>S: fd readable → unpark(VT) S->>C: some carrier (maybe different!) C->>VT: mount, continue after read() VT->>VT: return → TERMINATED

Key consequences:

  • A VT may resume on a different carrier. Never assume a carrier's identity or keep carrier-local state.
  • Thread.currentThread() returns the virtual thread, never the carrier.
  • Unmounting copies only the frames that changed (lazy copy), which is why parking costs around 100s of nanoseconds.

docs.title: What unmounts and what doesn't
docs.text:
Operation JDK 21–23 JDK 24+ Thread.sleep, LockSupport.park Unmounts Unmounts BlockingQueue.take/put, ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch Unmounts Unmounts Socket IO (java.net.Socket, SocketChannel, HttpClient, JDBC drivers using sockets) Unmounts (poller) Unmounts synchronized block where the VT blocks inside Pins Unmounts (JEP 491) Contended synchronized entry Pins Unmounts Object.wait() Pins (compensates by adding a carrier) Unmounts File IO (FileInputStream, Files.*) Captures the carrier; the pool compensates with an extra carrier Same DNS lookup (InetAddress) Captures the carrier, with compensation Same Native method / JNI / foreign function call that blocks Pins Pins Class initializer (<clinit>) blocking Pins Pins

"Captures with compensation" means the scheduler temporarily adds a carrier (up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize, default 256) so that the other VTs keep running.

docs.title: The scheduler knobs
docs.text:
System property Default Meaning jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism #cores Carriers that run VTs concurrently jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize max(parallelism, 256) Cap including compensation threads jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.minRunnable max(parallelism/2, 1) Minimum runnable carriers jdk.unparker.maxPoolSize – Timer threads that wake sleeping VTs

You almost never tune these. Watch for container CPU limits: availableProcessors() respects cgroups, so a pod limited to 2 CPUs gets 2 carriers.

docs.title: Memory: why a million threads fit
docs.text:
• A platform thread reserves its entire -Xss stack (1 MB virtual, committed lazily but never returned).
  • A VT's frames live in StackChunk heap objects that hold only the frames actually in use, often < 1 KB for a parked web request. 1M parked VTs need roughly 1 GB or less of heap, and they are garbage-collected like any other object.
  • GC treats stack chunks as ordinary heap objects. Generational ZGC (default generational from JDK 23) handles this well.

docs.title: Preemption: there isn't any (yet)
docs.text: VTs are not time-sliced. A VT that runs CPU work without blocking keeps its carrier until it blocks or finishes. With 8 carriers and 8 CPU-spinning VTs, all other VTs starve. That's why CPU work goes to a bounded platform pool (L7 pitfalls).

docs.title: L3: Pinning, and How JEP 491 Fixed synchronized
What is pinning?
docs.text:
A virtual thread is pinned when it cannot unmount from its carrier while blocked. The carrier OS thread blocks too. If all carriers are pinned, every virtual thread in the JVM stops making progress, even ones that have nothing to do with the lock.

sequenceDiagram participant VT1 as VT-1 participant C1 as Carrier-1 participant DB as Database participant VTx as VT-2..VT-10000 VT1->>C1: synchronized(cache) { VT1->>DB: jdbc query (blocks 200 ms) Note over VT1,C1: JDK 21: cannot unmount inside monitor<br/>→ Carrier-1 blocked 200 ms VTx--xC1: cannot use Carrier-1 Note over VTx: with 8 carriers, 8 such requests<br/>freeze the entire server DB-->>VT1: rows VT1->>C1: } monitor exit

docs.title: Why it happened on JDK 21–23
docs.text: HotSpot recorded monitor ownership by the carrier thread (through the lock record on the native stack). If the VT unmounted while holding the monitor, another VT mounted on that carrier would appear to own the lock.

docs.title: JEP 491 (JDK 24): synchronize virtual threads without pinning
docs.text:
The JVM now tracks monitor ownership by the virtual thread. In practice:

  • Blocking inside synchronized → unmounts.
  • Contended synchronized entry → the VT parks and unmounts. When the monitor is released, the VT is queued to the scheduler.
  • Object.wait() → unmounts.
  • -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads was removed. Use the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned instead.

Remaining pin cases on 24+: native frames on the stack (JNI calls, or a foreign-function call that calls back into Java) and blocking inside a class initializer.

docs.title: Detecting pinning
Fixing pinning on JDK 21–23
Short, CPU-only synchronized blocks are fine everywhere
docs.text: Pinning only hurts when you block while pinned. A synchronized method that increments a counter in nanoseconds never blocks, so it doesn't matter even on JDK 21. Don't blindly rewrite every synchronized keyword. Fix only the ones that wrap IO, sleeps, or long waits (JFR tells you which).

docs.title: Libraries to check (JDK 21–23)
docs.text:
Older versions of some drivers held monitors around socket IO. Upgrade before enabling VTs on 21:

Library VT-friendly from (approx.) PostgreSQL JDBC (pgjdbc) 42.6.0 MySQL Connector/J 9.0.0 Oracle JDBC 21.1+ (ojdbc11 23.x recommended) HikariCP 5.1.0 Apache HttpClient 5.2.2+ (ReentrantLock in the connection pool) Jetty 12 Tomcat 10.1.x / 11 Spring Framework 6.1 / Spring Boot 3.2 Kafka clients Check your version: callback and synchronized usage varies

On JDK 24+ most of these concerns disappear, apart from native/JNI-based clients.

docs.title: L4: 25 Worked Examples
docs.text:
L1 → L3

Each example shows the Java 8 way, the Java 21+ way, and the benefit. Imports are omitted for brevity. All examples assume var vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() is created in a try-with-resources block, unless noted.

docs.title: 1. Run a background task
2. Wait for several tasks
3. Fetch 1,000 URLs concurrently
4. Sleep without wasting a thread
docs.text:
Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
    while (true) {
        pollAndProcess();
        try { Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; }
    }
});
Benefit: 10,000 such pollers cost only a few MB. With platform threads they would cost 10 GB of stack reservations.

docs.title: 5. Read 500 files in parallel
docs.text:
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Map<Path, Future<Long>> lines = files.stream()
        .collect(toMap(p -> p, p -> ex.submit(() -> { try (var s = Files.lines(p)) { return s.count(); } })));
}

Note

File IO captures the carrier (the JDK compensates with extra carriers). It still works, and it's simpler than NIO2 AsynchronousFileChannel, but the gain is smaller than for network IO.

docs.title: 6. Timeout a single task
docs.text:
Future<Report> f = vt.submit(() -> reportService.build(id));
try {
    return f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
    f.cancel(true);                    // interrupts the VT → its blocking IO aborts
    return Report.partial(id);
}

docs.title: 7. Background job with a result callback
8. Distinguish VT from platform thread at runtime
docs.text: if (Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()) metrics.counter("on.vt").increment();

docs.title: 9. Thread-per-connection TCP server
docs.text: See L1 echo server. It scales to 100k+ connections with blocking code.

docs.title: 10. JDBC fan-out with a bounded connection pool
docs.text:
HikariDataSource ds = ...;  // maximumPoolSize = 20 — THE real limit
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Future<Customer>> fs = ids.stream()
        .map(id -> ex.submit(() -> customerDao.find(ds, id)))   // 5000 VTs, 20 connections
        .toList();
}
VTs queue on Hikari's getConnection() (it parks with a timeout via connectionTimeout). There's no thread explosion, and the database sees at most 20 sessions. Set connectionTimeout so requests fail fast instead of piling up.

docs.title: 11. Semaphore bulkhead per downstream
docs.text:
private final Semaphore paymentsPermits = new Semaphore(50);

PaymentResult charge(Payment p) throws Exception {
    if (!paymentsPermits.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new BulkheadFullException("payments");
    try { return paymentsClient.charge(p); }
    finally { paymentsPermits.release(); }
}
Benefit: the thread pool used to cap concurrency implicitly. With VTs you cap it explicitly per dependency, so a slow payments service can't consume all of your capacity.

docs.title: 12. Producer / consumer pipeline
docs.text:
BlockingQueue<Line> raw = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000);
BlockingQueue<Record> parsed = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000);
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    ex.submit(() -> { reader.forEach(l -> put(raw, l)); put(raw, Line.EOF); return null; });
    ex.submit(() -> { for (Line l; (l = raw.take()) != Line.EOF; ) parsed.put(parse(l)); parsed.put(Record.EOF); return null; });
    ex.submit(() -> { for (Record r; (r = parsed.take()) != Record.EOF; ) sink.write(r); return null; });
}
Bounded queues provide the backpressure, and blocking put and take cost nothing on VTs.

docs.title: 13. Scatter-gather with "first successful wins"
docs.text:
Java 8Java 21 
CompletableFuture<Quote> any = CompletableFuture.anyOf(
        supplyAsync(() -> vendorA.quote(item), pool),
        supplyAsync(() -> vendorB.quote(item), pool))
    .thenApply(Quote.class::cast);   // anyOf completes on first *completion*, even an exceptional one

try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Quote q = ex.invokeAny(List.of(() -> vendorA.quote(item), () -> vendorB.quote(item)),
                           500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);   // first SUCCESS; losers are cancelled
}

Benefit: invokeAny skips failures and cancels the losers, so you don't have to write that error handling yourself.

docs.title: 14. Parallel batch processing with progress
docs.text:
LongAdder done = new LongAdder();
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (Invoice inv : invoices) {
        ex.submit(() -> { emailInvoice(inv); done.increment(); });
    }
    ScheduledExecutorService progress = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
    progress.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> log.info("sent {}/{}", done.sum(), invoices.size()), 1, 1, SECONDS);
    // ex.close() at end of the block waits for all emails; then stop the progress reporter
    ex.shutdown(); ex.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.HOURS); progress.shutdownNow();
}

docs.title: 15. Retry with backoff (blocking style)
docs.text:
<T> T retry(Callable<T> call, int attempts, Duration base) throws Exception {
    for (int i = 1; ; i++) {
        try { return call.call(); }
        catch (IOException e) {
            if (i == attempts) throw e;
            long jitter = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(base.toMillis());
            Thread.sleep(base.multipliedBy(1L << (i - 1)).plusMillis(jitter));   // cheap on a VT
        }
    }
}
Benefit: no ScheduledExecutorService and no CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor chains. Sleeping is free.

docs.title: 16. Request-scoped context with ScopedValue
docs.text:
static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void handle(Request r) {
    ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, r.id()).run(() -> service.process(r));   // visible to all callees
}
void deepInsideService() { log.info("[{}] processing", REQUEST_ID.get()); }
Final in Java 25. Needs --enable-preview on 21–24. See Scoped Values.

docs.title: 17. Deadline across several calls
docs.text:
Instant deadline = Instant.now().plusMillis(800);
User u      = userClient.get(id, remaining(deadline));
Orders o    = orderClient.recent(id, remaining(deadline));
Recs recs   = recClient.forUser(id, remaining(deadline));

static Duration remaining(Instant d) {
    Duration left = Duration.between(Instant.now(), d);
    if (left.isNegative() || left.isZero()) throw new DeadlineExceededException();
    return left;
}

docs.title: 18. Structured fan-out with fail-fast (JDK 21–24 preview API)
docs.text:
OrderView view(long orderId) throws Exception {
    try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
        Subtask<Order> order     = scope.fork(() -> orders.get(orderId));
        Subtask<Payment> payment = scope.fork(() -> payments.forOrder(orderId));
        Subtask<Shipment> ship   = scope.fork(() -> shipping.forOrder(orderId));
        scope.join().throwIfFailed(IllegalStateException::new);
        return new OrderView(order.get(), payment.get(), ship.get());
    }
}

docs.title: 19. Same, with the Java 25 API (fifth preview)
docs.text:
OrderView view(long orderId) throws InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {                 // default Joiner: all must succeed
        Subtask<Order> order     = scope.fork(() -> orders.get(orderId));
        Subtask<Payment> payment = scope.fork(() -> payments.forOrder(orderId));
        Subtask<Shipment> ship   = scope.fork(() -> shipping.forOrder(orderId));
        scope.join();                                             // throws FailedException on first failure
        return new OrderView(order.get(), payment.get(), ship.get());
    }
}

docs.title: 20. Hedged request (tail-latency killer)
docs.text:
<T> T hedged(Callable<T> primary, Callable<T> backup, Duration hedgeAfter) throws Exception {
    try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        var cs = new ExecutorCompletionService<T>(ex);
        cs.submit(primary);
        Future<T> first = cs.poll(hedgeAfter.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        if (first == null) {                       // primary is slow: fire the backup
            cs.submit(backup);
            first = cs.take();
        }
        T result = first.get();
        ex.shutdownNow();                          // cancel whichever is still running
        return result;
    }
}
Benefit: cuts p99 latency dramatically for idempotent reads, at the cost of a few percent extra load.

docs.title: 21. Rate-limited crawler (permits + per-host limits)
docs.text:
Semaphore global = new Semaphore(200);
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Semaphore> perHost = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

void crawl(URI uri) throws InterruptedException {
    Semaphore host = perHost.computeIfAbsent(uri.getHost(), h -> new Semaphore(4));
    global.acquire();
    try {
        host.acquire();
        try { fetchAndEnqueueLinks(uri); } finally { host.release(); }
    } finally { global.release(); }
}

docs.title: 22. Kafka-style partition workers: order per key, parallel across keys
docs.text:
// One VT per partition key keeps per-key ordering while running all keys in parallel
ConcurrentHashMap<String, BlockingQueue<Event>> lanes = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void dispatch(Event e) {
    lanes.computeIfAbsent(e.key(), k -> {
        var q = new LinkedBlockingQueue<Event>(10_000);
        Thread.ofVirtual().name("lane-" + k).start(() -> drain(k, q));
        return q;
    }).add(e);
}
void drain(String key, BlockingQueue<Event> q) {
    try {
        for (Event e; (e = q.poll(30, SECONDS)) != null; ) handle(e);
    } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    finally { lanes.remove(key, q); }       // idle lane retires itself
}

Race on retirement

An event added between poll returning null and lanes.remove is lost. Use the race-free KeyedLanes in Case Studies for production.

docs.title: 23. Mixing CPU and IO correctly
docs.text:
ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(),
                                                   Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 0).factory());

Image handle(URI src) throws Exception {
    byte[] raw = http.download(src);                       // IO on the VT
    return cpu.submit(() -> resize(raw, 800, 600)).get();  // CPU on a bounded platform pool; VT parks
}
Benefit: CPU-heavy work never monopolizes the VT carriers, so IO-bound VTs keep flowing.

docs.title: 24. Graceful shutdown of a VT worker fleet
docs.text:
ExecutorService workers = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread.ofPlatform().unstarted(() -> {
    workers.shutdown();                                         // stop accepting
    try {
        if (!workers.awaitTermination(25, SECONDS)) workers.shutdownNow();  // interrupt stragglers
    } catch (InterruptedException e) { workers.shutdownNow(); }
}));

docs.title: 25. Benchmark: platform pool vs VTs (simple harness)
docs.text:
static Duration run(ExecutorService ex, int tasks, Duration ioLatency) throws Exception {
    long t0 = System.nanoTime();
    try (ex) {
        for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) ex.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(ioLatency); return null; });
    }
    return Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - t0);
}
// Measured, JDK 21, 4 vCPU:
// run(Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200),  10_000, 100ms) → 5,061 ms  (10000/200 × 100ms)
// run(Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1000), 10_000, 100ms) → 1,261 ms
// run(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), 10_000, 100ms) →   224 ms
Runnable version: examples/plain-java/PlatformVsVirtualBenchmark.java. Use JMH for real numbers (Benchmarking).

docs.title: L5: Patterns & Backpressure
docs.text:
L3 · 6–9 yrs

With platform threads, the pool size was your backpressure. Once you remove that limit, you must add explicit limits, or the first traffic spike turns 100k VTs into 100k simultaneous database queries.

flowchart LR In[Incoming requests<br/>unbounded VTs] --> RL{Admission control<br/>rate limiter / max in-flight} RL -->|reject 429/503| X[Fast failure] RL --> H[Handler VT] H --> B1{Bulkhead: DB<br/>Hikari pool = 30} H --> B2{Bulkhead: Payments<br/>Semaphore = 50} H --> B3{Bulkhead: Search<br/>Semaphore = 100} B1 --> DB[(PostgreSQL)] B2 --> PAY[Payments API] B3 --> OS[(OpenSearch)]

docs.title: Pattern 1: admission control (max in-flight)
docs.text:
public final class AdmissionFilter implements Filter {
    private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(5_000);   // from Little's Law + headroom

    @Override public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        if (!inFlight.tryAcquire()) {                          // never queue unboundedly
            ((HttpServletResponse) res).sendError(503, "Overloaded");
            return;
        }
        try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { inFlight.release(); }
    }
}

docs.title: Pattern 2: per-dependency bulkhead
docs.text: The Bulkhead from Synchronizers plus metrics: permits in use, rejections, and wait time. Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead is VT-friendly. Avoid ThreadPoolBulkhead, because it wraps calls in a platform pool.

docs.title: Pattern 3: rate limit (token bucket, VT-friendly)
docs.text:
public final class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity; private final double refillPerNano;
    private double tokens; private long last = System.nanoTime();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    public TokenBucket(long capacity, long perSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity; this.tokens = capacity; this.refillPerNano = perSecond / 1e9;
    }
    public void acquire() throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            long waitNanos;
            lock.lock();
            try {
                long now = System.nanoTime();
                tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) * refillPerNano); last = now;
                if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return; }
                waitNanos = (long) ((1 - tokens) / refillPerNano);
            } finally { lock.unlock(); }
            Thread.sleep(Duration.ofNanos(waitNanos));   // sleep OUTSIDE the lock; cheap on a VT
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Pattern 4: fan-out / fan-in with a deadline
docs.text:
Prefer StructuredTaskScope (Structured Concurrency). Without preview features:

<T> List<T> fanOut(List<Callable<T>> calls, Duration deadline) throws InterruptedException {
    try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        List<Future<T>> fs = ex.invokeAll(calls, deadline.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        return fs.stream().filter(f -> f.state() == Future.State.SUCCESS).map(Future::resultNow).toList();
    }
}

docs.title: Pattern 5: pipeline with bounded stages
docs.text: See example 12 in Worked Examples. Each stage gets N VTs and a bounded queue. Slow stages fill their input queue, which makes upstream put calls block. That's backpressure with no reactive library.

docs.title: Pattern 6: hedged requests
docs.text: See example 20. Use them only for idempotent calls, and cap the hedge rate (for example, at most 5% of requests).

docs.title: Pattern 7: async-to-sync bridge
docs.text:
Wrap a callback API so callers can write blocking code:

public Message receive(Duration timeout) throws Exception {
    var cf = new CompletableFuture<Message>();
    consumer.onMessage(cf::complete);
    consumer.onError(cf::completeExceptionally);
    return cf.get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);   // the VT parks; no thread wasted
}

docs.title: Pattern 8: per-key serialization (actor-lite)
docs.text:
public final class KeyedSerialExecutor {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    public <T> T run(String key, Callable<T> task) throws Exception {
        ReentrantLock l = locks.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ReentrantLock());
        l.lock();
        try { return task.call(); } finally { l.unlock(); }
    }
}
This is useful for wallet or cart updates where operations on one key must not interleave. Evict idle locks with Caffeine's weakValues(), or use striped locks (locks[Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), 1024)]).

docs.title: Pattern 9: one-loop-per-connection with blocking IO
docs.text: WebSocket or TCP protocols where each connection has a read loop and a write loop: two VTs per connection, coordinated with a BlockingQueue for outbound messages. Before VTs, this needed Netty or NIO selectors.

docs.title: Anti-pattern table
docs.text: Instead of… Do newFixedThreadPool(50, vtFactory) to limit concurrency newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() + Semaphore(50) Unlimited fan-out to a DB Hikari pool size + connectionTimeout CompletableFuture chains inside a VT handler Sequential blocking code Retrying without a deadline A deadline budget across retries (example 17)

docs.title: Migration roadmap
docs.text: flowchart TD     A[1. Upgrade JDK to 21 or 25 LTS<br/>no VTs yet — just run tests] --> B[2. Upgrade libs<br/>Spring Boot 3.2+, JDBC drivers, HTTP clients]     B --> C[3. Inventory risks<br/>synchronized+IO, ThreadLocal caches, pool-as-limit]     C --> D[4. Add explicit limits<br/>Hikari, semaphores, admission control]     D --> E[5. Enable VTs in a canary<br/>spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true]     E --> F[6. Observe<br/>JFR pinning, p99, DB connections, heap]     F --> G{Healthy?}     G -->|yes| H[7. Roll out + simplify code<br/>remove CF chains, reactive where not needed]     G -->|no| I[Fix pinning / limits] --> E

docs.title: Step 3: risk inventory checklist
docs.text:
# synchronized blocks that may wrap IO (relevant on JDK 21–23)
grep -rn "synchronized" src/main/java | grep -v "^.*//"
# ThreadLocal used as a cache
grep -rn "ThreadLocal<" src/main/java
# Pools used as concurrency limiters
grep -rn "newFixedThreadPool\|ThreadPoolTaskExecutor\|setMaxPoolSize" src/main/java
# Native / JNI
grep -rn "native \|System.loadLibrary" src/main/java
Finding Action synchronized around IO (JDK 21–23) Replace with ReentrantLock, or move to JDK 24+ ThreadLocal cache of an expensive object Make it a shared thread-safe instance, a small pool, or create it per use ThreadLocal context (MDC, security) Keep for now (it works). Plan a ScopedValue migration on Java 25 Thread pool sized to protect a downstream Replace with a Semaphore of the same size @Async pool with a bounded queue VTs remove the queue. Make sure the work's targets are bounded parallelStream() doing IO Move it to a VT executor Reactive code (WebFlux) with no streaming need Candidate for rewrite to MVC + VTs (optional, gradual)

docs.title: Before / after: a Java 8 service class
Rollout tips (from real migrations)
docs.text:
• Ship the JDK upgrade separately from enabling VTs, so you can attribute regressions.
  • Toggle with configuration (spring.threads.virtual.enabled) so you can roll back without a redeploy.
  • Compare these dashboards before and after: p50/p99 latency, throughput, DB active connections, heap after GC, CPU, and jdk.VirtualThreadPinned count.
  • Expect higher downstream load at the same traffic. The service now does more in parallel, so check the database's max_connections and downstream rate limits.

docs.title: 1. Pooling virtual threads
docs.text:
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100, Thread.ofVirtual().factory());   // ❌
A pool exists to reuse expensive threads, and VTs are not expensive. Pooling brings back queueing and loses the benefits. Fix: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() + Semaphore(100).

docs.title: 2. Pinning on JDK 21–23
docs.text: Blocking IO inside synchronized. Fix: ReentrantLock, or upgrade to JDK 24+. See L3.

docs.title: 3. CPU-bound work on VTs
docs.text: Video encoding on VTs monopolizes the carriers, because there's no preemption. Fix: send CPU work to a fixed platform pool sized to the core count.

docs.title: 4. Unbounded fan-out melts downstreams
docs.text: 100k VTs → 100k simultaneous HTTP calls → the downstream falls over, or you run out of ephemeral ports / file descriptors. Fix: bulkheads and admission control (L5).

docs.title: 5. ThreadLocal caches
docs.text: ThreadLocal<ObjectMapper> with 1M VTs means 1M ObjectMappers. Fix: ObjectMapper is thread-safe after configuration, so share one instance.

docs.title: 6. Huge ThreadLocal/MDC payloads
docs.text: Even context-only ThreadLocals get multiplied by the number of threads. Keep MDC tiny, or move to ScopedValue.

docs.title: 7. Expecting lower latency
docs.text: VTs improve throughput under concurrency. A single request's latency is unchanged, or slightly higher (around 1–2%).

docs.title: 8. Forgetting timeouts
docs.text: A VT blocked forever is a leak: it holds heap, sockets, and semaphore permits. Every IO call needs a timeout (HTTP connect/read timeouts, JDBC queryTimeout, Hikari connectionTimeout).

docs.title: 9. Assuming Thread.currentThread() identity is stable over the carrier
docs.text: Native code and libraries that key data by OS thread id (some profilers and old APM agents) may misbehave. Upgrade your APM agents.

docs.title: 10. Busy-wait spin loops
docs.text: while (!flag) {} on a VT never yields its carrier. Use LockSupport.park/unpark, CountDownLatch, or a queue.

docs.title: 11. Thread.yield() as a scheduling tool
docs.text: It's a hint at best. Don't design around it.

docs.title: 12. Calling join() on an executor's tasks inside synchronized (JDK 21–23)
docs.text: synchronized (x) { future.get(); } pins the carrier for the whole wait.

docs.title: 13. Daemon surprise
docs.text: VTs are daemon threads. A main that starts VTs and returns exits the JVM immediately, and in Spring, @Scheduled alone won't keep the JVM alive. Set spring.main.keep-alive=true.

docs.title: 14. Using parallelStream() from a VT for IO
docs.text: The work still runs on the common FJ pool (platform threads). Use the VT executor instead.

docs.title: 15. Over-subscribing a native resource
docs.text: File IO and DNS capture carriers. Reading 50k files at once spawns compensating carriers up to the 256 cap, and the remaining reads queue behind them. Fix: a Semaphore sized to the disk's concurrency.

docs.title: 16. Leaking executors
docs.text: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() assigned to a field but never closed still works (the threads are daemons), but you lose structured shutdown. Close it in @PreDestroy, or create it per scope with try-with-resources.

docs.title: 17. Mixing reactive and VT in one request
docs.text: Calling .block() inside a WebFlux handler is still wrong (it blocks an event-loop thread), even if the inner work uses VTs. Pick one model per request path.

docs.title: Thread dumps with millions of threads
docs.text:
jstack and ThreadMXBean show platform threads only (including carriers). For virtual threads, use:

jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json   # JSON: every VT, grouped by container
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/threads.txt                 # plain text

The JSON groups threads by thread container (executor or StructuredTaskScope), so you can see the tree of parent and child tasks. Parked VTs that aren't referenced from anywhere may be omitted.

{ "threadDump": { "threadContainers": [
  { "container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@5a2e4553",
    "parent": "<root>",
    "threads": [
      { "tid": "52", "virtual": true, "name": "order-17",
        "stack": [ "java.base/jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)",
                   "java.base/java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(LockSupport.java:371)",
                   "com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:162)", "..." ] } ] } ] } }

Here, HikariPool.getConnection shows up in thousands of VT stacks, which means connection pool exhaustion, not a JVM problem.

docs.title: JFR events for virtual threads
docs.text:
Event Default Meaning jdk.VirtualThreadStart / End Disabled Lifecycle (high volume) jdk.VirtualThreadPinned Enabled, 20 ms threshold Blocked while pinned jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed Enabled Scheduler rejected the start/unpark (resource exhaustion) 
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=app.jfr,settings=profile,duration=5m -jar app.jar
jfr summary app.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned --stack-depth 20 app.jfr

JDK Mission Control 9 (JMC) visualizes these events.

docs.title: Metrics to export
Debugging
docs.text:
• IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse step through VT code normally. Breakpoints suspend the VT.
  • Stack traces are complete and sequential, which is a huge win over CompletableFuture/reactive traces full of scheduler frames.
  • Name the VTs you create (Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-", 0)). Tomcat names request VTs such as tomcat-handler-N.

docs.title: Distributed tracing
docs.text:
OpenTelemetry's Java agent (1.32+) and Micrometer Tracing propagate context through ThreadLocal, which works on VTs. When you create VTs yourself, wrap the tasks so context propagates:

ExecutorService ex = Context.taskWrapping(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()); // OpenTelemetry
// Micrometer: ContextExecutorService.wrap(executor, () -> ContextSnapshotFactory.builder().build().captureAll())

docs.title: L9: Architect Level (10–15 years)
docs.text:
L4 · 10–15 yrs

At this level the question is no longer "how do I use a virtual thread". It is:

  • "What concurrency model should every service on our platform use, and where are the exceptions?"
  • "How does that choice change capacity planning, cost, failure modes, hiring, and operability?"

docs.title: 1. Platform decision framework
docs.text:
flowchart TD S[New service / endpoint] --> Q1{Streaming / long-lived<br/>push to many clients?} Q1 -->|Yes: SSE, WebSocket fan-out, backpressured streams| R[Reactive WebFlux / Netty<br/>or VT + bounded queues if simple] Q1 -->|No| Q2{Request/response<br/>mostly IO-bound?} Q2 -->|Yes| VT[Spring MVC + virtual threads<br/>DEFAULT] Q2 -->|No: CPU-bound| CPU[MVC + bounded platform pool<br/>for heavy compute] VT --> Q3{Gateway / BFF with<br/>very high fan-out & tiny CPU?} Q3 -->|Yes| GW[Either: reactive gateway<br/>or VT gateway — measure] Q3 -->|No| DONE[Ship it]

A sound platform rule, which the grocery platform in this org uses: "MVC on virtual threads by default; WebFlux only for gateway, BFF, delivery tracking, notifications, search, and the assistant (streaming)."

docs.title: 2. Capacity modelling with virtual threads
docs.text:
The scarce resources are no longer threads. They are:

Resource Limit source Model CPU Cores × target util λ_max = cores × util / cpu_time_per_req DB connections DB max_connections / replicas pool_per_pod = λ_pod × db_time; Σ pods × pool ≤ DB limit Downstream capacity Their SLO and rate limit Semaphore = λ × downstream_latency × 1.2 Heap Stack chunks + request objects in_flight × (stack + request garbage) File descriptors / sockets ulimit -n, ephemeral ports In-flight outbound connections

Worked example (grocery checkout, per pod):

  • Target 400 req/s per pod. CPU 4 ms/req → 1.6 cores busy (4 cores × 40% util): OK
  • p99 latency 300 ms → in-flight = 400 × 0.3 = 120 VTs (trivial)
  • Each request: 3 DB queries × 4 ms = 12 ms DB time → 400 × 0.012 = 4.8 connections → pool = 10
  • 20 pods × 10 = 200 connections against a DB limit of 500: OK
  • Payments: 50 req/s × 250 ms = 12.5 → Semaphore(16)

On Java 8 you'd size Tomcat to about 200 threads per pod "just in case", and still suffer thread exhaustion when payments slowed down to 5 s (400 × 5 = 2000 in-flight > 200 threads → the whole pod stalls). With VTs + Semaphore(16), only the payments path degrades and every other endpoint stays healthy. That isolation is the architectural win.

docs.title: 3. Failure-mode analysis
docs.text:
Failure Platform-thread service VT service (with bulkheads) VT service (no bulkheads) Downstream slows 10× Thread pool exhausts, all endpoints fail Only that dependency's calls fail fast In-flight grows; heap and DB connections exhausted DB pool exhausted Threads block on the pool, then the pool exhausts VTs wait up to connectionTimeout, then 503 Same, but with more waiters Traffic spike 5× Queueing in Tomcat accept queue Admission control sheds the excess GC pressure, cascading timeouts Pinning (JDK 21) n/a Throughput collapse under specific code paths Same

Lesson: virtual threads without limits are less safe than platform threads. The pool was an accidental bulkhead. Make it intentional.

docs.title: 4. Organization-wide adoption plan
docs.text:
1. Baseline: JDK 25 LTS, Spring Boot 3.5+/4.x, VT-ready drivers, current APM agent versions.
  2. Golden path template: service template with VTs on, admission filter, a bulkhead library, and JFR pinning alerts.
  3. Lint rules (ArchUnit / Error Prone): forbid Executors.newFixedThreadPool with a VT factory, forbid parallelStream in @Service IO classes, forbid ThreadLocal fields except in an allow-list.
  4. Load-test gate in CI: compare p99 and pinning between releases.
  5. Training: this playbook, L1 → L9.
  6. Reactive sunset (optional): migrate reactive services without streaming needs, one endpoint at a time.

docs.title: 5. VT vs reactive: the honest comparison
docs.text: See Virtual Threads vs Reactive. In short: VTs win on simplicity, debuggability, hiring, and library compatibility. Reactive still wins for streaming with backpressure, very high fan-out with tiny CPU (where ~1–5% lower overhead matters), and existing reactive ecosystems (R2DBC, reactive Kafka).

docs.title: 6. Things to watch beyond Java 25
docs.text:
• Structured concurrency finalization: the API changed significantly in 25 (open + Joiner). Wrap it behind an internal facade.
  • Custom VT schedulers (not yet public API): may later allow per-tenant or NUMA-aware scheduling.
  • Preemption of CPU-bound VTs: currently none. Keep heavy CPU work on platform pools.
  • JDBC/ORM: Hibernate and JDBC are blocking-first, which fits VTs. R2DBC usage will likely shrink.
